heading: OVERVIEW OF MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL
text:
The priority in caring for a casualty, should be to identify and stop life-threatening bleeding and prevent them from bleeding to death. Bleeding is considered life-threatening when--
- There is pulsing or steady bleeding from the wound.
- The overlying clothes are soaked with blood.
- Blood is pooling on the ground.
- There is a traumatic amputation of an extremity.
- Bandages or makeshift bandages used to cover the wound are ineffective and are steadily becoming soaked with blood.
- There was prior bleeding, and the patient is now in shock (unconscious, confused, and pale).

heading: OVERVIEW OF MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL
text: A TQ is immediately needed when any of the above examples are present on an extremity. Injury to a major vein or artery can result in shock or death from blood loss in minutes. Extremity (arm or leg) hemorrhage is a leading cause of preventable combat death. Using TQ(s) to stop the bleeding is essential to the survival of casualties with these types of injuries.

heading: OVERVIEW OF MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL
text: During CUF a TQ is the only medical intervention available to stop life-threatening bleeding from an extremity injury. Other wounds (such as neck, armpit, groin, or abdomen) are not treated during CUF. If the casualty is able, direct them to apply pressure to the wound as self-aid. Airway and other issues are not treated until the TFC phase.

heading: OVERVIEW OF MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL
text: It may be difficult to determine whether hemorrhage is life-threatening until the TFC phase when the wound can be exposed and evaluated. A suspected life-threatening hemorrhage is immediately treated.

heading: OVERVIEW OF MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL
text: During CUF, if a casualty shows to have massive bleeding, from an extremity, a hasty TQ is applied "high and tight" on the injured extremity and then cover should be acquired as quickly as possible. The equipment in the casualty's first aid kit should be used and not that of the responder. Do not put a TQ directly over the knee or elbow, over a holster, or cargo pocket that contains bulky items.

heading: OVERVIEW OF MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL
text: Direct pressure can and should be used as a temporary measure until a TQ or dressing is in place. It is difficult to use direct pressure alone to control significant bleeding or while moving the casualty. Direct pressure can be used if treatment no longer maintains control of the bleeding while a new treatment is started.

heading: OVERVIEW OF MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL
text: In CUF, consider placing one or more hasty TQs in a "high and tight" manner to an arm or leg to control massive life-threatening bleeding. This should be accomplished in less than one minute. If the casualty is conscious, the responder should direct the casualty to render self-aid and apply a TQ to themselves, if they have one. A TQ applied in the CUF must be re-evaluated in TFC.

heading: OVERVIEW OF MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL
text: To effectively perform first aid, Service members need a fundamental understanding of the key body systems, including their structures and functions. Knowledge of the respiratory, circulatory, and musculoskeletal systems is crucial as it helps in assessing injuries and providing the appropriate first aid without causing further harm to the casualty. Familiarity with these systems also aids in recognizing when they are damaged or not functioning properly. Injuries to or compromises of these vital systems can lead to severe, permanent injury or even death. Therefore, a solid grasp of these systems not only supports effective first aid intervention but also helps prevent intensifying the casualty's condition.

heading: CIRCULATORY SYSTEM
text: The heart and the blood vessels (arteries, veins, and capillaries) circulate blood throughout the body. The heart is divided into two separate halves, each acting as a pump. The left side pumps oxygenated blood (bright red) through the arteries into the capillaries. Nutrients and oxygen pass from the blood through the walls of the capillaries and into the cells. At the same time, waste products and carbon dioxide leave the cells and enter the capillaries. From the capillaries, the blood is carried through the veins to the right side of the heart and then into the lungs where it expels the carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen. Blood in the veins is dark red because of its low oxygen content. Blood does not flow through the veins in spurts as it does through the arteries. The entire system of the heart, blood vessels, and lymphatics is called the circulatory system.

heading: BLOOD VESSELS
text: The body has a complex network of blood vessels that are crucial for blood circulation. These vessels are three main types. First, arteries take oxygen-rich blood from the heart and branch into smaller arterioles, eventually leading to tiny capillaries. Next, capillaries play a key role in exchanging oxygen, nutrients, and wastes between blood and tissues. The blood, now lacking oxygen, moves into small veins called venules, which combine to form larger veins. Lastly, veins are responsible for carrying blood back to the heart, completing the circulation process.

heading: BLOOD VESSELS
text: The blood vessels in the body are all connected and work together. They help deliver oxygen and nutrients to every part of the body and get rid of waste materials. This shows how each type of blood vessel depends on the others, highlighting their important roles in a Service member's overall health.

heading: BLOOD
text: Blood is a mixture of plasma (liquid component), white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. The body contains about 5 to 6 quarts (about 5 liters) of blood. Once blood is pumped out of the heart, it takes 20 to 30 seconds to circulate through the body and return to the heart.

heading: BLOOD
text: Blood performs essential functions as it circulates through the body. It delivers oxygen and essential nutrients (such as fats, sugars, minerals, and vitamins) to the body's tissues. It carries carbon dioxide to the lungs and other waste products to the kidneys for elimination from the body. In addition, it carries components that fight infection and stop bleeding.

notices.text: If bleeding is not stopped, excessive blood loss can quickly lead to the death of the casualty. It is imperative that first aid providers quickly determine if a casualty is losing blood. Many injuries can result in blood vessels being torn which result in excessive blood loss.

heading: HEARTBEAT
text: The heart functions as a pump to circulate blood continuously through the blood vessels to all parts of the body. It contracts, forcing the blood from its chambers. The heart then relaxes, permitting its chambers to refill with blood.

heading: HEARTBEAT
text:
The rhythmical cycle of contraction and relaxation is called the heartbeat. The normal heart rate (heartbeats per minute) varies based on the age and physical condition of the individual at rest. For example--
- Adults: 60 to 100 heartbeats per minute.
- Children (1 to 6 years): 70 to 120 heartbeats per minute.
- Infants (6 to 12 months): 80 to 140 heartbeats per minute.
- Infants (0 to 5 months): 90 to 140 heartbeats per minute. Note. The typical pulse for Service members and athletes is 40 to 60 heart beats per minute and is lower than the average adult population due to physical conditioning.

heading: HEARTBEAT
text: It is common for a Service member's pulse to be elevated above the normal range during combat operations as this is both a stressful and high exertional state. Elevated pulse in combination with suspected injuries causing hemorrhage suggests developing shock.

heading: PULSE
text:
The heartbeat causes a rhythmical expansion and contraction of the arteries as it forces blood through them. This cycle of expansion and contraction can be felt (monitored) at various points in the body and is called the pulse. The common points for checking the pulse are at the--
- Side of the neck (carotid).
- Groin (femoral).
- Wrist (radial).
- Ankle (posterior tibial). Note. DO NOT use your thumb to check a casualty's pulse because you may confuse the beat of your own pulse with that of the casualty.

notices.text: It is imperative that first aid providers quickly determine if the casualty has a pulse (heartbeat). Absence of a pulse (heartbeat) will lead to the death of the casualty if not quickly restored.

heading: PULSE
text: The literature on combat casualty care raises questions about the reliability of traditional blood pressure measurements as indicators of specific pulse types. However, it underscores a crucial reality: as hemorrhage severity increases, more central pulses are likely to be lost, demanding prompt and decisive intervention. Identifying and responding to these central pulses swiftly is imperative in managing severe hemorrhage and ensuring the best possible outcomes for casualties.

heading: Carotid Pulse
text: To ascertain the carotid pulse, locate the pulse on the casualty's neck nearest to you. Gently place the tips of your first two fingers alongside their thyroid cartilage, commonly referred to as the Adam's apple (see figure 4-1). This method allows for an effective assessment of the pulse, rhythm, and strength.

heading: Femoral Pulse
text: To assess the femoral (groin) pulse, apply gentle pressure with the tips of your first two fingers to the center of the groin area (see figure 4-2). This method enables you to accurately detect the presence and strength of the femoral pulse.

heading: Radial Pulse
text: To ascertain the radial (wrist) pulse, position your first two fingers on the side of the casualty's wrist where the thumb is located (see figure 4-3 ). This technique allows for a precise assessment of the radial pulse's presence and strength.

heading: Posterior Tibial Pulse
text: To assess the posterior tibial (ankle) pulse, position your first two fingers on the inner side of the casualty's ankle (see figure 4-4). This method enables a reliable examination of the posterior tibial pulse's rhythm and strength.

heading: EQUIPMENT USED FOR MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL
text: Specialized equipment plays a crucial role in effectively managing massive bleeding, offering immediate and life-saving interventions. TQs, junctional tourniquets, hemostatic agents, hemostatic gauze, and pressure dressings, are among the tools used for this purpose. These items form integral components of the TCCC approach to massive bleeding control, empowering military personnel to address severe hemorrhage swiftly and efficiently in the field and enhancing the likelihood of survival for wounded individuals.

heading: TOURNIQUETS
text: TQs serve as critical devices for halting severe bleeding from extremities, such as arms or legs, by effectively restricting blood flow when applied higher to the injury site, thus preventing further blood loss.

heading: TOURNIQUETS
text: Considered the most vital lifesaving item in the first aid kit, TQs should be kept easily accessible and ready for use during combat missions. The "TQ, Nonpneumatic Combat Application One-Handed," commonly known as the combat application TQ, is the most prevalent type in military inventory, featuring key components such as the windlass rod for twisting and tightening, a windlass clip to secure the rod, a windlass safety strap for added security, and a routing buckle for TQ band management after looping it around an arm or leg.

heading: TOURNIQUETS
text: It's imperative that all personnel deployed on combat missions have a CoTCCC recommended TQ readily available in a standard location on their battle gear and are trained in its proper usage. Additionally, casualties should be capable of easily and swiftly accessing and applying their own TQs, emphasizing the importance of not storing TQs at the bottom of the pack, and prioritizing the use of the casualty's first aid kit TQ first.

heading: HEMOSTATIC DRESSING AND WOUND PACKING
text: Hemostatic dressings, engineered with clotting agents like kaolin or chitosan, are purpose-built to staunch bleeding efficiently. These dressings are either packed directly into deep or narrow wounds or applied directly onto a bleeding wound, accelerating blood clotting far more effectively than traditional dressings.

heading: HEMOSTATIC DRESSING AND WOUND PACKING
text: When severe bleeding is noted from a junctional area, such as the neck, axillary or inguinal locations of the body (areas were TQs cannot be applied) hemostatic dressings should be used for massive bleeding control. It's essential to note that they should not be used inside the abdomen or chest, where emergency bandages or other trauma dressings are more appropriate.

heading: HEMOSTATIC DRESSING AND WOUND PACKING
text: Each first aid kit is typically equipped with one hemostatic dressing and one dry sterile gauze. The hemostatic dressings recommended by the CoTCCC are known to be safe and include active ingredients that help blood to clot at the wound site. Hemostatic dressings are available in various types, one type of hemostatic dressing is impregnated with kaolin, another type contains celox granules, or the third type contains chitosan. Chitosan works by binding red blood cells and platelets to the surface of the dressing, enhancing clot formation. Importantly, despite being derived from shellfish, chitosan does not trigger allergic reactions in individuals with shellfish allergies.

heading: PRESSURE DRESSINGS
text: Pressure dressings play a crucial role in stemming bleeding by applying direct pressure on wounds. Typically comprised of an elastic bandage and a sterile pad, they are placed over the wound and securely fastened to maintain pressure on the injured area. These dressings not only aid in blood clotting but also compress the open blood vessel, assisting in controlling bleeding effectively. After bleeding has been stemmed with a hemostatic dressing or packing material, it's imperative to maintain pressure on the wound. This is achieved by applying a pressure dressing directly on top of the hemostatic dressing or packing material and wrapping it around the limb, ensuring comprehensive coverage of the wound and gauze applied previously.

heading: PRESSURE DRESSINGS
text: The CoTCCC-recommended emergency bandage or trauma dressing serves as a versatile solution for most wounds, particularly those not severe enough to require a TQ. These dressings can be used alone or in conjunction with other hemorrhage control methods, such as hemostatic gauze and normal gauze, to bolster their effectiveness in controlling bleeding by providing consistent pressure to the wound.

heading: TIER 1 SKILLS FOR MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL
text: The urgency of promptly stopping massive external bleeding cannot be overstated, as the longer a Service member bleeds from a major wound, the lower their chances of survival become. Severe injuries have the potential to cause death in as little as three minutes due to blood loss. During TFC, when evaluating the casualty for the location, type, and size of the wound or injury, it is essential to cut or tear their clothing and carefully expose the entire area of the wound. This procedure ensures proper visualization of the injury while minimizing the risk of further contamination. It's crucial not to touch the wound directly and to keep it as clean as possible to prevent complications. It's important to note that in a chemical environment, protective clothing should not be removed, and dressings should be applied over the protective clothing. The skills used by all Service members to control massive bleeding include the application of TQs, hemostatic dressings, and pressure bandages.

heading: APPLICATION OF TOURNIQUETS
text: In combat scenarios, especially while under enemy fire, a TQ stands as the primary means to control massive extremity bleeding, enabling individuals, battle buddies, or combat medics to swiftly manage lifethreatening hemorrhages until the casualty can be moved away from the firefight. Always prioritize treating life-threatening hemorrhage while seeking cover. The application of a TQ to a massive bleed is timesensitive, with the TQ aiming to halt bleeding within one minute and be fully secured within three minutes, casualties with uncontrolled massive bleeding can succumb within these initial minutes. Expecting pain during application is crucial as it signifies proper TQ application.

heading: APPLICATION OF TOURNIQUETS
text: The casualty may need to apply a one-handed TQ (see figure 4-5) to an upper extremity when applying self-aid. One-handed TQs are used to apply self-aid for bleeding from an injury to the upper arm or forearm. (One-handed windlass and one-handed ratchet TQs are the TQs of choice; they are effective and can be applied quickly).

heading: APPLICATION OF TOURNIQUETS
text: A hasty TQ is implemented as "high and tight" on the wounded extremity or when the bleeding source is ambiguous during the CUF phase. However, during TFC, all TQs should be deliberate, placed two to three inches above the wound directly on the skin, not over clothing. Once the casualty is in a safer position, the bleeding source should be reassessed, and the effectiveness of the TQs verified. If bleeding remains uncontrolled, a second TQ may be necessary, particularly for severe bleeding wounds of the thigh.

heading: APPLICATION OF TOURNIQUETS
text: It is crucial to recognize that TQs should be used cautiously, with the optimal safe duration being less than two hours. Beyond this timeframe, tissues may start to die, potentially leading to limb loss after six hours. Regular reassessment of TQ effectiveness is necessary, including checking for stopped bleeding, absent distal pulse, and ensuring no pulse below the TQ on the limb. Common errors when applying TQs include not using one, when necessary, not tightening it adequately, and using it for minimal bleeding. Additionally, TQs should never be removed except by medical personnel at a higher role of care. If the source of massive bleeding is evident, such as from an amputation or major wound, immediate bleeding control measures like applying a TQ or wound packing should be initiated, especially in areas where a TQ cannot be used, such as the groin, armpit, or neck. The following steps address tourniquet application in CUF for all Service Members, CLS, and medical personnel.

heading: APPLICATION OF TOURNIQUETS
text:
One-Handed (Windlass) TQ Application CUF:
- Remove TQ from JFAK and/or carrying pouch.
- Insert the wounded extremity through the loop of the self-adhering band.
- Position the TQ above the bleeding site, high on the extremity over the clothing/uniform.
- Ensure that all the slack in the self-adhering band is pulled through the routing buckle before the band is fastened back on itself and the windlass is twisted.
- Twist the rod until bleeding has stopped (complete steps 1-5 in under 1 min).
- Lock the windlass rod in place with the windlass clip.
- Route the self-adhering band around the rod and between the clips.
- Secure the windlass safety strap.
- If no other major bleeding is present, move to cover. Note. Do not document the TQ application time until the TFC phase.

heading: APPLICATION OF TOURNIQUETS
text:
One-Handed (Ratchet) TQ Application CUF:
- Remove TQ from the JFAK and/or carrying pouch.
- Insert the wounded extremity through the loop of the TQ band.
- Position the TQ above the bleeding site, high on the extremity over the clothing/uniform.
- Grasp the TQ loop with your teeth (or if able lean against a hard surface) to prevent slipping when tightening.
- Tighten the TQ strap as much as possible.
- Lift the lever arm of the ratcheting buckle and tighten by ratcheting the TQ until bleeding has stopped (complete steps 1-5 in under 1 min).
- Lock the ratchet on itself (it will click into place).
- If no other major bleeding is present, move to cover. Note. If bleeding is not controlled, continue to ratchet the maneuver device until bleeding has stopped. Do not document TQ application time until the TFC phase.

heading: APPLICATION OF TOURNIQUETS
text:
Two-Handed (Windlass) TQ Application CUF:
- Remove TQ from JFAK and/or carrying pouch.
- Insert the wounded extremity through the loop of the self-adhering band or route the band around the limb, passing the tip through the slit of the routing buckle.
- Position the TQ above the bleeding site, high on the extremity over the clothing/uniform.
- Ensure that all the slack in the self-adhering band is pulled through the routing buckle before the band is fastened back on itself and the windlass is twisted.
- Twist the rod until bleeding has stopped (complete steps 1-5 in under 1 min).
- Lock the windlass rod in place with the windlass clip.
- Route the self-adhering band around the rod and between the clips.
- Secure the windlass safety strap.
- If no other major bleeding is present, move to cover. Note. Do not document TQ application time until the TFC phase.

heading: APPLICATION OF TOURNIQUETS
text:
Two-Handed (Ratchet) TQ Application CUF:
- Remove the TQ from the casualty's JFAK and/or carrying pouch.
- Insert the wounded limb through the TQ strap loop or route the strap around the limb; pass the tip through the buckle.
- Position the TQ above the bleeding site, high on the extremity over the clothing/uniform.
- Pull the strap as tightly as possible, removing all excess slack.
- Lift the lever arm of the ratcheting buckle and tighten by ratcheting the TQ until bleeding has stopped (complete steps 1-5 in under 1 min).
- Lock the ratchet on itself (it will click into place).
- If no other major bleeding is present, move the casualty to cover. Note. If bleeding is not controlled, continue to ratchet the maneuver device until bleeding has stopped. Do not document TQ application time until the TFC phase.

heading: APPLICATION OF HEMOSTATIC DRESSING AND WOUND PACKING
text: Hemostatic dressings serve as effective tools for controlling bleeding in areas where a TQ cannot be applied effectively, such as the groin, armpit, or neck. These dressings should be applied with direct and firm pressure and held for at least three minutes.

notices.text: Do not pack hemostatic dressings into the abdomen or chest.

heading: APPLICATION OF HEMOSTATIC DRESSING AND WOUND PACKING
text: After the bleeding has been controlled, it's crucial to check for a distal pulse to ensure the dressing hasn't been applied too tightly. Adjust the dressing if a pulse is not felt to restore circulation.

notices.text: The emergency bandage must be loosened if the skin distal to the injury becomes cool, blue, numb, or pulseless.

heading: APPLICATION OF HEMOSTATIC DRESSING AND WOUND PACKING
text: Before applying the dressing, carefully examine the casualty for multiple wounds, as a projectile may have entered at one point and exited at another, with the exit wound typically being larger than the entrance wound.

heading: APPLICATION OF HEMOSTATIC DRESSING AND WOUND PACKING
text: When applying a bandage, prioritize using the casualty's emergency bandage. Apply it by opening the plastic dressing package, placing the sterile pad directly over the wound, wrapping the elastic tail around the extremity, running it through the plastic pressure bar, and securing the closure bar to prevent slipping without causing excessive pressure.

heading: APPLICATION OF HEMOSTATIC DRESSING AND WOUND PACKING
text: While hemostatic dressings should be packed into limb wounds, they should not be used in the abdomen or chest. For compressible hemorrhage in areas where a TQ cannot be applied effectively, such as the neck, armpit, and groin, use a CoTCCC-recommended hemostatic dressing.

heading: APPLICATION OF HEMOSTATIC DRESSING AND WOUND PACKING
text: Despite containing active hemostatic agents, hemostatic dressings require direct pressure for at least three minutes to be effective. Non-CoTCCC-recommended supplies may not be as effective in controlling massive hemorrhage.

notices.text: Continuously monitor the casualty for conditions necessitating basic lifesaving measures. Additionally, all open wounds should be checked for entry and exit points, with first aid administered accordingly.

If a projectile remains lodged in the body, do not attempt to remove it. Apply a dressing. Similarly, if an object is impaled in the wound, do not remove it; instead, apply a dressing around the object and stabilize it with additional bulky materials to prevent further injury.

heading: APPLICATION OF PRESSURE DRESSINGS
text: Depending on the nature of the injuries, the first responder may need to pack wounds and apply a pressure bandage. Hemostatic dressings, containing special clotting agents, are ideal for wound packing to promote blood clotting. If hemostatic dressings are unavailable, gauze bandage can be used to pack wounds.

notices.text: Avoid packing wounds in the chest or abdomen.

heading: APPLICATION OF PRESSURE DRESSINGS
text: Pressure dressings are crucial for maintaining the effectiveness of hemostatic dressings, ensuring sustained pressure on the bleeding sources. In situations where pressure dressings are not available, maintaining firm, direct pressure is essential until medical assistance arrives.

heading: APPLICATION OF PRESSURE DRESSINGS
text: When applying a pressure bandage over a packed wound, use short tugs while wrapping and continue with tension. Care should be taken to avoid wrapping the bandage too tightly, ensuring the skin below remains pink and warm, with a present pulse. Note. Service members assess tightness based on skin coolness and paleness rather than "capillary refill."

heading: APPLICATION OF PRESSURE DRESSINGS
text:
Hemostatic dressings are only applied during the TFC phase. The steps for wound packing and pressure bandage are as follows:
- Expose the wound, if not previously exposed.
- Remove clothing and equipment as required.
- Locate the source of the most active bleeding and apply direct pressure.
- Remove the hemostatic dressing from its sterile package.
- If a hemostatic dressing is not available, use gauze or clean, dry cloth material.
- Pack the hemostatic dressing tightly into the wound directly over the site that has the most active bleeding. Note. Fill and pack the whole wound cavity tightly while keeping firm pressure on the wound. More than one hemostatic dressing or gauze may be required to stop the blood flow. Note. If the hemostatic dressing or gauze does not extend 1 to 2 inches above the skin, place additional hemostatic dressing or gauze.
- After packing, continue to apply firm, manual pressure until the bleeding stops. Hold continuous direct pressure for a minimum of 3 minutes.
- Reassess to ensure bleeding has been controlled while maintaining pressure. Note: Ensure blood is not seeping through or around the hemostatic dressing. If bleeding has stopped, leave the hemostatic dressing in place while still maintaining pressure.
- If bleeding has not been controlled and packed initially with a hemostatic dressing, remove the ineffective hemostatic dressing and repack starting at step three of this skill.
- If the wound was previously packed with gauze or other materials, apply additional gauze or materials and pressure (for another 3 minutes) until bleeding has stopped.
- Remove the pressure bandage from its package.
- Place the pad (bandage) directly over the wound on the previously applied hemostatic dressing while continuing to apply direct pressure.
- Wrap the pressure/elastic bandage tightly around the extremity, focusing pressure over the wound and ensuring that the edges of the pad are covered. Note: If the bandage has a pressure bar, insert the elastic wrap completely into the pressure bar, pull the bandage tight, and reverse it back over the top of the pressure bar forcing it down onto the pad.
- Secure the hooking ends of the hood and loop straps or closure bar onto the last wrap of the bandage.
- Check for circulation below the pressure bandage by feeling for a distal pulse.
- Document all findings and treatments on a DD Form 1380 and attach it to the casualty. Note. If the skin below the pressure bandage becomes cool to touch, bluish, or numb, or if the distal pulse is no longer present, the pressure bandage may be too tight and should be loosened and reapplied. If bleeding reoccurs you may need to apply a limb or junctional tourniquet.

notices.text:
If a penetrating object is lodged in the casualty's body, bandage it in place. Do not remove the object.
- Ensure the hemostatic dressing or gauze extends 1-2 inches above the skin.

heading: APPLICATION OF PRESSURE DRESSINGS
text: Secure the pressure dressing tail with hooks or a knot, taping them down to prevent loosening. Pressure bandages should not create a TQ effect; if the pulse is absent below the bandage, it's too tight and needs to be loosened and retied.

heading: APPLICATION OF PRESSURE DRESSINGS
text: Signs of excessive tightness include bluish skin tint, coolness to touch, or numbness in the extremity below the bandage. All bandages should be reassessed after the casualty is relocated.

heading: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL
text: Tier 2 skills expand upon Tier 1 skills, which Service members apply to themselves or others in urgent situations. In the CUF phase, the tactical situation often limits the initiation of Tier 2 skills for hemorrhage control, typically extending only to the application of a hasty TQ. Tier 2 treatments such as the deliberate TQ and hemostatic pressure dressings are not applied during CUF due to the length of time to apply and the immediate threat to life from enemy fire.

heading: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL
text: Although Tier 1 and Tier 2 provide the same hemorrhage control treatment of hasty TQ during CUF, during TFC the Tier 2 CLS treats any massive bleeding, from an extremity, with deliberate TQs. Tier 2 personnel are also trained in junctional wound hemostatic pressure dressings.

heading: APPLICATION OF TOURNIQUETS
text: The CLS must possess proficiency in executing all Tier 1 massive bleeding control skills and be capable of directing or assisting Service members in their application. Emphasizing TQs as the primary method for bleeding control during CUF.

heading: APPLICATION OF TOURNIQUETS
text: During TFC, where time allows for thorough assessment, exposing the wound becomes feasible, aiding in and pinpointing the precise site of bleeding. Deliberate TQs applied in this phase, positioned two to three inches above the wound directly on the skin, optimize effectiveness while minimizing unnecessary impact on healthy tissue.

heading: APPLICATION OF TOURNIQUETS
text: The CLS conducts reassessment of TQs applied during CUF to ensure their efficacy. TQs hastily applied "high and tight" may need adjustment as medical personnel intervene, addressing the placement for optimal effectiveness.

heading: APPLICATION OF TOURNIQUETS
text: If bleeding persists despite a previously applied TQ, the CLS should promptly apply a second deliberate TQ adjacent to the original, positioned higher on the limb. Bleeding cessation is expected within one minute, with full TQ securing achieved within three minutes. Any life-threatening bleeding not identified during CUF warrants immediate intervention with a TQ, hemostatic, or pressure dressing.

heading: APPLICATION OF TOURNIQUETS
text: Documenting the time of TQ placement on both the TQ itself and the DD Form 1380 during TFC, rather than CUF, is crucial for subsequent medical personnel. Care should be taken to avoid placing TQs over joints or pockets containing bulky items, ensuring the TQs effectiveness.

heading: APPLICATION OF HEMOSTATIC DRESSING
text: While hemostatic dressings should be packed into wounds of the limbs, when the source of bleeding is too high on the limb for TQ application (such as the neck, armpit, and groin) they should NOT be packed into the abdomen or chest. For compressible (external) hemorrhage, places where a TQ cannot be effectively applied, use a CoTCCC-recommended hemostatic dressing.

heading: APPLICATION OF HEMOSTATIC DRESSING
text: Although the hemostatic dressing contains the active hemostatic agents, direct pressure must be applied for at least three minutes. Non-CoTCCC-recommended supplies may be available; however, they have not been shown to be effective in controlling massive hemorrhaging.

heading: APPLICATION OF DIRECT PRESSURE
text: After packing the wound with a hemostatic dressing or gauze, hold direct pressure for three minutes. Direct pressure can and should be used as a temporary measure until a TQ or dressing is in place. It is difficult to use direct pressure alone to control significant bleeding, or while moving the casualty. While packing a wound, maintain constant, direct pressure, at the source of the bleeding to be effective.

heading: APPLICATION OF WOUND PACKING
text: Wounds should not be blindly packed. Effort must be taken to locate the source of bleeding and apply direct pressure immediately while preparing the gauze.

heading: APPLICATION OF WOUND PACKING
text:
Wound packing:
- Identify and expose the wound.
- Locate the source of the most active bleeding and apply direct pressure, while preparing the hemostatic dressing.
- Remove the hemostatic dressing from its sterile package and pack it into the wound tightly, directly over the site of the most active bleeding.
- Fill and pack the whole wound cavity tightly while keeping firm pressure on the wound.
- Ensure the hemostatic dressing extends one to two inches above the skin.
- Hold continuous direct pressure for a minimum of three minutes.
- Reassess the wound to ensure that the bleeding has stopped.
- Apply a pressure bandage over the hemostatic dressing to secure it in place.
- Reassess the wound to ensure that the bleeding has stopped. If blood is seeping through or around the hemostatic dressing, the bleeding is not controlled, and the following steps should be applied:
- If extra hemostatic dressings are available, remove the initial, ineffective hemostatic dressing and replace them with new hemostatic dressings.
- If extra hemostatic dressings are unavailable, leave initial, ineffective hemostatic dressing in place and add extra gauze over the wound tract.
- If roller or compressed gauze was used initially, due to unavailability of hemostatic dressings, leave initial, ineffective roller or compressed gauze in place and add extra gauze over the wound tract.
- Once bleeding has been controlled, apply a pressure bandage over the wound packing material to secure it in place. Note. More than one hemostatic dressing may be required to stop the blood flow.

heading: APPLICATION OF PRESSURE DRESSINGS
text: Once bleeding has been controlled with a hemostatic dressing or packing material, pressure must be maintained on the wound. All hemostatic dressings for significant bleeding should be secured with pressure bandages.

heading: APPLICATION OF PRESSURE DRESSINGS
text: The pressure dressing is placed directly on top of the hemostatic dressing or packing material. While maintaining direct pressure on the hemostatic dressing or packing material, the CLS will wrap the pressure or elastic bandage tightly focusing pressure directly over the wound. Secure the pressure dressing tail either by hooks, or with a knot, and tape both down to ensure they do not come loose.

heading: APPLICATION OF PRESSURE DRESSINGS
text:
Pressure bandages should not have a TQ effect. If there is no pulse below the pressure bandage, it has been applied too tightly and will need to be loosened and retied. Another sign that the pressure bandage has been applied too tightly is the color of the skin. The skin will have a bluish tint and may be cool to the touch. The casualty will complain of numbness in the extremity below the bandage. All bandages should be reassessed by--
- Checking for circulation BELOW the pressure bandage by feeling for a distal pulse (a pulse below the bandage).
- Checking the skin BELOW the pressure bandage ensures the skin is not cool to the touch, has a bluish tint, or is numb.
- Checking every time a casualty is moved.

heading: APPLICATION OF PRESSURE DRESSINGS
text: The pressure dressing is too tight if the pulse below the pressure dressing is no longer present, or the skin is cool. If circulation is blocked or stopped, loosen, and re-tie the bandage. Dressings and bandages should be reassessed and checked routinely.

heading: APPLICATION OF JUNCTIONAL PRESSURE
text: Junctional pressure is an alternative method to control bleeding. This method uses pressure to press at the site or point where a main artery supplying the wounded area lies near the skin surface or over bone (see figure 4-6 on page 55). These areas are known as junctional areas and are difficult to stop the bleeding even though the vessels are larger than in the extremities. Junctional areas are located at the junction of the extremities and neck with the torso.

heading: APPLICATION OF JUNCTIONAL PRESSURE
text: Junctional hemorrhage can also occur on the extremities if the injury is too close to the torso for a TQ to be applied. Blood vessels at junctional areas are larger than in the limbs but can still be compressed with direct pressure. Junctional pressure may help in instances where bleeding is not easily controlled by TQs, where a hemostatic dressing has not yet been applied, or where pressure dressing may assist in clotting. Junctional pressure is a temporary measure that may buy time for more definitive treatment.

heading: Neck Junctional Hemorrhage Control
text: A neck wound should be packed with a hemostatic dressing using your fingers to ensure that the gauze is packed in all parts of the wound. The wound should be packed sufficiently to ensure that the gauze extends one to two inches above the skin surface. Direct pressure must be maintained continuously for three minutes and maintained throughout the application of the dressing. A pressure dressing is applied on top of the gauze.

heading: Neck Junctional Hemorrhage Control
text:
Neck junctional hemorrhage control:
- Consider body substance isolation
- Expose the injury and assess the bleeding source.
- Apply direct pressure to the bleeding source, use dressing from the casualty's IFAK or JFAK.
- Pack wound tightly with the hemostatic gauze until the wound cavity is filled. Note. These steps should be performed within 90 seconds.
- Ensure that the gauze extends 1 to 2 inches above the skin.
- Hold pressure for a minimum of three minutes.
- Reassess to ensure bleeding has been controlled while maintaining pressure.
- If bleeding has not been controlled.
- If packed with hemostatic dressing, and extra hemostatic dressings are available, remove and repack.
- If packed with gauze or initially packed with hemostatic dressing and no more hemostatic dressing is available, apply additional gauze and pressure (for three minutes) until the bleeding stops.
- Place an elastic bandage over the dressing leaving enough tail to tie it into a knot.
- While maintaining pressure, wrap diagonally across the chest under the opposite arm (armpit) around the back to the neck and back over the wound.
- Wrap the bandage (no less than 1 1/2 times) over the packing material covering it completely.
- Wrap around the neck and under the arm (on alternating sides of the tail, while maintaining tension/pressure), pulling elastic bandage tightly for pressure, covering the packing material. Note. Do not use the pressure bar on the neck.
- Secure the dressing by tying a non-slip knot with the end of the elastic bandage and its tail.
- Secure the elastic bandage tails with tape, wrapping a minimum of 1 1/2 times around the knot.
- Swath the upper arm (of the injured side) to the chest using a bandage.
- Continue to assess the wound for further bleeding.
- Document all findings and treatments on DD Form 1380.

heading: Axillary Junctional Hemorrhage Control
text:
The axillary (upper armpit) area is an area where the arm attaches to the torso. The axillary artery runs from the torso through the armpit and feeds oxygenated blood to both arms. Axillary junctional hemorrhage is very difficult to treat if attention to detail is not observed. The steps for controlling Axillary Junctional Hemorrhage are:
- Consider body substance isolation.
- Cut away any clothing (to expose injury) and lift the arm to assess the bleeding source.
- Apply direct pressure to the most active bleed. Prepare hemostatic dressing.
- Extend the casualty's arm at a 90-degree angle by placing it on your shoulder.
- Pack the wound tightly with the hemostatic gauze until the wound cavity is filled. Note. These steps should be performed within 90 seconds.
- Ensure that the gauze extends 1 to 2 inches above the skin.
- Hold pressure for a minimum of three minutes.
- If the bleeding has not been controlled.
- If packed with hemostatic dressing, and extra hemostatic dressings are available, remove and repack starting at step 5.
- If packed with gauze or initially packed with a hemostatic dressing and no more hemostatic dressing is available, apply additional gauze and pressure (for three minutes) until bleeding stops. Note. Clothing may need to be cut away to properly expose the injury. The best position to treat the casualty is the seated position. If the casualty cannot be treated in the seated position, you will need to sit the casualty up as much as possible to apply the elastic bandage.
- While maintaining pressure on the dressing/gauze, wrap the pressure (or elastic) bandage around the injured shoulder twice to ensure the gauze underneath is completely covered.
- Wrap the elastic bandage across, back and under the opposite armpit, anchoring around the opposite shoulder in a "figure 8" pattern.
- Depending on the bandage used, secure with the closure bar of tie tails of elastic bandage with a nonslip knot.
- Secure the pressure (elastic) bandage tails and knot using tape, wrapping a minimum of 1 1/2 times around the knot.
- Swat the upper arm to the side of the chest using a cravat.
- Continue to assess the wound for further bleeding.

heading: EXPEDIENT TECHNIQUES FOR HEMORRHAGE CONTROL
text: Expedient techniques for hemorrhage control are of paramount importance in TCCC due to their ability to rapidly address life-threatening bleeding in high-stress and time-critical combat situations. Expedient techniques enable military personnel to intervene quickly and effectively control hemorrhage and prevent further blood loss. These techniques, such as the use of TQs, pressure dressings, and hemostatic agents, are specifically designed to be simple, easily applied, and accessible to all Service members, regardless of medical training. By swiftly initiating hemorrhage control, expedient techniques significantly increase the chances of survival, allowing injured individuals to receive timely care, and ultimately improving their overall mission success, and preserving the fighting strength of the military forces.

heading: IMPROVISED TOURNIQUET
text: Using one of the CoTCCC-recommended TQs is the safe and preferred procedure for hemorrhage control. Improvised TQs are much less effective than commercially available TQs discussed in paragraph 4-37 on page 48. Improvised TQs are difficult to make and apply without extensive practice, however they may be needed in situations where commercially produced TQs are unavailable, or supplies have been exhausted.

notices.text:
The risks associated with using improvised TQs include:
- Damage may occur to the skin if the band is too narrow.
- Bleeding may worsen.
- Bleeding may not be completely controlled.
- Likely to loosen overtime from not being properly secured.

heading: IMPROVISED TOURNIQUET
text: If a TQ is not available, pack the wound and hold direct pressure over the source of the heaviest bleed, FIRST. If this fails to control the bleeding in an arm or leg, only then consider an alternate improvised TQ.

heading: IMPROVISED TOURNIQUET
text: An alternate improvised TQ uses other materials on hand. In constructing one, it is recommended that you fold a cravat (or other pliable material) to a width of approximately 1 1/2 to 2 inches and tighten it with some sort of windlass rod (a straight rod that can be used to twist the material tighter). Then secure the rod to ensure it does not loosen. Note. The cravat is included in the JFAK, however it is not part of the Army IFAK Generation 1 or 2. To resource the cravat for the Army IFAK, the nomenclature is: Sterile Burn Dressing Cravat, NSN: 6510-01-587-6579; Muslin Compressed Bandage NSN: 6510-00-201-1755.

heading: IMPROVISED TOURNIQUET
text: An improvised TQ should not be used except as an absolute last resort when there is no other option to control life-threatening bleeding. If no TQ is available, pack the wound and hold direct pressure over the main source of bleeding.

heading: IMPROVISED TOURNIQUET
text: Continue to check the TQ, as improvised TQs are prone to loosening due to (but not limited to) casualty movement, shifting fluid, and quality of improvised material.

heading: INGUINAL HEMORRHAGE CONTROL WITH AN IMPROVISED PRESSURE DELIVERY DEVICE
text: A pressure delivery device (PDD) is made using improvised materials, such as a shoe or boot, full water bottle, or canteen which applies additional pressure to the wound after it has been packed. A PDD may be needed to apply additional and targeted pressure to control inguinal or groin hemorrhage.

heading: INGUINAL HEMORRHAGE CONTROL WITH AN IMPROVISED PRESSURE DELIVERY DEVICE
text: For groin injuries packed with hemostatic dressings, use an improvised junctional PDD to secure the dressing. The PDD is placed in the groin while continuously maintaining pressure to the dressing.

heading: INGUINAL HEMORRHAGE CONTROL WITH AN IMPROVISED PRESSURE DELIVERY DEVICE
text: The PDD is then secured with a TQ, which is wrapped over the hips with the windlass or ratchet placed directly over the improvised device and tightened to add additional pressure. Two TQs placed together may be needed when improvising a PDD. Note. Junctional hemorrhages involve larger blood vessels requiring more pressure (and targeted pressure) than can be applied with a pressure dressing alone.

heading: INGUINAL HEMORRHAGE CONTROL WITH AN IMPROVISED PRESSURE DELIVERY DEVICE
text:
Inguinal (Groin) Hemorrhage Control with Improvised Junctional Pressure Device:
- Consider body substance isolation.
- Expose the injury and assess the bleeding source.
- Apply direct pressure to the wound using a hand, fist, or elbow and open the hemostatic gauze package.
- Tightly pack the wound with hemostatic gauze until the wound cavity is filled (finishing the packing within 90 seconds).
- Hold pressure for a minimum of 3 minutes.
- Reassess to ensure that the bleeding has been controlled while maintaining pressure.
- If packed with hemostatic dressing, and extra hemostatic dressings are available, remove and repack.
- If packed with gauze or initially packed with hemostatic dressing and no more hemostatic dressing is available, apply additional gauze and pressure (for three minutes) until bleeding stops.
- Select and position a pressure delivery device, such as a canteen, into the inguinal gutter while maintaining pressure.
- Select a TQ that can wrap around the casualty's waist/hip area or connect the two tourniquets together.
- Place the windlass or ratchet TQ directly over the middle of the pressure delivery device; ensure that the routing buckle is located towards the middle of the body.
- Remove all slack from the band or strap using a pushing motion across the casualty's body before tightening the TQ.
- Tighten the TQ and ensure that the bleeding is still controlled, and the distal pulse is absent. Note. If the bleeding is not controlled and the distal pulse (a pulse located below the TQ) is present, remove any remaining slack in the strapping (if possible) and twist or ratchet the TQ device until bleeding is controlled and/or a distal pulse is absent.
- Visually inspect the placement of the equipment, ensuring that the pressure delivery device is in place and the windlass or ratchet is properly positioned over the device.
- Document all findings and treatments on DD Form 1380.

heading: OVERVIEW OF AIRWAY CONTROL
text: After massive bleeding is controlled, the responder can move on to airway control, the first "A" in the MARCH-PAWS sequence. The casualty must have an open (unobstructed) airway. If the casualty is awake and talking, you can assume the casualty's airway is open. However, the casualty may still have difficulty breathing. If the casualty is unconscious, their airway must be inspected for any obvious blockages.

heading: OVERVIEW OF AIRWAY CONTROL
text: Humans must have oxygen to live. Through the breathing process, the lungs draw oxygen from the air and put it into the blood. The heart pumps the blood through the body to be used by the cells that require a constant supply of oxygen. Some cells are more dependent on a constant supply of oxygen than others. For example, cells of the brain may die within five minutes without oxygen. The brain, heart and lungs are very intolerant to lack of oxygen. The brain is considered one of the organs that is least tolerant to oxygen deprivation. Once these cells die, they are lost forever and do not regenerate. This could result in permanent brain damage, paralysis, or death.

heading: OVERVIEW OF AIRWAY CONTROL
text: Airway obstruction on the battlefield is often due to facial trauma. If the casualty is breathing on their own but unconscious or semi-conscious, and there is no airway obstruction, further airway management is achieved through a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA). First responders must assess casualties with facial trauma when contraindications exist to NPA use (such as basilar skull fractures, disruption of the midface, nasopharynx, or roof of the mouth).

heading: OVERVIEW OF AIRWAY CONTROL
text:
Unconscious casualties can also lose their airway as the muscles of their tongue may have relaxed. This causes the tongue to block the airway by sliding to the back of the mouth and covering the opening to the windpipe. The signs and symptoms of airway obstruction include:
- Casualty is in distress and indicating that they cannot breathe properly.
- Casualty making snoring or gurgling sounds.
- Visible blood or foreign objects are present in the airway.
- Severe trauma to the face is observed.

heading: RESPIRATION
text: Respiration is the process where we breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. The efficiency of this process can vary depending on someone's age and physical health. Generally, adults breathe 12 to 20 times a minute. But children and infants have different rates. For instance, children aged one to 10 years take 15 to 30 breaths per minute. Infants who are six to 12 months old breath faster, at a rate of 25 to 50 times per minute. Meanwhile, the youngest infants, those aged zero to five months, have a rate of 25 to 40 breaths per minute.

heading: ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF THE RESPIRATORY SYSTEM
text: The respiratory system consists of the airway, lungs, and rib cage. The airway consists of the nose, mouth, throat, voice box, and windpipe. Air passes to and from the lungs through the canal. The lungs are two elastic organs made up of thousands of tiny air spaces or sacs and covered by an airtight membrane. The bronchial tree is a part of the lungs. The rib cage is the structure that joins the spine in the back and the breastbone in front, which protects the heart and lungs. The top part of the rib cage is closed by the structure of the neck, and the bottom part is separated from the abdominal cavity by a large dome-shaped muscle called the diaphragm (figure 5-1 on page 60).

heading: ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF THE RESPIRATORY SYSTEM
text: The diaphragm and rib muscles, which are under the control of the respiratory center in the brain, automatically contract and relax. Inspiration increases and expiration decreases the size of the rib cage. When the rib cage increases and then decreases, the air pressure in the lungs is first less and then more than the atmospheric pressure, thus causing the air to rush into and out of the lungs to equalize the pressure.

heading: EQUIPMENT USED FOR AIRWAY CONTROL
text: The CoTCCC-recommended NPA with lubricant is a nonsterile, rubber tube-shaped device that is inserted into the nostril of a casualty. It acts as a wedge to keep the airway open by keeping the tongue from falling back into the space behind the mouth leading to the windpipe. Only an NPA, size 32 French, is found within the standard issued JFAKs. Sizing the NPA before insertion is not necessary but is important to minimize nasopharyngeal trauma or elicit the casualty's gag reflex. The lubricant is a water-based substance that assists in inserting the device into the nose. Use of an NPA is a Tier 2 skill.

notices.text: Do NOT use blood or other body fluids to lubricate the NPA. TIER 1 SKILLS FOR AIRWAY CONTROL

heading: EQUIPMENT USED FOR AIRWAY CONTROL
text: Tier 1 TCCC skills for airway control encompass techniques and procedures designed to address various challenges, including airway obstructions and respiratory distress. Proficiency in these skills is imperative for Service members operating in high-stakes, dynamic situations, and where swift and precise intervention can mean the difference between life, and death on the battlefield.

heading: SAFELY POSITION THE CASUALTY TO OPEN THE AIRWAY
text:
Check for responsiveness (figure 5-2 step A on page 61) and establish whether the casualty is conscious by gently shaking them and asking, "Are you OK?" Call for help (figure 5-2 step B on page 61) and then position the unconscious casualty so that they are lying in the recovery position, head tilted back; chin away from chest (figure 5-2 step C on page 61) by --
- Straightening the casualty's legs.
- Moving the casualty's arm that is nearest to you. Move it so that it is straight and above their head. Repeat the procedure for the other arm placing it by their side.
- Kneeling beside the casualty with your knees near their shoulders (leave space to roll their body).
- Placing one hand behind their head and neck for support. On your other hand, grasp the casualty under their arm (figure 5-2 step C on page 61).
- Rolling the casualty towards you using a steady, even pull. The casualty's head and neck should stay in line with their back.

heading: SAFELY POSITION THE CASUALTY TO OPEN THE AIRWAY
text: The recovery position allows blood and mucus to drain out of the casualty's nose and mouth and not drain back into the airway. However, if a neck injury is suspected and the jaw-thrust technique will be used, kneel at the casualty's head, looking towards their feet.

notices.text: If the casualty is lying on their chest (prone position), cautiously roll the casualty as a unit so that their body does not twist. The twisting may further complicate a back, neck, or spinal injury.

heading: AIRWAY OBSTRUCTIONS
text:
Oxygen flows to and from the lungs requires an unobstructed airway, yet obstructions can arise due to various factors:
- Unconsciousness may lead to the tongue falling back into the throat, obstructing the airway if not properly managed.
- Foreign objects, particularly food, may become lodged in the throat during eating, especially when large pieces are swallowed without proper chewing, exacerbated by factors like alcohol consumption or slipping dentures.
- Regurgitation of stomach contents or the formation of blood clots due to head and facial injuries can further contribute to airway blockage.
- Ensure correct positioning and maintenance of the airway in injured or unconscious casualties to mitigate these risks.

heading: AIRWAY OBSTRUCTIONS
text: Upper airway obstruction, a potentially life-threatening emergency, can occur as either a partial or complete blockage. The severity and nature of the obstruction underscore the importance of rapid recognition and immediate intervention to prevent respiratory compromise. Identifying the signs early and responding effectively are crucial in maintaining the airway and supporting breathing, which are vital for the casualty's survival. This situation demands prompt and decisive action to alleviate the obstruction and ensure an open airway.

heading: Partial Airway Obstruction
text: The casualty may still have an air exchange. A good air exchange means that the casualty can cough forcefully, though they may be wheezing between coughs. The rescuer should not interfere and should encourage the casualty to cough up the object obstructing their airway on their own. Weak coughing with a high-pitched noise between coughs may indicate a poor air exchange. You should assist the casualty and treat them as though they had a complete obstruction.

heading: Complete Airway Obstruction
text: A complete obstruction (no air exchange) is indicated if the casualty cannot speak, breathe, or cough at all. They may be clutching their neck and moving erratically. In an unconscious casualty, a complete obstruction is also indicated if after opening their airway you cannot ventilate them. A casualty, experiencing a partial foreign body airway obstruction, with poor air exchange, or a complete airway obstruction will not survive without medical intervention. Both conditions are treated the same.

heading: OPENING THE AIRWAY OF AN UNCONSCIOUS OR NOT BREATHING CASUALTY
text: The tongue is the single most common cause of an airway obstruction (see figure 5-3). In most cases, simply using the head-tilt/chin-lift or jaw thrust technique can open the airway. This action pulls the tongue away from the air passage in the throat (see figure 5-4).

heading: OPENING THE AIRWAY OF AN UNCONSCIOUS OR NOT BREATHING CASUALTY
text: Call for help and then position the casualty. Move (roll) the casualty onto their back as described in paragraph 5-10 on page 60.

heading: OPENING THE AIRWAY OF AN UNCONSCIOUS OR NOT BREATHING CASUALTY
text: If a foreign body is seen in the airway, an attempt to remove it should be made. Do not put your fingers in the mouth to try to find or remove any unseen objects that might be causing an obstruction as this may push the object further into the airway. Open the airway using the head-tilt/chin-lift method. Note. If foreign material or vomitus is visible in the mouth, it should be removed as quickly as possible.

heading: Remove any visible objects, but do not perform a blind finger
text: sweep.

notices.text: The head-tilt/chin-lift technique is an important procedure in opening the airway; however, use extreme care because excess force in performing this maneuver may cause further spinal injury. In a casualty with a suspected neck injury or severe head trauma, the safest approach to opening the airway is the jaw-thrust technique because in most cases, it can be accomplished without extending the neck.

heading: Head-Tilt/Chin-Lift Method
text: Place one hand on the casualty's forehead and apply firm, backward pressure with the palm to tilt the head back. Place the fingertips of the other hand under the bony part of the lower jaw and lift, bringing the chin forward. The thumb should not be used to lift the chin (see figure 5-5). Note. The fingers should not press deeply into the soft tissue under the chin because the airway may be obstructed.

heading: Jaw-Thrust Method
text: The jaw-thrust method may be accomplished by the rescuer grasping the angles of the casualty's lower jaw and lifting with both hands, one on each side, displacing the jaw forward and up (see figure 5-6). The rescuer's elbows should rest on the surface on which the casualty is lying. If the lips close, the lower lip can be retracted with the thumb. If mouth-to-mouth breathing is necessary, close the nostrils by placing your cheek tightly against them. The head should be carefully supported without tilting it backwards or turning it from side-to-side. If this is unsuccessful, the head should be tilted back slightly. The jaw-thrust is the safest first approach to opening the airway of a casualty who has a suspected neck injury because in most cases it can be accomplished without extending the neck. Note. If the casualty's lips are still closed after the jaw has been moved forward, use your thumbs to retract the lower lip, and allow air to enter the casualty's mouth.

heading: Jaw-Thrust Method
text: The jaw-thrust method, commonly emphasized in training, can sometimes serve as a distraction in the field. Neck injuries in trauma cases are typically associated with dramatic incidents such as falls and motor vehicle accidents. Most neck injuries occur upon impact, and the extent of injury is usually immediate and unchangeable at the scene. If neck trauma is present, it is often necessary to perform a jaw-thrust maneuver to secure an airway and maintain that position until additional personnel arrive. This intervention allows the responder to proceed with the MARCH sequence.

heading: MANAGING THE AIRWAY
text: If the casualty is breathing independently yet is unconscious or semiconscious, and there is no airway obstruction, managing the airway is best accomplished using an NPA. An NPA is suitable for both conscious and unconscious individuals and is effective in helping to open or maintain an open airway. This method ensures that the airway remains clear, facilitating easier breathing and potentially preventing further complications.

heading: MANAGING THE AIRWAY
text: Casualties with severe facial trauma can often protect their own airways by sitting up and leaning forward. Assisting a conscious casualty by helping them assume any comfortable sitting-up position that allows them to breathe easily. If the casualty is unconscious but breathing, the casualty should be placed in the recovery position (figure 5-7 on page 65).

heading: MANAGING THE AIRWAY
text: The recovery position allows blood and mucus to drain out of the casualty's nose and mouth and not drain back into the airway. The recovery position also helps to protect against inhaling vomit if the casualty throws up. If a casualty can breathe on their own, let them assume the best position (position of comfort) that allows them to breathe, including sitting up.

heading: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR AIRWAY CONTROL
text: The primary objective of Tier 2 airway control skills is to confirm the initiation of Tier 1 skills, with the addition of Tier 2 insertion of a nasopharyngeal airway and monitor the casualty for any signs of airway compromise, as outlined in paragraph 5-3. If the casualty shows signs of not breathing spontaneously, it's imperative to promptly notify medical personnel. Medical personnel may then require assistance from the CLS in administering breathing assistance using a bag valve mask (BVM) device, as depicted in figure 5-8. In instances where respirations are observed to be diminished, providing ventilation support with a BVM becomes necessary, and the CLS may be requested to assist in its usage by medical personnel.

heading: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR AIRWAY CONTROL
text: Casualties requiring ongoing BVM support due to lack of spontaneous breathing effort, if not just administered a sedating pain medication, might indicate an injury or condition warranting earlier or immediate evacuation (such as severe traumatic brain injury or TBI). If definitive treatment or evacuation is not available, consider triaging the casualty to expectant if resources are limited or better applied to more likely survivable casualties.

heading: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR AIRWAY CONTROL
text: Ventilations can be performed alone or with two people working together. The mask is held using the "E-C" holding technique (figure 5-9 on page 66). The mask is sealed over the casualty's mouth so that air does not escape (figure 5-10 on page 66). The mask is then squeezed firmly for one to two seconds and five to six seconds apart. The Deployed Medicine website has an instruction video on the proper application of the one and two-person BVM.

heading: EXPEDIENT TECHNIQUES FOR AIRWAY CONTROL
text: Expedient techniques for airway control are critically important in TCCC due to the immediate threat posed by compromised airways in combat situations. Injured Service members may experience airway obstructions, respiratory distress, or loss of consciousness, which can rapidly progress to life-threatening situations. Expedient airway control techniques, such as the head tilt/chin lift, jaw thrust maneuver and use of NPAs may enable prompt restoration of adequate breathing and oxygenation. These techniques can be quickly implemented by trained personnel, ensuring timely intervention even in chaotic and high-stress environments. By swiftly addressing airway compromises, through the use of expedient techniques in TCCC play a vital role in preserving life, preventing further complications, and maximizing the chances of survival for injured military personnel on the battlefield.

heading: OPENING THE OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY - CONSCIOUS CASUALTY
text: Clearing an airway obstruction in a conscious casualty can be managed while they are either standing or sitting. However, it's critical to recognize that an obstructed airway can lead to oxygen deficiency in the brain, resulting in respiratory arrest, unconsciousness and, if not promptly corrected, death.

heading: OPENING THE OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY - CONSCIOUS CASUALTY
text: To assess and manage airway obstruction, start by asking the casualty if they can speak or if they are choking. Additionally, check for the universal choking sign (see figure 5-11 on page 67). If the casualty can speak or cough effectively, encourage them to continue coughing. This indicates that they still have good air exchange, and you should not interfere with their efforts to expel the obstruction.

heading: OPENING THE OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY - CONSCIOUS CASUALTY
text: However, if you notice high-pitched sounds when the casualty breathes or coughs, indicating poor air exchange, or if the casualty is unable to breathe, immediate action is required. Call for help and prepare to perform manual thrusts to clear the obstruction. Use abdominal thrusts, also known as the Heimlich maneuver, by positioning your hands between the waist and the rib cage and delivering quick upward thrusts. For individuals in advanced stages of pregnancy, those who are markedly obese, or if there is a significant abdominal wound, use chest thrust instead. This involves placing your hands in the center of the breastbone and pushing sharply inward and upward.

heading: OPENING THE OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY - CONSCIOUS CASUALTY
text: Quick action is essential in these situations to restore breathing and prevent further complications, including death. Always ensure to assess the situation carefully and apply the appropriate technique based on the casualty's condition

heading: Apply Abdominal Thrusts
text:
Prior to applying abdominal thrust, first responders should administer five back blows. Abdominal thrust can be accomplished by using the following procedures:
- Stand behind the casualty and wrap your arms around their waist.
- Make a fist with one hand and grasp it with the other. The thumb side of your fist should be against the casualty's abdomen, in the midline and slightly above the casualty's navel, but well below the tip of the breastbone (figure 5-12 on page 68).
- Press the fists into the abdomen with a quick backward and upward thrust (figure 5-13 on page 68).

heading: abdominal thrust procedure abdominal thrust
text:
- Each thrust should be a separate and distinct movement.
- Continue performing abdominal thrusts until the obstruction is expelled or the casualty becomes unresponsive.
- If the casualty becomes unresponsive, call for help as you proceed with the steps to open the airway.

heading: Apply Chest Thrusts
text:
An alternate technique to the abdominal thrust is the chest thrust. This technique is useful when the casualty has an abdominal wound, is pregnant, or when the casualty is so large that you cannot wrap your arms around the abdomen. To apply chest thrusts with casualty sitting or standing:
- Stand behind the casualty and wrap your arms around their chest with your arms under their armpits.
- Make a fist with one hand and place the thumb side of the fist in the middle of the breastbone (take care to avoid the tip of the breastbone and the margins of the ribs).
- Grasp the fist with the other hand and exert thrusts (figure 5-14 on page 69).
- Each thrust should be delivered slowly, distinctly, and with the intent of relieving the obstruction.
- Perform chest thrusts until the obstruction is expelled or the casualty becomes unresponsive.
- If the casualty becomes unresponsive, call for help as you proceed with steps to open the airway, and perform rescue breathing.

heading: OPENING THE OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY - CASUALTY LYING DOWN OR UNRESPONSIVE
text: When an individual who is choking becomes unresponsive while lying down, or if an unconscious person is discovered and the cause of their condition is unknown, specific emergency protocols must be followed to address potential airway obstruction.

heading: OPENING THE OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY - CASUALTY LYING DOWN OR UNRESPONSIVE
text:
If a conscious individual begins choking and subsequently loses consciousness, immediate action is required:
- Summon help right away to ensure assistance is on the way.
- Open the casualty's airway to assess and manage the obstruction.
- Perform a finger sweep only if there is visible obstruction in the mouth to avoid pushing the obstruction deeper.
- Attempt to rescue breathing, which involves assessing whether the air can flow into the lungs. Refer to detailed instructions on mouth-to-mouth resuscitation provided in paragraph 6-49 on page 81. If breathing efforts fail due to a blockage, swiftly move to clear the airway using procedures outlined in paragraph 5-39.

heading: OPENING THE OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY - CASUALTY LYING DOWN OR UNRESPONSIVE
text:
In scenarios where a casualty is found already unresponsive, the procedure slightly differs:
- Quickly assess the situation to understand the context and severity.
- Call for immediate assistance.
- Position the casualty on their back to manage and secure the airway effectively.
- Check for a pulse to determine the urgency of cardiovascular support.
- Open the airway using recommended techniques.
- Confirm if the casualty is not breathing and, if so, proceed to attempt rescue breathing as per the guidelines detailed in paragraph 6-49 on page 81.

heading: OPENING THE OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY - CASUALTY LYING DOWN OR UNRESPONSIVE
text: These critical steps are designed to maximize the chances of recovery by ensuring that the airway is cleared, and that breathing is restored at the earliest possible opportunity. Quick and effective intervention is crucial in such emergencies, underscoring the importance of thorough training and readiness.

heading: OPENING THE OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY - CASUALTY LYING DOWN OR UNRESPONSIVE
text:
If you are still unable to ventilate the casualty, perform 6 to 10 manual (abdominal or chest) thrusts. To perform the abdominal thrusts:
- Kneel astride the casualty's thighs (see below figure 5-15).
- Place the heel of one hand against the casualty's abdomen (in the midline slightly above the navel but well below the tip of the breastbone). Place your other hand on top of the first one. Point your fingers toward the casualty's head.
- Press into the casualty's abdomen with a quick, forward, and upward thrust. You can use your body weight to perform the maneuver. Deliver each thrust quickly and distinctly.
- Repeat the sequence of abdominal thrusts, finger sweeping, and rescue breathing (attempt to ventilate) as long as necessary to remove the object from the obstructed airway.
- If the casualty's chest rises, proceed to feel for their pulse.

heading: OPENING THE OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY - CASUALTY LYING DOWN OR UNRESPONSIVE
text:
To perform chest thrusts the unresponsive casualty is placed on their back, face up, and open their mouth. The first responder kneels close to the side of the casualty's body and--
- Locates the lower edge of the casualty's ribs with their fingers by running theirs fingers up along the rib cage to the notch (figure 5-16 step A on page 71).
- Places the middle finger on the notch in the casualty's chest and the index finger next to the middle finger on the lower edge of the casualty's breastbone.
- Place the heel of the other hand on the lower half of the breastbone next to the two fingers (figure 5-16 step B on page 71).
- Remove the fingers from the notch and place that hand on top of the positioned hand on the breastbone, extending or interlocking the fingers (figure 5-16 step C on page 71).
- Straighten and lock elbows with their shoulders directly above the hands without bending the elbows, rocking, or allowing the shoulders to sag.
- Apply enough pressure to depress the breastbone 1 1/2 to 2 inches and then release the pressure completely (figure 5-16 step D on page 71). This press and release process is delivered quickly and distinctly, six to 10 times. Figure 5-17 on page 71 shows another view of the breastbone being depressed.

notices.text: Rescuers may feel ribs fracture, and this is OK since it's a lifethreatening situation.

heading: OPENING THE OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY - CASUALTY LYING DOWN OR UNRESPONSIVE
text: The first responder repeats the sequence of the chest thrust, finger sweep, and rescue breathing as long as necessary to clear the object from the obstructed airway. If the casualty's chest rises, proceed to feeling for their pulse.

heading: OPENING THE OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY - CASUALTY LYING DOWN OR UNRESPONSIVE
text:
If rescue breathing cannot be administered due to airway obstruction, remove the airway obstruction by--
- Placing the casualty on their back, face up, turn the unresponsive casualty as a unit, and call out for help.
- Performing a finger sweep.
- Using the tongue-jaw lift by opening the casualty's mouth by grasping both their tongue and lower jaw between your thumb and fingers and lifting (tongue-jaw lift) (see figure 5-18). If you are unable to open their mouth, cross your fingers and thumb (crossed-finger method) and push their teeth apart (see figure 5-19) by pressing your thumb against their upper teeth and pressing your finger against their lower teeth.

heading: (tongue-jaw lift) (crossed-finger method)
text: - Insert the index finger of the other hand down along the inside of their cheek to the base of the tongue. Use a hooking motion from the side of the mouth toward the center to dislodge the foreign body (see figure 5-20).

notices.text: Take care not to force the object deeper into the airway by pushing it with the finger.

heading: OVERVIEW OF RESPIRATION AND BREATHING
text: After establishing an open airway, it is important to evaluate the casualty's respirations and maintain that airway in an open position. This is the "R" of MARCH-PAWS. Respiratory distress means difficulty breathing (rapid or abnormally slow breathing), in other words, it is difficult for the casualty to get air in or out. Airway and respiration are not addressed in CUF; however, they must be addressed in TFC.

heading: OVERVIEW OF RESPIRATION AND BREATHING
text: The pleural space between the lungs and chest wall naturally has negative pressure, which helps the lungs to collapse (exhale) and expand (inhale). With either a blunt or penetrating injury to the chest wall or lungs, air may counteract the lung's natural tendency to expand and collapse. This is due to positive pressure replacing negative pressure. It results in air being trapped in the pleural space, putting pressure on the affected lung. This forces the lungs to collapse and reduces the ability to get oxygen to the body.

heading: OVERVIEW OF RESPIRATION AND BREATHING
text: While it may be easy to see a gunshot wound or shrapnel wound to the chest, it is important to evaluate casualties for additional injuries from blunt force trauma which may have been caused from an explosive device or from the chest hitting the steering wheel during a high-impact vehicle accident.

heading: OVERVIEW OF RESPIRATION AND BREATHING
text:
Signs of future life-threatening respiration issues include bruising, contusions (swelling around the chest, back, or rib cage), crepitus (crackling, popping, grating) that are felt or heard, or other deformities of the chest not normally seen without removing the clothing. Signs of respiratory distress include:
- Difficulty in breathing.
- Struggling to get air in and out.
- Breathing is too weak to be effective (less than six times per minute).
- Rapid breathing (greater than 20 times per minute). Note. The above signs may also indicate a penetrating chest wound injury. Report findings of respiratory distress to medical personnel.

heading: CONTROL
text:
In TCCC, various specialized equipment is used to address respiration and breathing control in combat situations. These tools are designed to promptly manage compromised airways and provide respiratory support. The primary equipment used includes:
- NPA.
- BVM.
- Chest Seal.
- 10-14-gauge catheter over needle device.

heading: CONTROL
text: An NPA is a flexible tube inserted through the nose into the oropharynx to maintain an open airway and facilitate adequate breathing. It is particularly useful when there is a risk of tongue obstruction or in cases where the patient is conscious and able to maintain their own airway.

heading: CONTROL
text: A BVM device consists of a self-inflating bag and a mask that is manually squeezed to deliver positive pressure ventilation. It is used when there is a need for artificial respiration to support or control the patient's breathing.

heading: CONTROL
text: A chest seal is an airtight dressing that is applied over a penetrating chest wound to prevent the entry of air into the pleural cavity, reducing the risk of a tension pneumothorax. It allows for the restoration of normal respiratory function by maintaining appropriate chest pressure. The CoTCCC-recommended chest seal is a vented (preferred) self-adhering chest seal (see figure 6-1 on page 74) is used for treating and sucking chest wounds or open pneumothorax.

heading: CONTROL
text: The equipment is essential components of TCCC's approach to respiration and breathing control. Utilizing this equipment enables military personnel to manage airway obstructions, provide respiratory support, and prevent potentially life-threatening complications associated with compromised breathing in combat scenarios.

heading: CONTROL
text: The CoTCCC-recommended catheter-over-needle device is used to treat tension pneumothorax. The recommended catheter-over-needle device is either a 10-gauge, 14-gauge, or 3 1/4 inch long device (see figure 6-2).

heading: TIER 1 SKILLS FOR RESPIRATION AND BREATHING CONTROL
text:
Often the act of just opening and maintaining the airway will allow the casualty to breathe properly. The first responder opens the casualty's airway maintaining the head position to keep the airway open. Failure to maintain the open airway will prevent the casualty from receiving an adequate supply of oxygen. While maintaining an open airway the first responder checks for breathing, respiration rate (breaths per minute) and respiration quality (shallow and labored) by placing the casualty on their back and assessing their breathing by observing the casualty's chest by--
- Looking for the chest to rise and fall.
- Listening for air escaping during exhalation by placing your ear near the casualty's mouth.
- Feeling for the flow of air on your cheek (see figure 6-3).
