heading: PREVENTION OF SHOCK
text: It is more effective to prevent shock through hemorrhage control than to treat it once it has developed. Even in cases where shock is already present, the most critical first action is to control any bleeding. Continuously reassess all bleeding control measures, such as tourniquets and pressure dressings, to ensure they remain effective and are adjusted tightly as soon as possible. This is a crucial step in treating shock.

heading: PREVENTION OF SHOCK
text: Internal bleeding caused by blunt or penetrating trauma to the chest or abdomen may not be immediately controlled and can lead to shock later on. Continuous assessment of the casualty is essential. Even if a casualty is not currently in shock but has sustained serious injuries, they should be carefully monitored for signs of developing shock. It's important not to wait until signs and symptoms of shock appear. While medical personnel will provide comprehensive treatments, controlling any external bleeding early can save valuable time.

heading: EQUIPMENT USED FOR CIRCULATION CONTROL
text: At present, no specialized equipment has been designated exclusively for managing circulation control. The equipment mentioned in the earlier section of this publication serves to support and enhance circulation control measures.

heading: TIER 1 SKILLS FOR CIRCULATION CONTROL
text: The best way to prevent shock is to control bleeding. Responders should continuously monitor and reassess the effectiveness of bleeding control measures to ensure they are working, TQ application, wound packing with hemostatic dressing, a pressure dressing, or a combination of these.

heading: TIER 1 SKILLS FOR CIRCULATION CONTROL
text: After reassessing TQs and hemostatic dressings, the TCCC guideline on shock states: "Assess for hemorrhagic shock" (altered mental status in the absence of brain injury or weak and absent radial pulse). Reassess all bleeding control measures are still effective and TQs remain tight.

heading: BASIC MEASURES TO CONTROL CIRCULATION
text: Control bleeding and then take steps to prevent shock by elevating the casualty's legs higher than the casualty's heart if their airway tolerates lying flat on their back.

heading: BASIC MEASURES TO CONTROL CIRCULATION
text:
Conduct a bleeding re-check by:
- Reassess every TQ and dressing that may have been applied earlier.
- Expose the area and determine if bleeding is controlled.
- Expose and clearly mark all TQ sites with the time of TQ application if not previously done.
- When time and the tactical situation permit, check for further bleeding, and for pulses further out on the limb than the TQ.

heading: POSITION THE CASUALTY FOR SHOCK
text: Move the casualty under a permanent or improvised shelter to shade them from direct sunlight. If the casualty is conscious, place the casualty in the shock recovery position (see figure 7-1), which is on their back with their feet elevated slightly above the level of their heart. This will help their blood circulation. A log, field pack, box, rolled field jacket, or other stable objects can be used to elevate their feet. If a sitting position makes it easier for the casualty to breathe, that is fine.

heading: POSITION THE CASUALTY FOR SHOCK
text:
The following steps will also significantly help in the prevention of shock:
- Loosen clothing at the neck, waist, or anywhere is binding.
- Prevent the casualty from getting chilled or overheated. Using a blanket or clothing, cover the casualty to avoid loss of body heat by wrapping the blanket completely around the casualty. Note. Ensure no part of the casualty is touching the ground, as this increases loss of body heat.
- Calm and reassure the casualty by--
- Taking charge and showing self-confidence.
- Assuring the casualty that they are being taken care of.
- Watch the casualty closely for life-threatening conditions and check for other injuries, if necessary.
- Seek medical aid.
- Record the treatment on DD Form 1380.

notices.text: Do not loosen clothing if in a chemically contaminated area.
If the casualty has a fractured lower extremity, do not place the casualty in the shock position until the fracture has been splinted.

heading: FOOD OR DRINK
text: When providing first aid for shock, DO NOT give the casualty any food or drink. If you must leave the casualty or if they are unconscious, turn their head to the side (see figure 7-2) to prevent them from choking, if they vomit.

heading: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR CIRCULATION CONTROL
text: Tier 2 skills for this section specifically address the crucial aspect of circulation control. Emphasizing the need for rapid and appropriate interventions to prevent further harm and optimize the chances of survival for wounded Service members. Circulation control involves techniques and procedures aimed at managing bleeding and vascular injuries. These are often encountered in high-stakes and dynamic combat environments.

heading: PELVIC FRACTURES
text:
Pelvic fractures can be a cause of massive internal bleeding and impact circulation, which is the "C" in the MARCH-PAWS sequence. A pelvic fracture may be suspected if the casualty's injuries are a result of blunt force or blast trauma with one or more of the following:
- Pelvic pain.
- Major lower-limb amputation or lower-limb near amputations.
- Pelvic deformities, penetrating injuries, or bruising near the pelvis.
- Pelvic instability or crepitus, which is a crinkly, grating feeling, or sound under the skin.
- Unconsciousness or shock.

heading: PELVIC FRACTURES
text: If a pelvic fracture is suspected, the casualty will require advanced evaluation by medical personnel, and you should notify medical personnel of the potential for a pelvic fracture as soon as possible.

heading: PRESSURE BANDAGE REASSESSMENT
text: The regular reassessment of pressure bandages is crucial in managing wounds effectively. The CLS are tasked with ensuring that there is no ongoing bleeding from the wound site. Additionally, it's important to check for circulation below the pressure bandage by feeling for a distal pulse--that is, a pulse found below the level of the bandage.

heading: PRESSURE BANDAGE REASSESSMENT
text: If the skin below the bandage is cool, bluish, numb, or if the distal pulse is absent, these may be signs that the bandage is applied too tightly, potentially hindering blood flow. In such cases, the bandage should be loosened and then securely retied to ensure proper circulation is restored.

heading: PRESSURE BANDAGE REASSESSMENT
text: All dressings and bandages must be checked routinely, especially every time a casualty is moved. This practice helps to monitor the effectiveness of the initial treatment and to make timely adjustments as needed.

heading: PRESSURE BANDAGE REASSESSMENT
text: In situations where a pressure bandage or hemostatic dressing fails to control bleeding, a TQ should be applied approximately two to three inches above the site of bleeding, if feasible. If placing a TQ is not possible and the existing bandage is either ineffective or saturated with blood, replace it with a fresh hemostatic dressing. Ensure to pack the wound thoroughly with the hemostatic material, applying constant, direct pressure at the bleeding source for optimal effectiveness.

heading: EXPEDIENT TECHNIQUES FOR CIRCULATION CONTROL
text: Medical personnel may not always be readily available. Nonmedical personnel must rely on themselves, other Service members' knowledge, fundamentals of first aid for circulation control, until medical assistance arrives. This section will provide additional first aid, non-TCCC, procedures that nonmedical personnel can use for circulation control.

heading: TECHNIQUES FOR NON-MEDICAL PERSONNEL
text: When medical personnel are not immediately available, non-medical personnel must depend on themselves and the knowledge of other Service members. The fundamentals of first aid for controlling circulation are crucial until professional medical help arrives. This section aims to provide essential, non- TCCC first aid procedures that non-medical personnel can use effectively to maintain circulation control.

heading: TECHNIQUES FOR NON-MEDICAL PERSONNEL
text: Non-medical personnel are often the first responders in critical situations, making it essential for them to be familiar with basic first aid techniques. Understanding and applying these methods can be lifesaving when delays in professional medical treatment occur. Training in these expedient techniques empowers individuals to act confidently and efficiently, providing critical care in emergencies.

heading: TECHNIQUES FOR NON-MEDICAL PERSONNEL
text: The guidance provided here includes several key first aid actions that non-medical personnel can take to manage circulation issues effectively. These include methods to minimize bleeding, stabilize the affected individual, and prepare for the arrival of medical professionals. Each technique has been chosen for its simplicity and effectiveness, ensuring that those with minimal medical training can apply them under pressure.

heading: TECHNIQUES FOR NON-MEDICAL PERSONNEL
text: It is vital for all personnel, especially those in high-risk environments, to be trained in these techniques. Such training ensures that every member of a team can provide essential care in emergencies, enhancing overall safety and increasing the likelihood of positive outcomes in critical situations.

heading: TREATMENT FOR ANAPHYLACTIC SHOCK
text: Anaphylactic shock is a severe and life-threatening allergic reaction that significantly impacts the circulatory system. This medical emergency is marked by a swift release of histamines and other chemicals into the body, leading to vasodilation and increased permeability in blood vessels. Such changes can disrupt the adequate perfusion of vital organs and tissues, putting the casualty's life at great risk.

heading: TREATMENT FOR ANAPHYLACTIC SHOCK
text: Vasodilation, a key feature of anaphylactic shock, involves the relaxation of smooth muscle cells within blood vessel walls, causing these vessels to widen and blood pressure to drop significantly. This physiological process can rapidly deteriorate the casualty's condition.

heading: TREATMENT FOR ANAPHYLACTIC SHOCK
text: The treatment of anaphylactic shock is urgent and time sensitive. Immediate actions include calling for medical help and, if available, using the casualty's epinephrine auto-injector. Anaphylactic reactions can manifest within seconds or minutes after exposure to an allergen, affecting the skin, respiratory, and circulatory systems.

heading: TREATMENT FOR ANAPHYLACTIC SHOCK
text: Prompt recognition and response to anaphylactic shock are critical. Assessing both the signs and symptoms early on is essential for effective intervention. Quick and accurate identification of the condition allows for the necessary steps to be taken to mitigate its life-threatening effects.

heading: TREATMENT FOR ANAPHYLACTIC SHOCK
text:
To effectively check for anaphylactic shock, Service members should follow a systematic approach:
- Assess Symptoms:
- Observe for sudden and severe symptoms like difficulty breathing, wheezing, or shortness of breath.
- Check for a rapid or weak pulse.
- Look for swelling of the face, lips, or tongue.
- Note any hives or widespread skin redness.
- Be alert to signs of confusion, dizziness, or loss of consciousness.
- Ask Questions:
- Inquire about any known allergies or recent exposures to potential allergens.
- Ask if they have ingested or come into contact with a known allergen recently.
- Observe Breathing:
- Check for signs of respiratory distress, such as rapid or labored breathing.
- Listen for wheezing or other abnormal breathing sounds.
- Check Circulation:
- Assess the pulse to determine its rate and strength.
- Look for signs of poor circulation, such as pale or bluish skin.
- Look for Other Symptoms:
- Be aware of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or a feeling of impending doom.

heading: TREATMENT FOR ANAPHYLACTIC SHOCK
text: If anaphylactic shock is suspected, immediate medical assistance is crucial. The primary treatment involves administering epinephrine (adrenaline). If an epinephrine auto-injector is available, assist the affected individual in using it, or administer it yourself if you are allowed and trained. Dosage guidelines are typically provided with the injector--0.15 milligrams (mg) for children and 0.3 mg for adults weighing more than 66 pounds.

heading: TREATMENT FOR ANAPHYLACTIC SHOCK
text:
Further doses of epinephrine may be necessary, administered every 5 to 10 minutes if prescribed and symptoms persist. Additionally, provide supportive measures for treating shock, respiratory failure, circulatory collapse, or cardiac arrest:
- Position the casualty supine with legs elevated if injuries permit.
- Perform rescue breathing and external chest compressions if required.
- Monitor vital signs every three to five minutes until the casualty is stable.

heading: TREATMENT FOR ANAPHYLACTIC SHOCK
text: Record all first aid actions on DD Form 1380 and request MEDEVAC immediately. Use CASEVAC only if MEDEVAC is unavailable and transport the casualty to the nearest MTF as soon as possible. Anaphylaxis is life-threatening, and immediate action is crucial. Seek professional medical help promptly and provide supportive care while awaiting arrival of medical personnel.

heading: OVERVIEW OF HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
text: The "H" in MARCH-PAWS stands for hypothermia prevention. Hypothermia begins when the body's core temperature drops below 97 degrees Fahrenheit (F). It can be mild (93-96 degrees F), moderate (89-93 degrees F), or severe (less than 89 degrees F), depending on the temperature. To accurately diagnose hypothermia, the core temperature must be measured rectally with a special low-range thermometer, as mouth and ear measurements won't work well in cold environments.

heading: OVERVIEW OF HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
text: Hypothermia can be caused by being in a cold environment or by losing a lot of blood, a condition known as hypovolemia. This is when there's a significant drop in the volume of blood circulating in the body. Both environmental exposure and loss of blood can lead to dangerously low body temperatures, which can be life-threatening if not treated.

heading: OVERVIEW OF HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
text: Environmental hypothermia happens when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it, often from being in cold weather for too long. Hypothermia from hypovolemic shock happens due to a large loss of blood or fluids, making it hard for the body to keep warm. Both causes can lead to serious health issues, including death, if not managed quickly.

heading: OVERVIEW OF HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
text: Hypothermia can happen suddenly, like from falling into cold water, or slowly, if someone is exposed to cold conditions for a long time. It can even happen in mild temperatures if a person is wet, which makes it easier to lose body heat. Factors like wet clothing, not enough food, exhaustion, and drinking alcohol or using drugs can make hypothermia worse.

heading: OVERVIEW OF HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
text: Massive bleeding can cause hypothermia, which in turn can cause more bleeding because cold temperatures can prevent blood from clotting properly. This is a problem even in warm weather, and especially for people in shock who can't generate enough body heat. It's crucial to stop this cycle to save the person's life.

heading: SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS OF HYPOTHERMIA
text:
In the TFC phase of care, the focus has shifted from immediate life-threatening hemorrhage control during CUF phase, to the reassessment of all previous interventions. This is followed by the prevention and treatment of other injuries and complications such as hypothermia. It is important to identify the signs of hypothermia. Some easily recognizable signs of hypothermia are:
- Vigorous shivering is typically present.
- Shivering may decrease or cease as the core temperature continues to fall.
- Conscious, but usually apathetic or lethargic.
- Confusion.
- Sleepiness.
- Slurred speech or mumbling.
- Slow breathing and drowsiness.
- Weak pulse.
- Low or unattainable blood pressure.
- Change in behavior with or without poor control over body movements, and with or without slow reactions.

heading: SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS OF HYPOTHERMIA
text:
The signs and symptoms of hypothermia may vary depending on the severity and can be categorized into mild, moderate, and severe stages:
- Mild Hypothermia:
- Shivering.
- Cold and pale skin.
- Numbness or tingling in extremities.
- Fatigue and drowsiness.
- Slurred speech.
- Impaired coordination and fine motor skills.
- Moderate Hypothermia:
- Intense shivering or shivering stops.
- Difficulty in speaking and thinking clearly.
- Clumsiness and lack of coordination.
- Cold, pale, or blue-gray skin.
- Slow breathing and heart rate.
- Weak pulse.
- Severe Hypothermia:
- Shivering may stop completely.
- Confusion and disorientation.
- Loss of consciousness.
- Very cold, pale, or bluish skin.
- Slow or irregular breathing.
- Weak or absent pulse.

heading: FIRST AID FOR HYPOTHERMIA
text: The goals for first aid for hypothermia are to rescue, examine, insulate, and rapidly transport. If untreated, hypothermia is a true medical emergency and requires evacuation. Evacuate as soon as possible with the casualty lying down.

notices.text: Do not allow the casualty to use tobacco, consume alcohol, or caffeinated drinks.

heading: FIRST AID FOR HYPOTHERMIA
text:
Re-warming techniques include--
- Remove the casualty from the cold environment.
- Replace wet clothing with dry clothing.
- Cover the casualty with insulating material or blanket.
- Wrap the casualty from head to toe.
- Avoid unnecessary movement from the casualty.
- If the casualty is conscious, slowly give high caloric sweet warm fluids.
- Seek medical aid.

heading: FIRST AID FOR HYPOTHERMIA
text: Hypothermia is a serious condition that requires professional evaluation and treatment. Attempting to rewarm a severely hypothermic person should be done by medical professionals using appropriate techniques. While waiting for help to arrive, focus on preventing further heat loss and providing support to the person.

heading: PREVENTION OF HYPOTHERMIA
text: Preventing hypothermia is critical in reducing the effects of heat loss and preventing deaths from uncontrolled bleeding. Immediate action to prevent hypothermia should commence right after an injury occurs. Without preventative measures, there is a real risk that a casualty may succumb to hemorrhage from a wound that could otherwise be survivable. As blood loss itself can lead to hypothermia, it is vital for first responders and CLS to control bleeding and actively engage in both passive and active measures to prevent the casualty's body temperature from dropping.

heading: PREVENTION OF HYPOTHERMIA
text: The quicker hypothermia prevention begins, the less severe its impact will be on the casualty's bleeding and potential shock. Minimizing exposure to the elements is essential. Actions such as replacing wet clothing with dry ones and placing the casualty on an insulated surface should be prioritized. Environmental factors such as daily temperature fluctuations, nightfall, changes in altitude, and wind exposure must also be considered as they can significantly affect body heat retention.

heading: PREVENTION OF HYPOTHERMIA
text: Prevention of hypothermia is far more manageable than treating it once it has set in. Starting hypothermia prevention measures early is crucial because a decreased body temperature can adversely affect blood clotting processes, heightening the risk of continued bleeding--even in warm conditions.

heading: PREVENTION OF HYPOTHERMIA
text: CLS personnel must be proactive in assuming that every casualty is at risk of developing hypothermia, utilizing all known prevention techniques. If a casualty is already hypothermic, the response should be even more aggressive, treating the condition as a direct threat to the casualty's life.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF HYPOTHERMIA
text: To prevent hypothermia, it is essential to keep the casualty warm, even in very hot environments. This is particularly crucial when a casualty is suffering from hemorrhagic shock due to blood loss, as they are at an extreme risk for developing hypothermia. Both active and passive methods should be employed to ensure the casualty's body temperature is maintained. This involves proactive measures such as providing thermal blankets, using heat packs, and minimizing exposure to cold or windy conditions. Maintaining warmth not only aids in preventing hypothermia but also helps stabilize the casualty's overall condition.

heading: EQUIPMENT USED FOR HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
text: The hypothermia control equipment falls into either active warming (external source of heat) or passive warming blankets, or a poncho liner to treat or prevent hypothermia. The most common equipment seen is the hypothermia prevention and management kit, blankets, or ponchos.

heading: ACTIVE HYPOTHERMIA MANAGEMENT AND MATERIAL
text: Medical personnel will distribute active hypothermia blankets based on the unit mission and load. Active hypothermia blankets are activated when their heating elements are exposed to air and can produce temperatures reaching 104 degrees F for up to eight hours. Active hypothermia blankets are applied to a casualty who cannot generate their own heat, but not directly on their skin, because the activated blankets can cause burns.

heading: ACTIVE HYPOTHERMIA MANAGEMENT AND MATERIAL
text: Apply the active warming blanket from the active hypothermia materials to the casualty's torso, not directly on the skin, and cover the casualty with the passive hypothermia shell. Continue to reassess the casualty to determine if additional methods are needed to prevent or treat hypothermia. The heat reflective shell will help to retain the heat produced by the ready-heat blanket. It has an incorporated hood and Velcro closures down each side to allow exposure of an arm or a leg. Such exposure allows the medic to attend to IVs and TQs.

heading: ACTIVE HYPOTHERMIA MANAGEMENT AND MATERIAL
text: If an active hypothermia device is not available, a combination of the passive warming blanket and active warming blanket may be used. Active hypothermia treatment uses heating sources such as the readyheat blanket to warm the casualty. This requires a chemical reaction with oxygen, so at higher altitudes there may not be enough oxygen to sustain the chemical reaction required to generate heat.

heading: ACTIVE HYPOTHERMIA MANAGEMENT AND MATERIAL
text: You must determine based on the environmental conditions whether the casualty needs both the outer shell and the heating blanket. It is sufficient to just keep them covered with the shell, because it is already hot outside.

heading: ACTIVE HYPOTHERMIA MANAGEMENT AND MATERIAL
text: If no active rewarming equipment is available, then use passive warming devices that will retain heat and keep the casualty dry. The casualty should be assessed for hemorrhagic shock and ensure bleeding is controlled.

notices.text: Active warming is contraindicated in a casualty who is showing signs and symptoms of hyperthermia from heat related illness.

heading: PASSIVE HYPOTHERMIA MANAGEMENT AND MATERIAL
text: Passive hypothermia blankets are designed to retain the casualty's body heat by enclosing them within a thermal barrier, keeping them off the cold ground. While passive strategies prevent further cooling, they do not actively warm the casualty. Therefore, it's critical to avoid placing the casualty directly onto cold, wet, or damp surfaces; instead, a blanket or poncho should be positioned underneath them to provide insulation. In the absence of specialized re-warming equipment, dry blankets, poncho liners, sleeping bags, or similar items should be used to retain heat and keep the casualty dry and elevated from the ground.

heading: PASSIVE HYPOTHERMIA MANAGEMENT AND MATERIAL
text: Key considerations include recognizing that blood loss can significantly reduce body temperature, even in warmer climates. When using a blanket or any passive heating material, it is crucial to wrap the casualty completely, including their head, but ensure the face remains uncovered to prevent breathing obstructions. Leaving any part of the body exposed can result in heat loss and worsen hypothermia. These measures are vital in managing a hypothermic casualty, especially in the absence of active warming tools.

heading: TIER 1 SKILLS USED FOR HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
text:
The first responder must prevent, and address hypothermia compounded by massive blood loss. This is not hypothermia due to cold weather, but can be prevented by--
- Keeping clothing or uniform on the casualty.
- Replacing extremely wet clothing if possible and keeping the casualty dry.
- Keeping the casualty off the ground, by placing a barrier between the casualty and the ground or lifting them off the ground, if possible. Note. Contact with the ground increases loss of body heat.
- Using dry blankets, poncho liners, sleeping bags, or anything that will retain heat.
- Minimizing the casualty's exposure to the environment.

heading: TIER 2 SKILLS USED FOR HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
text: The Tier 2 TCCC skills emphasize advanced yet practical approaches to managing battlefield casualties under hypothermic conditions. Personnel trained in Tier 2 TCCC are equipped with the knowledge and skills to effectively use available medical equipment to prevent and treat hypothermia. This includes the application of specialized gear such as hypothermia prevention and management kits, which are designed to maintain body temperature and prevent further heat loss in injured soldiers. In addition, Tier 2 personnel are trained to monitor vital signs closely, ensuring that the core body temperature is maintained within a safe range, thereby reducing the risk of hypothermia-related complications.

heading: EXPEDIENT SKILLS USED FOR HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
text: In situations where standard medical supplies are not available, field expedient techniques for hypothermia control become crucial. Soldiers are taught to use their environment and available resources to prevent and manage hypothermia. For instance, using space blankets or even regular blankets to wrap the victim can significantly reduce heat loss. If these are not available, utilizing materials such as leaves, grass, or even newspapers as insulation can be a life-saving improvisation. Creating a barrier between the victim and the cold ground, such as with a sleeping pad, backpack, or any available material, can also prevent further body heat loss. These improvised methods are essential skills in TCCC, enabling soldiers to provide effective hypothermia care even in resource-limited settings.

heading: SYMPTOMS, AND TREATMENTS
text: As discussed in paragraph 3-96 on page 39, PAWS is the second part of the MARCH-PAWS casualty assessment and is conducted after the MARCH portion. The MIST reporting was introduced as a standard component of the MEDEVAC request during Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan.

heading: SYMPTOMS, AND TREATMENTS
text: While not officially part of the NATO and U.S. standard MEDEVAC request, MIST reporting has become customary in some operations. Often referred to as the 10th line in the 9-line MEDEVAC request, the completed DD Form 1380 serves as the MIST report. However, the high volume of casualties expected during large scale combat operations may make it challenging to complete MIST reporting for each casualty.

heading: SYMPTOMS, AND TREATMENTS
text: The MIST report facilitates the transfer of medical information to the receiving health care provider by providing a structured approach to the casualty handoff. A MIST report delivers additional evacuation information that might be required by theater commanders and assists the receiving MTF in preparing for specific inbound casualties. However, transmitting a MIST report for each casualty during operations and mass casualty incidents may not always be timely or feasible.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF PAIN AND ANTIBIOTICS
text: The combat wound medication pack (CWMP) is both the "P" (pain) and the "A" (antibiotics) in the MARCH-PAWS sequence. Pain is common with battlefield injuries. Some injuries and levels of pain can be treated safely by using pain medications (also known as analgesics) in the CWMP. These include fractures, burns, and eye injuries.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF PAIN AND ANTIBIOTICS
text: The CWMP is a prepackaged medication packet with drugs and dosages specifically chosen for use in combat casualty care. The CWMP contains drugs for mild to moderate pain (Meloxicam and Acetaminophen) and an antibiotic specific for penetrating wounds (Moxifloxacin). The CWMP should be used only for combat related injuries and is not for routine use. It may be procured through medical logistics systems as a prepackaged blister pack or, may be locally packaged by medical personnel.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF PAIN AND ANTIBIOTICS
text: For pain relief on the battlefield of mild to moderate pain that will not keep the casualty out of the fight, ensure they take their CWMP. The casualty should take all three medications in the CWMP. This can give significant pain relief and will not alter the casualty's mental status. This is a good option when the casualty's pain and wounds are not severe enough to keep them out of the fight. Note. If the casualty has wounds or pain severe enough to render them unable to fight, then medical personnel have other options for more effective pain relief. The medications given by medical personnel will generally require that the casualty be disarmed because the medications can alter the casualty's mental status.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF PAIN AND ANTIBIOTICS
text: CWMP is a prepackaged pill pack containing CoTCCC-recommended medications for use in combat casualty care. The CWMP is found in the casualty's first aid kit. It contains medications for pain and antibiotics that can be taken by mouth.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF PAIN AND ANTIBIOTICS
text: The medication in the CWMP should be taken as soon as possible after life-threatening conditions have been addressed. All medications administered should be documented along with the time given on the DD Form 1380.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF PAIN AND ANTIBIOTICS
text:
The CWMP contains the following components:
- Two 500mg caplets of acetaminophen (total 1,000mg) in extended-release form.
- One 400mg tablet of moxifloxacin.
- One 15mg tablet of meloxicam.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF PAIN AND ANTIBIOTICS
text: Each of the three medications in these dosages is contained in a blister pack. Note. The popular nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin interfere with platelet function and blood clotting and can significantly increase the risk of bleeding in combat casualties.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF PAIN AND ANTIBIOTICS
text: Acetaminophen and meloxicam do not alter platelet function and are safe and effective for use in combat casualties. Meloxicam does not alter platelet function and is the preferred Non-Steroidal Anti- Inflammatory Drug for personnel who may see combat in the next 7-10 days.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF PAIN AND ANTIBIOTICS
text:
The CWMP should be given when the casualty:
- Is conscious and able to swallow.
- It has mild to moderate pain.
- Is still able to fight if needed.
- Has any penetrating wounds or break of the skin.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF PAIN AND ANTIBIOTICS
text:
The CWMP should NOT be given if the casualty:
- Is unable to swallow or take oral meds, such as when the casualty is unconscious, or has severe facial trauma, or burns.
- Has known allergies to the CWMP medications.
- If the casualty is unconscious, refer them to medical personnel as soon as possible. Note. If the casualty has a break in the skin in a traumatic injury, they should take the CWMP. Otherwise, consult with medical personnel before giving it.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF PAIN AND ANTIBIOTICS
text: Battlefield wounds are often dirty and susceptible to infection. Early administration of antibiotics from the CWMP may reduce the chance of later infections. Wound infections can kill the casualty or delay their recovery. The CWMP should be given as soon as possible for wounds after life-threatening issues have been addressed.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF WOUNDS
text: Beyond MARCH, there are additional or secondary injuries that should be identified and may need treatment. The secondary injuries identified in TCCC are organized by eye trauma, head injury, burns, and fractures. These secondary injuries are treated in TFC.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF WOUNDS
text: Wound management is the "W" in the MARCH-PAWS sequence. Once the casualty's hemorrhage has been controlled, earlier control interventions are completed, and wound management must be rechecked. All wounds must be frequently reassessed to ensure continued hemorrhage control.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF WOUNDS
text:
The first responder or CLS should confirm all wounds have been addressed and reassess for re-bleeding under gauze or bandages to ensure bleeding has been controlled. The first responder or CLS must look for blood flowing around or under TQs, bandages, and dressings. If the bleeding has not been controlled, tighten the TQ or pressure bandage for that wound if possible, and redress any wounds as necessary. Also, check other wounds to make sure that:
- Eye injuries are shielded.
- Open chest wounds are accounted for.
- All wounds are wrapped.
- Fractures are splinted.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF WOUNDS
text: Wounds should always be monitored and frequently reassessed to ensure hemorrhage has been controlled. Any wounds that continue to bleed must be packed with new hemostatic dressing. Once the dressing has been applied with pressure for three minutes, carefully observe for blood continuing to flow from under the gauze to determine if bleeding has been controlled. When the bleeding has stopped, a new pressure bandage should be applied over the hemostatic dressing.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF WOUNDS
text: Any previously untreated wounds should be dressed by applying (or packing) gauze with direct pressure. Non-life-threatening bleeding usually does not need hemostatic dressing. If dressings or gauze are not available, use clean, dry cloth such as torn clothing, or a cravat if available.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF WOUNDS
text:
Minor wounds include minor lacerations and abrasions, such as road rashes. Other wounds that may need to be dressed include major wounds that are no longer bleeding, such as:
- Amputation stumps.
- Gunshot wounds that required a TQ.
- Major lacerations.
- Shrapnel wounds, possibly with shrapnel still in place.
- Impaled objects.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF WOUNDS
text:
Applied pressure bandages must be continuously reassessed for:
- Increased pain.
- Skin color.
- Loss of the pulse.

heading: MANAGEMENT OF WOUNDS
text: If any of the above develops, it might indicate an emergency. Ensure that the applied bandage isn't too tight and loosen it as needed while keeping the bleeding controlled. Note. Pulses are reassessed after dressings are placed to ensure that they are not too tight. Do not ever apply a dressing and forget it! This page intentionally left blank.

heading: OVERVIEW OF EYE TRAUMA
text: The eye is a vital sensory organ, and blindness is a severe physical handicap. Timely first aid for eye injuries may relieve pain and may help prevent shock, permanent eye injury, and possible loss of vision. The eye is very sensitive: any injury can be easily aggravated if it is improperly handled. Injuries in the eye may be quite severe. Cuts of the eyelids can appear to be very serious, but if the eyeball is not involved, a person's vision usually will not be damaged. However, lacerations (cuts) of the eyeball can cause permanent damage or loss of sight.

heading: OVERVIEW OF EYE TRAUMA
text:
Exposure to intense light can burn an individual. Infrared rays, eclipse light (if the casualty has looked directly at the sun), or laser burns cause injuries of the exposed eyeball. Ultraviolet (UV) rays from arc welding can cause a superficial burn to the surface of the eye. These injuries are generally not painful but may cause permanent damage to the eyes. Immediate first aid is usually not required. Loosely bandaging the eyes may make the casualty more comfortable and protect their eyes from further injury caused by exposure to other bright lights or sunlight. Eyesight is one of our most important senses. Damage to an eye can be irreversible if not treated correctly and as early as possible. The following signs should make you suspect a penetrating eye injury:
- Bleeding surrounding the eye, inside the eyeball, or coming from the eyeball.
- Obvious penetration of shrapnel or debris into the eyeball or eye socket.
- Protruding objects from the globe of the eyeball.
- Swelling or lacerations of the globe of the eyeball.
- Protrusion of the globe of the eyeball from the eye socket.
- Reduced vision and swelling of the eye area.
- Misshapen or distorted parts of the eye from normal.

heading: EQUIPMENT USED FOR THE TREATMENT OF EYE TRAUMA
text:
The rigid eye shield is a barrier to environmental hazards and to protect the eye by providing a safe enclosure, until additional medical attention is available. The rigid eye shield is normally plastic or metallic, with a domed shape to enhance the protection of eye injuries, without applying pressure. It may be selfadhering or require tape. If a rigid eye shield is not available, or already used, the following may be used as an improvised or expedient rigid eye shield:
- Protective glasses.
- Clean cup.
- Dip can.

heading: EQUIPMENT USED FOR THE TREATMENT OF EYE TRAUMA
text: The Military Acute Concussion Evaluation 2 Card is an acute assessment tool for all medically trained personnel who treat Service members involved in a potentially concussive event. The Military Acute Concussion Evaluation 2 incorporates current state-of-the-science traumatic brain injury information, which looks at the systems in charge of integrating balance, vision, and movement.

heading: TIER 1 SKILLS USED TO TREAT EYE TRAUMA
text: If a penetrating eye injury is seen or suspected, the first responder must shield the injured eye. The casualties injured eye must be covered with a rigid eye shield, not a pressure patch. In typical situations, a concave shield is placed over the injured eye, (not both eyes), and taped in place. If there is a protruding object in the eye, bandage in place -- do not remove the object. Do not waste critical time by conducting further treatment. The casualty should be evacuated as soon as possible.

notices.text: DO NOT apply pressure to the injured eye.

heading: TIER 1 SKILLS USED TO TREAT EYE TRAUMA
text: The rigid eye shield is secured over the injured eye with tape at a 45-degree angle across the forehead and cheek. Rigid eye shields should be placed over both eyes only when you are sure and at least suspect that both eyes have been injured. If a rigid eye shield is not available, tactical eyewear may be used to protect the eyes from further trauma.

heading: TIER 1 SKILLS USED TO TREAT EYE TRAUMA
text: When only one eye has been injured, do not place a shield over the uninjured eye to prevent eye movement. Movement has not been shown to worsen the outcome for the injured eye. Blindness, resulting from placing eye shields over both eyes unnecessarily, makes an otherwise ambulatory casualty a litter casualty, and is psychologically stressful. The first responder should be prepared to render first aid for lacerations of the eyelid, foreign bodies in the eye, extrusions of the eye, and chemical burns of the eye.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR LACERATIONS OF THE EYELID OR EYEBALL WITH EYE-SHIELD
text: Lacerated or torn eyelids may bleed heavily, but bleeding usually stops quickly. Cover the injured eye with a sterile dressing. DO NOT put pressure on the wound because you may injure the eyeball. Handle torn eyelids very carefully to prevent further injury. Place any detached pieces of the eyelid on a clean bandage or dressing and immediately send them with the casualty to the medical facility.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR LACERATIONS OF THE EYELID OR EYEBALL WITH EYE-SHIELD
text: Lacerations or cuts to the eyeball may cause serious and permanent eye damage. Cover the injury with a loose sterile dressing. DO NOT put pressure on the eyeball because additional damage may occur.

notices.text: DO NOT apply pressure when there is a possible laceration of the eyeball. The eyeball contains fluid. Pressure applied over the eye will force the fluid out, resulting in permanent injury. APPLY A PROTECTIVE DRESSING WITHOUT ADDED PRESSURE.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR LACERATIONS OF THE EYELID OR EYEBALL WITH EYE-SHIELD
text: Survey the situation; if the injury is from chemical exposure, immediately wash the eye. Otherwise, DO NOT put anything on the eye ITSELF, especially if you think the eye is cut.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR LACERATIONS OF THE EYELID OR EYEBALL WITH EYE-SHIELD
text:
If necessary, remove the casualty's headgear. Position and treat the casualty as follows:
- The conscious casualty will be placed in a seated position.
- The unconscious casualty will be placed in a supine position with their head slightly elevated.
- Gently clean any dirt or blood from the affected area around the eye.

notices.text: DO NOT put pressure on the eye or remove anything from the eye surface. This could cause additional harm, such as loss of eyesight or loss of the eye.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR LACERATIONS OF THE EYELID OR EYEBALL WITH EYE-SHIELD
text:
Examine the eyes for the following:
- Objects protruding from the eyes.
- Look for foreign objects in or on the eyes and damage to the eyes.
- Swelling or lacerations of the eyes.
- Bloodshot appearance of the white of the eyes.
- Bleeding--
- Surrounding the eye.
- From inside the eyeball.
- Coming from the eyeball.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR LACERATIONS OF THE EYELID OR EYEBALL WITH EYE-SHIELD
text: Ask the casualty if they are wearing contact lenses, but DO NOT force the eyelids open. Record and communicate to medical personnel (first responders, emergency medical technicians, or combat medics) that contact lenses are being worn.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR LACERATIONS OF THE EYELID OR EYEBALL WITH EYE-SHIELD
text:
Categorize the injury as follows:
- Injury to the tissue surrounding the eye (lacerations and contusions).
- Injury to the eyeball.
- Extrusion (the eye is protruding out of the eye socket).
- Foreign bodies.
- Protruding (impaled) objects. Note. Torn eyelids should be handled carefully. Wrap any fragments in a separate moist dressing and evacuate with the casualty.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR LACERATIONS OF THE EYELID OR EYEBALL WITH EYE-SHIELD
text:
Provide first aid for the injury as follows:
- Control bleeding with light pressure from a dressing.

notices.text:
Pressure is used for orbital injuries, DO NOT use any pressure if injury to the eyeball itself is suspected. Injuries to the eye itself require an immediate covering with an eye shield.
- Gently clean any dirt or blood from the affected area around the eye.
- Cover the eyelid with the rigid eye-shield provided in the first aid kit, or anything that provides a hard cover over the eye such as--
- Eye protective gear, ballistic glasses, or goggles.
- The bottom of a disposable cup for example, one made of extruded polystyrene (foam), plastic, or paper. Note. This helps prevent any undue pressure or further damage to the eye.
- Secure the shield by applying tape from the cheek to the forehead (figure 10-1 on page 100). If no tape is available, use gauze, cloth dressing, shoelace, or string to secure in place.
ALWAYS use a rigid eye-shield to provide a barrier to prevent further damage. NEVER place anything under the rigid eye-shield or directly on the eye.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR LACERATIONS OF THE EYELID OR EYEBALL WITH EYE-SHIELD
text: Preserve any avulsed (detached) skin or tissue in a clean sterile gauze soaked in saline (if available) and transport it with the casualty for possible grafting.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR LACERATIONS OF THE EYELID OR EYEBALL WITH EYE-SHIELD
text:
While seeking CASEVAC or MEDEVAC:
- Do not cause further injury.
- Limit movements that could cause further injury to the eye.
- Do not administer medication to prevent coughing, sneezing, or vomiting.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR LACERATIONS OF THE EYELID OR EYEBALL WITH EYE-SHIELD
text: Consider giving the entire combat pill pack if medical treatment takes more than three hours from the time of injury and if giving the medication to the casualty does not cause nausea.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR LACERATIONS OF THE EYELID OR EYEBALL WITH EYE-SHIELD
text:
Record first aid administered on the DD Form 1380. Evacuate the casualty:
- On their back, with the head elevated and immobilized.
- With their corrective eyeglasses, even if they are broken.
- Ensure the casualty's personal belongings, such as identification and any critical medications, accompany them during evacuation.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR LACERATIONS OF THE EYELID OR EYEBALL WITH EYE-SHIELD
text: Do not cause further injury to the eye or casualty while waiting for evacuation. Provide assurance to the casualty and stay with the casualty until relieved by medical personnel or competent authority.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR FOREIGN BODIES IN THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: With impaled objects or significant sized foreign bodies, both eyes are usually bandaged to help secure the foreign body in the injured eye. In a battlefield environment, leave the uninjured eye uncovered so that the casualty can see.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR FOREIGN BODIES IN THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text:
Survey the situation, if the injury is from chemical exposure, immediately wash the eye. Otherwise, DO NOT put anything on the eye ITSELF, especially if you think the eye is cut. Examine the eyes as follows:
- Look at the eyes -- are the pupils equal and round?
- Look for bleeding or foreign bodies in the eye.

notices.text:
DO NOT put pressure on the eye or remove anything from the eye surface. This could cause additional harm, such as loss of an eye.
- Foreign bodies in the eye are treated by appropriate medical personnel or by the casualty if it can easily be removed (for example, a surface non-embedded material such as an eyelash or speck of dirt).

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR FOREIGN BODIES IN THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text:
Use the rigid eye-shield provided in the first aid kit, or anything that provides a hard cover over the eye, such as--
- Eye protective gear, ballistic glasses, or goggles.
- The bottom of a disposable cup, for example one made of extruded polystyrene (foam), plastic, or paper. Note. This helps prevent any undue pressure or further damage to the eye. DO NOT put any pressure on the eye.
- Secure the rigid eye-shield by applying tape from the cheek to the forehead. If tape is unavailable, use gauze, cloth dressing, shoelace, or string to secure in place. Note. In hazardous conditions (such as combat or unsure footing), leave the good eye uncovered long enough to ensure the casualty's safety.

notices.text: Removing foreign bodies from the eye is NOT a first aid procedure. Seek medical treatment.
DO NOT attempt to remove a foreign object stuck to or sticking into the eyeball. A medical officer (physician) must remove such objects.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR FOREIGN BODIES IN THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Apply dry sterile dressings to build around and support the object. This will help prevent further contamination and minimize movement of the object. Cover the injured eye with a paper cup or cardboard cone.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR FOREIGN BODIES IN THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Seek further medical aid immediately.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR FOREIGN BODIES IN THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text:
Obtain details about the injury--
- Source and type of foreign bodies if known.
- Whether the foreign bodies were windblown, or by what type of high-velocity mechanism.
- Time of onset and length of discomfort.
- Any previous injuries to the eye.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR FOREIGN BODIES IN THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text:
Do not cause additional injury to the eye--
- Do not probe for foreign bodies.
- Do not put pressure on the eyeball.
- Do not remove the impaled object.
- Limit movements that could cause further eye injury.
- Do not administer medication to prevent coughing, sneezing, or vomiting.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR FOREIGN BODIES IN THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Consider giving the entire combat pill pack if medical treatment takes more than three hours from the time of injury, and if giving the medication to the casualty does not cause nausea.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR FOREIGN BODIES IN THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Record the first aid administered and other information as required on the DD Form 1380 (provided in the first aid kit).

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR FOREIGN BODIES IN THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Do not cause further injury to the eye or casualty while waiting for evacuation. Provide assurance and stay with the casualty until relieved by medical personnel or competent authority.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR EXTRUSIONS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Service members may encounter casualties with severe eye injuries that include an extruded eyeball (eyeball out-of-socket). In such instances, you should gently cover the extruded eye with a loose moistened dressing and cover the unaffected eye. DO NOT bind or exert pressure on the injured eye while applying the dressing. Keep the casualty quiet, place them on their back, treat for shock, and evacuate them immediately.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR EXTRUSIONS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Survey the situation and remove or avoid hazards.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR EXTRUSIONS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Remove the casualty's headgear, if necessary.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR EXTRUSIONS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text:
Position a--
- Conscious casualty in a seated position.
- Reassure and inform the conscious casualty of the first aid steps that you are providing.
- Unconscious casualty lying on their back with their head slightly elevated.

notices.text: DO NOT put pressure on the eye or remove anything from the eye surface. This could cause additional harm, such as loss of eyesight or loss of the eye.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR EXTRUSIONS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text:
Examine the eyes for--
- Objects protruding from the eye or eyes.
- Swelling or lacerations of the eyes.
- Bloodshot appearance of the eyes.
- Bleeding--
- Surrounding the eye.
- From inside the eyeball.
- Coming from the eyeball.
- Contact lenses. Ask the casualty if they are wearing contact lenses, however, do not force the eyelids open.
- Extrusion (the eye is protruding from the socket).

notices.text: DO NOT attempt to reposition the eyeball or replace it in the eye socket.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR EXTRUSIONS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text:
Provide appropriate first aid for the injury as follows:
- Position the casualty face up.
- Cut a hole into several layers of dressing material and then moisten it. Use sterile or the cleanest water if available, preferably potable.
- Gently place the dressing so the injured eyeball protrudes through the hole, with minimal contact. Surround and protect the eyeball, minimizing the movement of the dressing. The dressing should be built up higher than the eyeball. Note. If available, place a paper cup or cone-shaped piece of cardboard over the eye. This material should not touch the eye. Do not apply pressure to the injury site. Apply roller gauze to hold the cup in place.
- The provided rigid eye-shield will not be deep enough to properly protect the eye extrusion injury.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR EXTRUSIONS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Call for medical aid immediately and arrange for MEDEVAC as soon as possible.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR EXTRUSIONS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text:
While calling for CASEVAC or MEDEVAC --
- Limit movements that could cause further eye injury.
- Do not administer medication to prevent coughing, sneezing, or vomiting.
- Consider giving the entire combat pill pack if medical treatment takes more than three hours from the time of injury, and if giving the medication to the casualty does not cause nausea.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR EXTRUSIONS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text:
Record first aid administered on the DD Form 1380. Evacuate the casualty:
- On their back, with the head elevated and immobilized.
- With their corrective eyeglasses, even if they are broken.
- Ensure the casualty's personal belongings, such as identification and any critical medications, accompany them during evacuation.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR EXTRUSIONS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Do not cause further injury to the eye or casualty while waiting for evacuation. Provide assurance and stay with the casualty until relieved by medical personnel or competent authority.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR CHEMICAL BURNS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Injuries from chemical burns require immediate first aid. Mainly acids or alkalis cause chemical burns. The first aid measures consist of flushing the eyes immediately with large amounts of water for at least 5 to 20 minutes, or as long as necessary to flush out the chemical and, once flushed, bandaging the eyes. If the burn is an acid burn, you should flush the eye for at least 5 to 10 minutes. If the burn is an alkali burn, you should flush the eye for at least 20 minutes. After the eye has been flushed, evacuate the casualty immediately.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR CHEMICAL BURNS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text:
When an individual suffers burns of the face from a fire, the eyes will close quickly due to extreme heat. This reaction is a natural reflex to protect the eyeballs; however, the eyelids remain exposed to possibly being burned. If a casualty receives burns of the eyelids or face--
- DO NOT apply dressing.
- DO NOT touch.
- SEEK medical assistance immediately.

notices.text: DO NOT attempt to force open the eyes with thermal burns.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR CHEMICAL BURNS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Reassure the casualty and quickly survey the situation.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR CHEMICAL BURNS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text:
Quickly identify the substance that the casualty was exposed to such as-- Note. Do not delay first aid to perform this step. Time is critical and the eyes must be irrigated as soon as possible.
- Alkali substances, which are the most dangerous of all substances are due to the penetrating factor. Common substances that contain the hydroxides of ammonia, lye, potassium, magnesium, and lime are--
- Fertilizers.
- Cleaning products such as drain cleaners, and oven cleaners.
- Plaster and cement.
- Acid substances are usually less severe than alkali burns. Common acids contain sulfuric, hydrochloric, nitric, acetic, chromic, and hydrofluoric acids are--
- Glass polish, vinegar, and nail polish remover.
- Automobile battery acid.
- Irritants and substances that have a neutral power of hydrogen tend to cause more discomfort to the eye. Examples of irritants that may cause this damage are--
- Most household detergents.
- Pepper spray.
- Smoke from burning chemicals or rubber.

notices.text: DO NOT put pressure on the eye or remove anything from the eye surface. This could cause additional harm, such as loss of eyesight or loss of the eye.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR CHEMICAL BURNS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text:
Check for the following signs and symptoms:
- Irritation.
- Pain and redness.
- Watering and tearing.
- Possible erosion of the corneal surface.
- Inability to keep the eye open.
- Swelling of the eyelid.
- Blurred vision.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR CHEMICAL BURNS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text:
Initiate first aid for the chemical burn as follows:
- IMMEDIATELY flood the eye with water.
- Keep irrigating the eye with running water from a faucet, low-pressure hose, bottle, cup, or intravenous setup (if available).
- Hold the irrigating tip 1 to 1 1/2 inches away from the casualty's eye or eyes, direct the irrigating solution gently from the inner eye (nearest the nose) to the outer eye (towards the ear) from the casualty's unaffected eye.
- Start the transport and continue washing out the eye or eyes for at least 20 minutes or until the casualty's arrival at the MTF.
- Dry the area around the eye or eyes by gently patting with gauze sponges or other appropriate clean material. Do not touch the casualty's eye.
- Cover the injured eye or eyes with the rigid eye-shield provided in the first aid kit, or an appropriate device that provides a hard cover over the eye such as:
- Eye protective gear, ballistic glasses, or goggles.
- The bottom of a disposable cup made of extruded polystyrene (foam), plastic, or paper.
- Secure the rigid eye-shield by applying tape from the cheek to the forehead. If tape is unavailable, use gauze, cloth dressing, shoelace, or string to secure in place. Note 1. In hostile environments (such as combat or unsure footing), the eyes may have to remain uncovered so the casualty can see getting away from danger. Note 2. Burned eyelids swell to protect the underlying eyes. The eyes should be protected with the rigid eye-shield to prevent further injury.

notices.text: ALWAYS use a rigid eye-shield to provide a barrier to prevent further damage. NEVER place anything under the shield or directly on the eye.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR CHEMICAL BURNS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Seeking MEDEVAC for the casualty.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR CHEMICAL BURNS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Do not cause further injury to the eye by limiting movement that could cause further eye injury. Do not administer medication that prevents coughing, sneezing, or vomiting.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR CHEMICAL BURNS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Consider giving the entire combat pill pack if medical treatment takes more than three hours from the time of injury, and if giving the medication to the casualty does not cause nausea.

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR CHEMICAL BURNS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Record the first aid given on the DD Form 1380 (provided in the first aid kit).

heading: INITIATE FIRST AID FOR CHEMICAL BURNS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD
text: Evacuate the casualty without causing further harm.

heading: TIER 2 SKILLS USED TO TREAT EYE TRAUMA
text:
If a penetrating eye injury is noted or suspected, four steps must be taken:
- Perform a rapid field test of visual acuity. Rapid visual acuity testing includes:
- Read print.
- Count fingers.
- Identity hand motion.
- Sense light perception.
- Cover the affected eye with a rigid eye shield, NOT a pressure patch. A pressure dressing could result in permanent loss of vision. Place a rigid eye shield on only one eye, unless both eyes are injured. Covering both eyes turns an otherwise ambulatory casualty into a litter casualty. Tactical eyewear is always a good way to prevent eye issues and can be used for protection if no eye shield is available.
- Administer the casualty's complete CWMP, including all the medications contained in it. One of the medications is 400mg of moxifloxacin, which can be administered to prevent infection.
- Document all findings and treatments on the casualty's DD Form 1380.

heading: TIER 2 SKILLS USED TO TREAT EYE TRAUMA
text: Pressure on the eye could force the interior contents of the eye out of the eyeball through a cut or laceration. For protruding or impaled objects extending past the eye shield, cut a hole in the eye shield to allow the object to fit through, and secure it in place. If the eye shield cannot be applied around the impaled object, then use an improvised eye shield to avoid pressure on the eye.

heading: EXPEDIENT SKILLS USED TO TREAT EYE TRAUMA
text:
There are several expedient skills that can be employed to provide immediate care for eye trauma. Eye trauma should always be evaluated and treated by a qualified medical professional as soon as possible. The following are some skills or techniques that may be used in the initial management of eye trauma:
- Protecting the eye: If there is a foreign object, such as debris or a penetrating object, near or embedded in the eye, it's crucial to prevent further injury. Avoid touching or rubbing the eye, as this can exacerbate the damage. Place a protective shield or cup over the eye, if available, to prevent accidental contact.
- Flushing the eye: If there are chemicals or irritants in the eye, use immediate and gentle irrigation with clean water, or saline solution can help flush out the substance. Tilt the head to the side and pour a gentle stream of fluid over the eye from the inner corner to the outer corner. Use a clean container or a commercially available eye wash bottle.
- Covering injuries: If there is a cut or laceration around the eye, apply a sterile dressing or clean cloth to cover the wound. Avoid applying pressure directly on the eye. Secure the dressing in place with a bandage or adhesive tape.
- Immobilizing the eye: If there is a suspected or evident fracture of the eye socket or orbit, it may be necessary to immobilize the eye to prevent further injury. Place a protective shield or a cup over the eye and use a bandage or tape to secure it in position. This can help stabilize the injured area until medical attention is available.
- Applying cold compresses: In cases of eye trauma accompanied by swelling or bruising, a cold compress can be applied gently over the closed eyelid. This can help reduce swelling and alleviate pain. Use a clean cloth or ice pack wrapped in a towel. Avoid placing ice directly on the skin.

heading: EXPEDIENT SKILLS USED TO TREAT EYE TRAUMA
text: The above expedient skills are meant to provide initial first aid and should not replace professional medical care. The casualty should be evacuated as soon as possible to supporting MTF to ensure a thorough evaluation and appropriate treatment for eye trauma.

heading: OVERVIEW OF HEAD INJURIES
text: Head injuries are a common concern that can occur due to accidents, falls, or sports-related incidents. When the head experiences a forceful impact, it can result in different types of injuries. Understanding head injuries can help Service members take the necessary precautions to protect themselves or others from potential harm. It is critically important to report findings of a head injury to medical personnel at the scene since a lack of rapid, and appropriate medical care can worsen the head injury, and the eventual outcome. Head trauma can be either blunt or penetrating. Head injuries can be broadly classified as open or closed head injuries.

heading: OPEN HEAD INJURY
text: An open head injury, also known as an open skull injury, is a type of injury that occurs when there is a break or penetration of the skull, exposing the brain to the external environment. It typically involves visible damage to the scalp, skull, or meninges (protective coverings of the brain). The signs and symptoms of an open head injury can vary depending on the severity and specific location of the injury. Open head injuries are considered medical emergencies. If an open head injury is suspected, it is crucial to seek immediate medical attention for evaluation, diagnosis, and appropriate treatment.

heading: OPEN HEAD INJURY
text:
The common signs and symptoms associated with an open head injury are:
- Visible head wound. An open head injury often involves a visible wound or laceration on the scalp or skull. There may be bleeding, or an open fracture where the bone is exposed.
- Profuse bleeding. Open head injuries can cause significant bleeding due to damage to blood vessels. Blood may be visible on the scalp, face, or in severe cases, there may be profuse bleeding from the head wound.
- Skull deformity. In some cases, an open head injury may cause a visible deformity or depression in the skull, indicating a skull fracture or bone displacement.
- Loss of consciousness. Depending on the severity of the injury, loss of consciousness can occur, ranging from a brief period to an extended duration.
- Clear fluid or blood drainage. Leakage of clear fluid (cerebrospinal fluid) or blood from the nose, ears, or wound can indicate a more severe injury and should be treated as an emergency.
- Severe headache. An intense and persistent headache is common following an open head injury.
- Nausea and vomiting. Feelings of nausea and vomiting may be present after an open head injury.
- Confusion and disorientation. The Service member may exhibit confusion, memory loss, difficulty concentrating, or may appear disoriented.
- Seizures. Seizures can occur after an open head injury, especially if the brain is directly affected.
- Changes in speech or vision. The person may have difficulties with speech, vision problems, double vision, or other sensory disturbances.
- Weaknesses or numbness. Weakness or numbness in certain body parts can be a sign of nerve damage resulting from the head injury.

heading: CLOSED HEAD INJURY
text: A closed head injury refers to trauma to the head that does not involve an open wound or penetration of the skull. Instead, the injury occurs internally, within the skull. Closed head injuries are often the result of blunt force impacts, falls, or accidents, where the brain is subjected to sudden acceleration, deceleration, or rotational forces. Concussions are the most common type of a closed head injury. Closed head injuries may not be obvious or detectable.

heading: CLOSED HEAD INJURY
text: Closed head injuries can range in severity from mild concussions to more severe forms, such as contusions, diffuse axonal injuries, or intracranial hemorrhages. It is essential to seek medical attention if a closed head injury is suspected, as the impact on the brain can have serious consequences and requires appropriate evaluation and management.

heading: CLOSED HEAD INJURY
text:
The signs and symptoms of a closed head injury can vary depending on the severity of the injury. Mild cases may be present with subtle symptoms, while more severe injuries can have immediate and pronounced effects. The common signs and symptoms associated with a closed head injury are:
- Headache or pressure in the head.
- Nausea and vomiting.
- Dizziness and balance problems.
- Confusion and disorientation.
- Memory loss or difficulty concentrating.
- Mood and behavior changes.
- Sensory changes, such as blurred vision, or ringing in the ears.
- Sensitivity to light and sound.
- Loss of consciousness (in severe cases).

heading: CLOSED HEAD INJURY
text: It is important to seek medical attention if any of these signs are present after a head injury, as they can indicate a range of severity from a mild concussion to more serious brain trauma. The above symptoms can occur immediately after the injury or may develop gradually over time. Symptoms may vary from person to person.

heading: CONCUSSIONS
text: A concussion is a type of traumatic brain injury that occurs when the brain experiences a sudden and forceful movement within the skull. It is typically caused by a blow, jolt, or bump to the head or body, which can disrupt the normal functioning of the brain.

heading: CONCUSSIONS
text: Concussions can occur in various situations, such as sports-related injuries, falls, motor vehicle accidents, or any other incident involving a significant impact to the head. Concussions can happen even without a direct impact to the head. The forceful movement or shaking of the body can still cause the brain to move inside the skull, leading to a concussion.

heading: CONCUSSIONS
text:
The primary characteristic of a concussion is a temporary disruption of brain function. Concussions may not always involve a loss of consciousness. In fact, most concussions occur without a person losing consciousness. Common symptoms of a concussion can include:
- Headache or pressure in the head.
- Dizziness or feeling lightheaded.
- Confusion or feeling mentally foggy.
- Memory problems or difficulty concentrating.
- Fatigue or feeling tired.
- Nausea or vomiting.
- Sensitivity to light or noise.
- Changes in sleep patterns.
- Irritability or changes in mood.
- Blurred vision or difficulty with balance.

heading: CONCUSSIONS
text: It's important to seek medical attention if a concussion is suspected, as health care professionals can evaluate the severity of the injury and provide appropriate guidance for recovery. The initial management of a concussion involves rest and avoiding activities that could further injure the brain. Physical and cognitive rest are recommended to allow the brain to heal properly. In some cases, individuals may need to temporarily limit activities like school or work to promote recovery. A gradual return to normal activities is typically recommended under the guidance of a health care professional.

heading: CONCUSSIONS
text: Every concussion is unique, and the symptoms and recovery time can vary from person to person. With proper rest, most individuals recover fully from a concussion. However, in some cases, symptoms may persist or worsen, and a condition known as post-concussion syndrome may develop.

heading: CONTUSIONS RELATED TO HEAD INJURIES
text: A contusion refers to a type of injury characterized by damage to the tissue or blood vessels beneath the skin, usually resulting from a blunt force impact. It is commonly known as a bruise. When a contusion occurs, blood vessels are damaged, leading to bleeding and the subsequent discoloration of the skin.

heading: CONTUSIONS RELATED TO HEAD INJURIES
text: In relation to head injuries, contusions can occur because of a direct blow or trauma to the head. When the head experiences a significant impact, the brain can collide with the inner surface of the skull, leading to contusions. These types of injuries are known as cerebral contusions.

heading: CONTUSIONS RELATED TO HEAD INJURIES
text: Cerebral contusions can be classified as coup-contrecoup injuries, which means that contusions can occur both at the site of impact (coup) and on the opposite side of the brain due to the brain rebounding and hitting the skull (contrecoup). These injuries are concerning because they involve damage to the brain tissue itself.

heading: CONTUSIONS RELATED TO HEAD INJURIES
text: The severity of a cerebral contusion can vary, ranging from mild to severe. In more severe cases, contusions can lead to increased pressure within the skull, swelling of the brain, and potentially lifethreatening complications.

heading: CONTUSIONS RELATED TO HEAD INJURIES
text:
It is crucial to seek immediate medical attention if a head injury is suspected, as prompt evaluation and treatment are essential to prevent further complications. Symptoms of a cerebral contusion may include:
- Changes in vision.
- Confusion.
- Difficulty speaking.
- Dizziness.
- Headache.
- Loss of consciousness.
- Nausea.
- Seizures.
- Vomiting.
- Weaknesses.

heading: CONTUSIONS RELATED TO HEAD INJURIES
text: Treatment for cerebral contusions focuses on managing the underlying injury and preventing further damage. It may involve measures such as rest, pain management, observation, close monitoring of neurological status, and, in more severe cases, surgical intervention to relieve pressure and remove any blood clots or damaged tissue.

heading: EQUIPMENT USED FOR THE TREATMENT OF A HEAD INJURY
text: Treating a head wound requires few essential pieces of equipment. Service members will need disposable gloves to protect themselves and the injured person from any potential infection. Sterile gauze pads or clean clothes are vital for covering and applying pressure to the wound to stop the bleeding. Adhesive bandages or medical tape are used to secure the gauze in place. Additionally, a mild antiseptic solution or wipes are important for cleaning the wound to prevent infection. Lastly, a cravat or gauze bandage can be used to create a makeshift dressing or sling to support the head if there is a suspected skull or neck injury.

heading: TIER 1 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF A HEAD INJURY
text: Service members may not have the time or expertise to conduct extensive treatment for a head injury. Service members experiencing any of the symptoms explained in paragraph 11-17 should be evacuated as soon as tactically feasible.

heading: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF A HEAD INJURY
text: Service members experiencing any of the symptoms explained in paragraph 11-17 should be evacuated as soon as tactically feasible. However, the CLS should complete the injury/evaluation/distance (commonly known as I.E.D.) checklist that is outlined in DODI 6490.11. This checklist is used to gather information, and to identify the signs and symptoms of a head injury.

heading: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF A HEAD INJURY
text: Commanders or their representatives are required to assess all Service members involved in potentially concussive events, including those without apparent injuries, as soon as possible using the injury/evaluation/distance checklist (figure 11-1).
