- TQ: R Arm - If a TQ is applied to the right arm, write the type of TQ (hasty or deliberate) used, and the time of TQ application.
- TQ: L Arm - If a TQ is applied to the left arm, write the type of TQ (hasty or deliberate) used, and the time of TQ application.
- TQ: R Leg - If a TQ is applied to the right leg, write the type of TQ (hasty or deliberate) used, and the time of TQ application.
- TQ: L Leg - If a TQ is applied to the left leg, write type of TQ (hasty or deliberate) used, and the time of TQ application.
- Time - Write the time that vital signs are taken.
- Pulse (rate and location) - Write casualty's pulse rate.
- Blood Pressure - Write casualty's blood pressure.
- Respiratory Rate - Write casualty's respiratory rate.
- AVPU - Write casualty's level of consciousness.
- Pain Scale (0-10) - Write casualty's level of pain in numeric rating scale of 0 to 10, with 0 being no pain and 10 being the worst pain.
- Back of Card (figure 15-2 on page 154):
- Battle Roster # - Write first letter of casualty's first name, then first letter of casualty's last name, write the last four numbers of the casualty's identification number. In figure 15-2, the Service member's battle roster number is "LD2270."
- Evacuation (EVAC) - Mark an "X" on the casualty's evacuation precedence (Urgent, Priority, or Routine).
- C - Mark an "X" for all Circulation hemorrhage control interventions. For TQ, mark category (Extremity, Junctional, and, or Truncal) and write name of TQ(s) used. For dressings, mark category (Hemostatic, Pressure, and, or Other) and write type of dressing(s) used.
- A - Mark an "X" for all airway interventions (Intact, NPA, cricothyroidotomy (known as CRIC), endotracheal (known as ET) tube, supraglottic airway (SGA) and write the type of device(s) used.
- B - Mark an "X" for all Breathing interventions oxygen (O2), needle decompression (Needle- D), Chest-Tube, (Chest-Seal) and write the type of device(s) used.
- C: Fluid - Circulation resuscitation interventions. Write name, volume, route, and time of any fluids given.
- C: Blood Product - Circulation resuscitation interventions. Write name, volume, route, and time of any blood products given. Note. When more space is needed for documentation, attach another DD Form 1380 to the original by safety pin or other means. The second form will be labeled DD Form 1380 #2, showing the Service member's name and unit.
- Analgesic Medications - Write name, dose, route, and time that any analgesics are given.
- Antibiotic Medications - Write name, dose, route, and time that any antibiotics are given.
- Other Medications - Write name, dose, route, and time of any other administered medications.
- Other - Mark an "X" for other treatments administered (combat pill pack, eye shield (mark right (R) or left (L)), splint, hypothermia prevention) and the type of device(s) used.
- Notes - Use this space to record any other pertinent information or clarifications.
- First Responder Name - Print the first responder's name (Last, First).
- First Responder Last 4 - Write the last four numbers of the first responder's social security number or identification number.
- Attach the completed DD Form 1380 to the casualty in a visible area where follow on medical staff will see it. Note. Do not attach DD Form 1380 to the casualty's body armor, as this equipment most likely will be separated from the casualty once they arrive at the MTF.

heading: figure 15-2, the Service member's battle roster number is "BL6553."
text: First responders and CLS personnel are advised to fill out the DD Form 1380 to the best of their ability. DD Form 1380 is crucial as it records evidence of initial treatment and provides subsequent levels of medical care with essential information. This documentation is vital for medical personnel to assess and determine the appropriate continuation of care for the casualty. This process ensures that each step of medical intervention is informed and based on prior actions taken, facilitating a cohesive and effective treatment pathway.

heading: MEDICAL EVACUATION REQUEST
text:
Every Service member should be able to initiate a 9-line MEDEVAC request. The standard MEDEVAC request has nine lines. However, lines one through five are required before a MEDEVAC can be launched. Using a phonetic alphabet and following the unit's normal communications procedures, call in:
- Grid location.
- Radio frequency and call sign.
- Number of casualties by precedence.
- Equipment that needs to be brought by the evacuation team.
- Number of litter and ambulatory casualties.

heading: MEDICAL EVACUATION REQUEST
text: Before initiating a 9-line MEDEVAC request, collect all the information needed. When calling in, be sure to follow all appropriate communication protocols and guidance.

heading: MEDICAL EVACUATION REQUEST
text: Depending on operational, mission variables, and availability, evacuation options may involve MEDEVAC, CASEVAC, or a combination of the two. During CASEVAC, casualties are moved without medical regulating and do not possess a protected status under the Geneva Conventions. As such, CASEVAC platforms may be engaged by enemy forces. With MEDEVAC, patients may be regulated or unregulated and the ambulance is properly marked, MEDEVAC cannot be used for nonmedical missions without losing its protected status. The 9-line MEDEVAC request is communicated through the designated evacuation system or Patient Evacuation Coordination Cell, depending on orders and the tactical SOP.

heading: MEDICAL EVACUATION REQUEST
text: When a Service member requests a MEDEVAC, they are not directly coordinating with a medical provider but are explaining the requestor's evacuation requirements with someone who coordinates the movement assets. Although they still require some general information about the status of the casualty, much of the information that they need to coordinate evacuation is not clinical and relates to logistical and operational issues.

heading: MEDICAL EVACUATION REQUEST
text: Communicate with medical providers on the evacuation asset if possible and relay the MIST report. Provide additional information as appropriate. For additional information on MEDEVAC request refer to ATP 4-02.2.

heading: EVACUATION EQUIPMENT AND CASUALTY PACKAGING
text: Essential evacuation equipment (for example, litters, packaging materials, and BVMs) should be prepared by other unit personnel while medical treatment continues and coordinating with the casualty treatment team to save time. For example, other unit members can prepare litters while treatment is being provided. Do not delay getting casualties onto litters. The first responder and CLS can better prevent hypothermia by getting casualties off the ground.

heading: LITTERS
text: Casualty movement in TFC may be better accomplished using litter due to the tactical situation and the need to move casualties rapidly. The litter exists only to facilitate casualty movement, and the casualty can be placed in the best position that facilitates their care and comfort. Casualties do not have to be placed on their backs on a litter. It is easier to move them if they are already on the litter; however, they must be secured to the litter before movement. Litter is also usually better for moving a casualty long distance.

heading: LITTERS
text: All unit members should know how to open and set up litters and rehearse their use during pre-mission training. All unit members should know who will carry litter or where litter is located on vehicles.

heading: LITTERS
text:
Selecting the proper litter is dependent on several different factors:
- The evacuation platform.
- The terrain at the location of pick-up.
- The casualty's injuries.
- The availability of different types of litters.

heading: LITTERS
text: Two of the more common litters often used are the quad-folding litter and the lightweight flexible stretchers. Each of them has advantages and disadvantages and maybe the proper litter depends on the situation. For example, flexible litter can be moved using a one-person drag (terrain permitting) but are more difficult to carry longer distances than a quad-folding litter.

heading: LITTERS
text: Each unit will have litters that have been proven to support their mission profile, and it is important to be aware of the limitations and advantages of each litter at your disposal before being deployed in a situation where you will require them.

heading: CASUALTY PACKAGING
text: When preparing a casualty for evacuation, the first responder or CLS need to anticipate the environmental factors that could prevent the casualty from remaining stable. Examples include extreme noises, vibrations, high winds from propeller washing, and exposure to cold environments from either altitude or low ambient temperatures. A plan should be developed to mitigate each of those potential threats when preparing for your casualty.

heading: CASUALTY PACKAGING
text: All loose ends of bandages, medical equipment, and hypothermia prevention materials should be secured. The first responder or CLS should prevent dressings and other medical items from being blown around by the rotor wash or becoming entangled with other equipment.

heading: CASUALTY PACKAGING
text: Loose materials can catch on anything from tree limbs to body-armor of litter bearers, to parts of the aircraft or vehicles. Any snag like this can cause delays in evacuation or even further injury to casualties or providers. Blankets and foil-based hypothermia materials are especially susceptible to being caught in the wind.

heading: CASUALTY PACKAGING
text: Hypothermia prevention equipment should be tucked and secured beneath the casualty and litter straps. Loose edges can be caught up in wind or rotor wash or snagged on objects in the helicopter as the casualty is loaded aboard.

heading: CASUALTY PACKAGING
text: The TQs should remain visible and not be hidden. The DD Form 1380 should be attached to the casualty.

heading: Evacuation Considerations for Suspected Spinal Injuries
text: A spinal injury should be expected in certain situations, like fast-roping falls or being near a significant blast. In those cases, when tactically feasible, ensure the C-spine is immobilized and the casualty is kept straight during evacuation. Keep the litter type and evacuation platform in mind and ensure the evacuation ground or air vehicle can accommodate the selected litter.

heading: Walking Wounded
text: Not all casualties require a litter for evacuation. For those casualties who are still ambulatory, provide instructions or assistance as needed. Depending on the nature of their injuries, they may be able to assist with carrying litters or providing security.

heading: Walking Wounded
text: It is best to guide disoriented or visually impaired casualties by having them place their hand on the shoulder of the casualty in front of them, or a nonmedical attendant as they move to the evacuation platform. Instruct them on repeatedly checking their own wounds and dressings to ensure that bleeding remains controlled throughout the evacuation process.

heading: CASUALTY STAGING
text: A particular importance when moving more than one casualty is the process of staging the casualties. Based on the guidance from the MEDEVAC personnel, certain casualties have priority and may need to be loaded last, so that they are the first ones offloaded at the destination.

heading: CASUALTY STAGING
text: If not given specific guidance, place the most serious casualty in a position where they are loaded last, and have casualties who may be less severely injured loaded before them. The first responder or CLS may also need to assist in marking the LZ, providing security, or assisting in marshalling the aircraft or litterbearer teams.

heading: EVACUATION CARE AFTER-ACTION REVIEW
text: It is critical that documentation of personnel, injury, and treatment be annotated using DD Form 1380 and should be completed prior to any handoff of the casualty. If care cannot be documented using the DD Form 1380 at the point of care by the first responder or CLS, it should be documented using the TCCC after action review, found on the JTS website, as soon as possible (within 72 hours) after treatment. The nonmedical first responder or CLS should follow up with the supporting unit medical personnel to complete and submit the TCCC after action review.

heading: In the operational environment, Service members are exposed to risks and receive
text: injuries beyond those caused by an operational event. First aid skills play a vital role in ensuring the safety and well-being of Service members. As personnel participate in outdoor activities and training, the potential for accidents or injuries increases. Having a solid foundation in first aid equips Service members with the necessary knowledge and abilities to respond swiftly and effectively in times of emergencies. Whether it's treating minor cuts and bruises, providing initial care for more serious injuries, or even saving lives, the importance of first aid skills cannot be overstated. By acquiring these skills, Service members not only become more responsible and capable individuals, but they also contribute to creating a safer environment for themselves and others.

heading: OVERVIEW OF BITES AND STINGS
text: Bites and stings are common occurrences that can happen in almost every environment. From pesky mosquito bites to venomous snakebites, these encounters with creatures big and small can lead to a range of discomfort, pain, and even potential danger. Understanding the various types of bites and stings, their causes, and proper treatment is crucial for minimizing the associated risks and ensuring a swift recovery.

heading: OVERVIEW OF BITES AND STINGS
text: Poison and venom are terms often used interchangeably, but they have distinct differences in their mode of delivery and the way they affect living organisms. A poison is a substance that is harmful or lethal when ingested, inhaled, or absorbed through the skin. It is typically produced by plants, animals, or microorganisms as a defensive mechanism. Poisonous substances can be found in various forms, such as toxins in certain plants, chemicals in household products, or even certain medications when taken in excessive amounts. The key characteristic of poison is that it needs to be ingested or absorbed into the body to cause harm.

heading: OVERVIEW OF BITES AND STINGS
text: Venom is a specialized secretion that is actively injected into another organism. It is typically produced by certain animals, such as snakes, spiders, scorpions, and some insects. Venom is delivered through specialized organs, such as fangs, stingers, or spines, and is primarily used for hunting or self-defense. Unlike poison, venom is actively injected into the victim's bloodstream, tissues, or body cavities, often leading to localized or systemic effects, which can range from pain and swelling to paralysis or even death. The main distinction between poison and venom lies in their delivery method. Poison is harmful when ingested or absorbed, while venom is specifically injected into another organism through specialized organs.

heading: OVERVIEW OF BITES AND STINGS
text: If bites and stings are not treated promptly and correctly, they may cause serious illness or death. The severity of a snakebite depends upon whether the snake is venomous or nonvenomous, the type of snake, the location of the bite, and the amount of venom injected. Bites from humans and other animals, such as dogs, cats, bats, raccoons, and rats, can cause severe bruises and infection and tears or lacerations of tissue. Awareness of the potential sources of injuries can reduce or prevent them from occurring. Knowledge and prompt application of first aid measures can lessen the severity of injuries from bites and stings and keep the Service member from becoming a serious casualty.

heading: HUMAN OR ANIMAL BITES
text:
First aid for human or animal bites aims to prevent infection and provide initial care for the wound. To perform first aid for a human or animal bite:
- Remove yourself from further harm. If dealing with an animal bite, ensure that you are no longer at risk of being bitten again.
- Control bleeding. If the bite wound is bleeding, apply direct pressure with a clean cloth or sterile gauze to stop or minimize the bleeding. Elevating the wound, if possible, can also help reduce bleeding.
- Clean the wound. Rinse the bite wound thoroughly with clean water or saline solution to flush out any dirt, bacteria, or saliva that may have entered the wound. Gently remove any debris from the wound using mild soap and water.
- Apply an antiseptic. After cleaning, apply an antiseptic solution or ointment to the wound to help reduce the risk of infection. Follow the instructions on the product label and ensure it is suitable for use on open wounds.
- Cover the wound. Use a sterile dressing or clean bandage to cover the wound. This will protect it from further contamination and promote healing. Change dressing regularly to maintain cleanliness.
- Seek medical attention. It is important to seek medical evaluation for all animal bites, especially those from unfamiliar or wild animals, deep wounds, or those that become red, swollen, or increasingly painful. A health care professional can assess the severity of the bite, prescribe antibiotics if necessary, and administer tetanus prophylaxis if required.

heading: HUMAN OR ANIMAL BITES
text: If someone gets bitten by an animal, whether known, unknown, wild, or domestic, the primary concern is rabies. Unless the animal is someone's pet and verified to be up to date on rabies, the individual who has been bitten must get the rabies post-exposure vaccine. Seemingly minor bites can lead to infection, so it is essential to consult a health care professional to determine the appropriate course of action and receive any necessary medical treatment. Note. If unable to capture or kill the animal, provide medical personnel with any information that will help identify it.

heading: MARINE (SEA) ANIMALS
text: Except for sharks and barracuda, most marine animals will not deliberately attack. The most frequent injuries from marine animals are wounds by biting, stinging, or puncturing. Wounds inflicted by marine animals can be very painful but are rarely fatal.

heading: MARINE (SEA) ANIMALS
text: Wounds from sharks, barracuda, and crocodilian can involve major trauma because of bites and lacerations. Bites from large marine animals are potentially the most life-threatening of all injuries from marine animals. Major wounds from these animals can be treated by controlling the bleeding, preventing shock, giving basic life support, splinting the injury, and by securing prompt medical aid.

heading: MARINE (SEA) ANIMALS
text: Turtles, moray eels, and corals normally inflict minor wounds. Treat by cleansing the wound(s) thoroughly and by splinting if necessary.

heading: MARINE (SEA) ANIMALS
text: Jellyfish, anemones, and others marine animals inflict injury by means of stinging cells in their tentacles. Contact with the tentacles produces burning pain with a rash and small hemorrhages on the skin. Shock, muscular cramping, nausea, vomiting, and respiratory distress may also occur. Gently remove the clinging tentacles with a towel and wash or treat the area. Use diluted ammonia or alcohol, a meat tenderizer, and talcum powder. If symptoms become severe or persist, seek medical assistance.

heading: MARINE (SEA) ANIMALS
text: Spiny fish, urchins, stingrays, and cone shells inject their venom by puncturing the skin with their spines. General signs and symptoms include swelling, nausea, vomiting, generalized cramps, diarrhea, muscular paralysis, and shock. Deaths are rare. Treatment consists of soaking the wound(s) in hot water (when available) for 30 to 60 minutes. This inactivates the heat sensitive toxin. In addition, further first aid measures should be taken such as controlling bleeding or applying a dressing. This should be carried out as necessary.

notices.text: Be careful not to scald the casualty with water that is too hot because the pain of the wound will mask the normal reaction to heat.

heading: SNAKE BITES
text: Snakebites can occur unexpectedly during outdoor activities or encounters with snakes in their natural habitats. Understanding how to identify snakes, knowing the proper steps to take after a snakebite, and having a grasp of basic first aid techniques can significantly increase the chances of a positive outcome in such situations. Snakes are categorized between nonvenomous and venomous snakes.

heading: SNAKE BITES
text: Snakes can be categorized into various groups based on different characteristics. One common classification system categorizes snakes into four main categories of colubrid snakes, constrictor snakes, nonvenomous snakes, and venomous snakes. These categories may overlap, and some snakes may possess traits from multiple categories. Understanding the different categories of snakes can aid in snake identification, assessing potential risks, and knowing how to respond appropriately in various situations.

heading: Colubrid Snakes
text: Colubrid snakes represent the largest snake family and include a wide range of non-venomous species. These snakes have diverse habitats, sizes, and feeding habits. Common colubrid snakes include rat, king, gopher, and water snakes.

heading: Constrictor Snakes
text: Constrictor snakes are non-venomous snakes that subdue their prey by coiling around them and squeezing until they can no longer breathe. Constrictors then swallow their prey whole. Well-known constrictor snakes include boas, pythons, and anacondas.

heading: Non-venomous Snakes
text: Non-venomous snakes include snakes that lack venom glands or fangs and pose no direct threat to humans. Non-venomous snakes play an essential role in controlling rodent populations and maintaining ecological balance. Examples of non-venomous snakes are boas, pythons, corn, and garter snakes.

heading: Non-venomous Snakes
text: There are approximately 130 different varieties of nonvenomous snakes in the U.S. They have ovalshaped heads and round eyes. Unlike venomous snakes, discussed below, nonvenomous snakes do not have fangs with which to inject venom. Figure 16-1 depicts the characteristics of a nonvenomous snake.

heading: Venomous Snakes
text: Venomous snakes possess venom glands and specialized fangs to inject venom into their prey or as a defense mechanism. It is important to exercise caution and seek immediate medical attention in the event of a venomous snakebite.

heading: Venomous Snakes
text: It is important to note that the distribution of venomous snakes may vary within states, and some species may be specific to certain regions. When spending time in areas known to have venomous snakes, it is crucial to be aware of the local species, understand their habitats and behavior, and take appropriate precautions to avoid encounters and bites.

heading: Venomous Snakes
text: Venomous snakes in other parts of the world include sea snakes, the Fer-De-Lance, the Bushmaster, tropical rattlesnake in tropical Central America; the Malayan pit viper in the tropical Far East; the cobra in Africa and Asia; the mamba (or black mamba) in central and southern Africa; and the krait in India and Southeast Asia.

heading: Categories of Venomous Snakes
text:
Venomous snakes can be categorized into several groups based on their characteristics and taxonomic classification. The following are some common categories of venomous snakes:
- Vipers.
- Elapids.
- Rear-Fanged Snakes.
- Burrowing Asps.
- Sea Snakes.

heading: Categories of Venomous Snakes
text: These categories provide a general overview of the different types of venomous snakes based on their taxonomic families and key characteristics. It's important to note that there may be variations within each category, and some venomous snakes may exhibit characteristics from multiple families.

heading: Categories of Venomous Snakes
text: This family of snakes includes some of the most well-known venomous snakes. Vipers are characterized by their large, triangular heads, heat-sensing pits between their eyes and nostrils, and hinged fangs that can fold back when not in use. Examples include rattlesnakes, copperheads, and cottonmouths or water moccasins. See figure 16-2 for characteristics of a venomous pit viper and figure 16-3 on page 163 provides examples of viper snakes.

heading: Rattlesnake
text:
In the U.S, there are several species of venomous snakes. The following are some of the venomous snakes commonly found in different regions of the country:
- Rattlesnakes: Rattlesnakes are a group of venomous snakes known for the rattling sound they produce by shaking their tails. Species such as the eastern and western diamondback, timber and Mojave rattlesnakes are found in various parts of the U.S.
- Copperheads: Copperheads are venomous snakes with distinctive copper-colored heads. They are commonly found in the eastern and southeastern regions of the U.S.
- Cottonmouths or Water Moccasins: Cottonmouths or Water Moccasins are venomous semi-aquatic snakes primarily found in the southeastern U.S. They are known for their aggressive behavior and are often encountered near bodies of water.
- Coral Snakes: Coral snakes are venomous snakes with colorful bands of red, yellow, and black. The Eastern and Texas Coral Snakes are found in specific regions of the southern U.S.
- Various Pit Vipers: Pit vipers include venomous snakes that possess heat-sensing pits between their eyes and nostrils. Along with rattlesnakes and copperheads, this category includes species such as the eastern and western Massasauga Rattlesnakes, and the Mojave Desert Sidewinder.

heading: Rattlesnake
text: The casualty's condition provides the best information about the seriousness of the situation and how much time has passed since the bite occurred. Pit viper bites are characterized by severe burning pain. Discoloration and swelling around the fang marks usually begins within five to ten minutes after the bite. If only minimal swelling occurs within 30 minutes, the bite will almost certainly have been from a nonvenomous snake or possibly from a venomous snake, which did not inject venom. The venom destroys blood cells, causing a general discoloration of the skin. Blisters and numbness in the affected area follow this reaction. Other signs, which can occur, are weakness, rapid pulse, nausea, shortness of breath, vomiting, and shock.

heading: Rattlesnake
text:
The venom of viper bites affects the circulatory system and destroys muscle. Severe pain, swelling and change in skin color usually develop within five to 10 minutes and slowly spreads. After several hours, the following signs and symptoms will occur:
- Further swelling and changes in skin color.
- Bleeding blisters.
- Numbness of the affected area.

heading: Rattlesnake
text:
Other signs and symptoms which may occur include:
- Weaknesses.
- Rapid pulse.
- Nausea.
- Vomiting.
- Shortness of breath.
- Sweating.
- Shock.

heading: Rattlesnake
text: Elapids are a family of venomous snakes known for their fixed front fangs and potent neurotoxic venom. They generally have slender bodies and smooth scales. Famous elapid snakes include cobras, coral snakes, kraits, and mambas. Corals (figure 16-4), cobras (figure 16-5), kraits, and mambas all belong to the same group even though they are found in different parts of the world. All four inject their venom through short, grooved fangs, leaving a characteristic bite pattern.

heading: example snake example
text: To identify a coral snake, a common phrase used in the U.S. is "Red or yellow, kill a fellow; red on black, venom lack." This phrase refers to the color pattern on the snake's bands and serves as a mnemonic device to help distinguish coral snakes from non-venomous snakes with similar markings, such as milk or scarlet kingsnakes. Coral snakes have red bands touching yellow bands, while non-venomous snakes have red bands touching black bands. It's important to remember that this phrase is specific to the U.S. and may not apply to coral snake species found in other regions. When encountering any snake, it is advisable to maintain a safe distance and seek professional assistance if unsure of its venomous nature.

heading: example snake example
text: The venom from corals, cobras, kraits, and mambas, which belong to the elapid family, notably affects the central nervous system, producing a distinct set of symptoms that diverge from those caused by pit vipers. Initially, these bites may result in only minimal pain and swelling, leading many individuals to underestimate the severity of the bite. Typically, the onset of neurological symptoms occurs within one to seven hours postbite, including blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, drowsiness, and an increase in salivation and sweating.

heading: example snake example
text: If the bite is not addressed quickly with appropriate medical intervention, more severe symptoms can manifest, such as nausea, vomiting, respiratory difficulties, shock, and eventually more critical conditions like paralysis, convulsions, and coma. This progression underscores the necessity of recognizing the potential danger of elapid bites early and seeking immediate medical treatment to mitigate these serious outcomes.

heading: example snake example
text: While most rear-fanged snakes are non-venomous, some species within this family possess venomous rear fangs. These fangs are located toward the back of the mouth and are used to subdue their prey. Rearfanged venomous snakes include boomslangs, mangrove, and vine snakes.

heading: example snake example
text: Burrowing asps are a family of venomous snakes primarily found in Africa and parts of the Middle East. They have small, fixed front fangs and are adapted for burrowing in sandy or loose soil. Examples include the stiletto snakes and mole vipers.

heading: example snake example
text: Sea snakes are a group of venomous snakes that have adapted to life in aquatic environments. They have paddle-shaped tails and can be found in the coastal waters of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Sea snakes have highly potent venom but are generally not aggressive towards humans.

heading: example snake example
text: Sea snakes (figure 16-6 on page 165) are found in the warm water areas of the Pacific and Indian Oceans, along the coasts, and at the mouths of some larger rivers. Their venom is VERY venomous, but their fangs are only 1/4 inch long.

heading: Venomous Snakebite
text: Venomous snakes DO NOT always inject venom when they bite or strike a person. However, all snakes may carry tetanus (lockjaw); anyone bitten by a snake, whether venomous or nonvenomous, should immediately seek medical attention.

heading: Venomous Snakebite
text: Venom is injected from the venom sacs through grooved or hollowed fangs. Depending on the species, these fangs are either long or short. Pit vipers have long hollow fangs. These fangs are folded against the roof of the mouth and extend when the snake strikes. This allows them to strike quickly and then withdraw. Cobras, coral snakes, kraits, mambas, and sea snakes have short, grooved fangs. These snakes are less effective in their attempts to bite, since they must chew after striking to inject enough venom (poison) to be effective.

heading: Venomous Snakebite
text: In the event you are bitten, do not attempt to identify and or kill the snake. Freshly killed snakes can continue to bite due to reflexive action. Snake identification is not critical. Medical personnel will treat symptoms by geography and not someone's best guess at a species.

heading: Venomous Snakebite
text: The venoms of different snakes cause different effects. Pit viper venom (hemotoxin [blood toxin]) destroys tissue and blood cells. Cobras, adders, and coral snakes inject powerful venom (neurotoxin [nerve toxin]) which affects the central nervous system, causing respiratory paralysis. Water moccasins and sea snakes have venom that is both hemotoxic and neurotoxic.

heading: FIRST AID FOR A SNAKEBITE
text:
In the event of a snakebite, prompt first aid is crucial to minimizing the potential effects of the venom. To perform first aid for a snakebite:
- Stay calm and call for medical assistance immediately. Provide medical personnel with information about the snake, if possible, but do not attempt to capture or kill the snake as it may increase the risk of further bites.
- Keep the bitten Service member as still and calm as possible. Restrict movement and avoid unnecessary exertion, as it can accelerate the spread of venom in the bloodstream.
- Remove any constricting items, such as jewelry or tight clothing, from the affected area, as swelling may occur.
- Position the affected limb slightly below the level of the heart, if possible. This can help slow the spread of venom.
- Cleanse the wound gently with mild soap and water to reduce the risk of infection. Do not apply ice or use a TQ, as they are not effective and can cause additional harm.
- Apply a sterile bandage or dress over the bite, ensuring it is snug but not too tight. This can help immobilize the area and reduce the spread of venom.
- Encourage the person to remain calm and still, while waiting for medical help to arrive. Monitor their vital signs, such as breathing and heart rate, and be prepared to administer CPR if necessary.

heading: FIRST AID FOR A SNAKEBITE
text: The above steps are general guidelines and may vary depending on the snake species and the region. It is crucial to seek medical attention immediately after a snakebite, as they can provide appropriate antivenom treatment and further evaluate the situation.

notices.text: DO NOT attempt to cut open the bite or suck out the venom. If the venom should seep through any damaged or lacerated tissues in your mouth, you could immediately lose consciousness or even die.

heading: FIRST AID FOR A SNAKEBITE
text: If accompanying the casualty on CASEVAC to an MTF, observe the casualty carefully for signs and symptoms of an allergic reaction. Continue to monitor the airway, breathing, circulation, vital signs (for first aid purposes; pulse, and respiration), and distal pulse of the bitten extremity, treating for shock, and conserving body heat.

heading: INSECT (ARTHROPOD) BITES AND STINGS
text: An insect bite or sting can cause great pain, allergic reaction, inflammation, and infection. If not treated correctly, some bites or stings may cause serious illness or even death. When an allergic reaction is not involved, first aid is a simple process. In any case, medical personnel should examine the casualty at the earliest possible time. It is important to identify spiders, bees, or creatures that cause bites or sting, especially in cases of an allergic reaction.

heading: INSECT (ARTHROPOD) BITES AND STINGS
text: The insects found throughout the world that can produce a bite or sting are too numerous to mention in detail. Commonly encountered stinging or biting insects include the brown recluse spiders, black widow spiders, tarantulas, scorpions, urticating caterpillars, bees, wasps, centipedes, conenose beetles (kissing bugs), ants, and wheel bugs. Upon being reassigned, especially to overseas areas, take the time to become acquainted with the types of insects to avoid.

heading: INSECT (ARTHROPOD) BITES AND STINGS
text: Arthropods are segmented invertebrates with jointed antennae and legs. They include insects, arachnids, centipedes, and millipedes. See figure 16-7 for examples of venomous arthropods.

heading: INSECT (ARTHROPOD) BITES AND STINGS
text:
Of all deaths due to venomous stings or bites in a year, most are caused by arthropods. Most injuries resulting from venomous arthropods can be prevented by doing the following:
- If you are allergic to certain stings or bites, be prepared with the proper medication.
- Ask the local inhabitants about the local venomous and harmful arthropods.
- Avoid touching unfamiliar arthropods or allowing them to touch you.
- Watch where you put your hands and feet.
- Before using it, check places where harmful arthropods may hide.
- Closets, wall spaces, doorways, and eaves.
- Outdoor privies and latrine boxes.
- Bed clothing, beds, and sleeping bags.
- Shoes, boots, and clothing.
- Logs, felled trees, and leaves.
- Rocks, boards, and debris.
- Avoid beehives, ant and wasp nests, and spider webs.
- Wear foot protection (shoes, boots, and sandals) always.
- Hang up clothes.
- Practice good sanitation by removing debris, trash, and board piles.
- Avoid wearing deodorants, colognes, perfumes, or cosmetics with fragrances.

heading: INSECTS
text: An insect is a small invertebrate animal characterized by having a segmented body, three pairs of legs, and often one or two pairs of wings. Insects are a diverse group, with over a million known species, and they play important roles in ecosystems as pollinators, decomposers, and prey for other organisms.

heading: INSECTS
text:
First aid treatment for insect bites can vary depending on the type of insect and the individual's reaction. The general first aid steps for treating insect bites are:
- Remove the stinger (if applicable): In the case of stinging insects like bees or wasps, it's important to remove the stinger as quickly as possible to prevent further venom injection. Gently scrape it off the skin using a blunt edge like a credit card or your fingernail. Avoid squeezing the venom sac, as it may release more venom.
- Wash the bite area: Clean the bite site with mild soap and water to reduce the risk of infection. Be gentle and avoid excessive scrubbing.
- Apply a cold compress: To alleviate pain, reduce swelling, and minimize itching, apply a cold compress or an ice pack wrapped in a cloth to the bite area. Do this for 10-15 minutes at a time, several times a day.
- Use over-the-counter remedies: Over-the-counter topical creams, ointments, or sprays containing ingredients such as hydrocortisone, calamine lotion, or antihistamines can help relieve itching and inflammation. Follow the instructions and precautions on the product packaging.
- Take oral antihistamines: If itching or swelling persists, you can take over-the-counter oral antihistamine to help reduce allergic reactions and relieve symptoms. Consult a pharmacist or health care professional for appropriate dosage and recommendations.
- Avoid scratching: Although it may be tempting, refrain from scratching the insect bite to prevent further irritation, infection, or the development of a secondary skin condition.
- Monitor for severe reactions: In rare cases, insect bites can cause severe allergic reactions, known as anaphylaxis. If you experience symptoms such as difficulty breathing, dizziness, swelling of the face or throat, or a widespread rash, seek immediate medical attention.

heading: INSECTS
text: If the insect type is unknown or if the Service member is experiencing severe or worsening symptoms, it is best to consult a health care professional for proper evaluation and guidance.

heading: ARACHNIDS
text: An arachnid is a class of joint-legged invertebrate animals that include spiders, scorpions, ticks, and mites. Arachnids are part of the phylum Arthropoda, which also includes insects, crustaceans, and millipedes.

heading: ARACHNIDS
text: Arachnids are characterized by having two main body segments: the cephalothorax (a fused head and thorax region) and the abdomen. They typically have four pairs of legs attached to the cephalothorax and possess specialized mouthparts called chelicerae, which are used for feeding and defense. Most arachnids also have specialized structures like spinnerets for producing silk (used by spiders for web-building) and a pair of pedipalps that may serve various functions depending on the species.

heading: ARACHNIDS
text: While spiders are perhaps the most well-known arachnids, other arachnids exhibit unique features. Scorpions have large pincers and a long tail ending in a venomous stinger. Ticks and mites are tiny arachnids that often parasitize animals, including humans, and can transmit diseases. Some arachnids, such as daddy longlegs and sun spiders, have distinct body shapes and behaviors.

heading: ARACHNIDS
text: Arachnids play diverse roles in ecosystems. Spiders, for example, are predators of insects and help control their populations. Arachnids have adapted to various habitats worldwide, from deserts to forests to aquatic environments. Arachnids are a diverse group of invertebrates that exhibit a wide range of adaptations, behaviors, and ecological roles within the animal kingdom.

heading: SPIDERS
text:
Among the many species of spiders found around the world, a few are known for their potentially dangerous bites. The most well-known dangerous spider species are the:
- Brazilian Wandering Spider.
- Sydney Funnel-web Spider.
- Black Widow Spider.
- Brown Recluse Spider.

heading: SPIDERS
text: The Brazilian Wandering Spider is found in South and Central America and is known for its highly venomous bite. It is considered one of the most venomous spiders in the world. Their venom can cause severe pain, priapism (prolonged erection), and, in rare cases, can be life-threatening.

heading: SPIDERS
text: The Sydney Funnel-web Spider is found in Australia, the Sydney Funnel-web Spider is highly venomous and can be aggressive when threatened. Their venom is potent and can cause severe symptoms, including muscle spasm, difficulty breathing, and in rare cases, it can be fatal. Prompt medical attention is crucial if bitten.

heading: SPIDERS
text: The Black Widow Spider is found in various parts of the world. Females have a distinctive black body with a red hourglass-shaped mark on the abdomen. Their venom contains neurotoxins that can cause intense pain, muscle cramps, nausea, and in severe cases, can affect the nervous system. While bites are rarely fatal, medical attention is still recommended.

heading: SPIDERS
text: The Brown Recluse Spider is found primarily in the U.S. Their bites can cause tissue necrosis (cell death), leading to an ulcerous wound that may require medical attention. Other symptoms can include pain, itching, and systemic effects.

heading: SPIDERS
text: While these spiders are considered dangerous, actual bites and severe reactions are relatively rare. Most spiders are not aggressive and will only bite in self-defense. If bitten by a spider and experiencing severe symptoms, seek immediate medical attention.

heading: SPIDERS
text: Specific risks associated with spider bites can vary depending on a Service member's health, sensitivity, and potential allergies. Therefore, it is always advisable to exercise caution around spiders and seek professional medical advice if a bite occurs.

heading: SCORPION
text:
The most dangerous scorpions are typically found in regions with warm climates, particularly in arid or desert areas. Some locations known for housing dangerous scorpion species are:
- North Africa.
- Middle East.
- Mexico.
- Brazil.
- India.

heading: SCORPION
text: Countries in North Africa, such as Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Egypt, are home to highly venomous scorpion species. These species include the Deathstalker scorpion and the Androc tonus australis.

heading: SCORPION
text: Several countries in the Middle East have venomous scorpions, including Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, Jordan, and Yemen. The Deathstalker scorpion is found in this region, along with other dangerous species such as the Arabian Fat-tailed scorpion and the Palestine Yellow scorpion.

heading: SCORPION
text: Mexico is known for its diverse scorpion fauna, and it is home to several highly venomous species. The Bark scorpion is found in various parts of the country, including the notorious Arizona Bark scorpion, which is also found in the southwestern U.S.

heading: SCORPION
text: In Brazil, the Brazilian Yellow scorpion is considered one of the most venomous scorpions. It is primarily found in southeastern and southern regions of the country.

heading: SCORPION
text: India is home to several dangerous scorpion species. The Indian Red scorpion and the Indian Black scorpion are found to live in this region.

heading: SCORPION
text: While these regions have known populations of dangerous scorpions, encounters with venomous scorpions and severe envenomation are relatively rare. However, it is always advisable to exercise caution and take necessary precautions when in scorpion-prone areas. Figure 16-8 provides an example of a scorpion.

heading: CENTIPEDES
text: A centipede is a type of arthropod characterized by elongated, multi-segmented creatures with numerous pairs of legs, ranging from tens to hundreds depending on the species. Centipedes are found in various habitats worldwide, including forests, deserts, and tropical regions.

heading: CENTIPEDES
text:
While most centipedes are not considered dangerous to humans, some larger species possess venomous pincers or fangs located on their first pair of legs. When threatened or provoked, they can deliver a painful sting or bite. The severity of the reaction to a centipede sting can vary depending on the species and the individual's sensitivity to the venom. Centipede bites are painful but not life-threatening. If a Service member is stung by a centipede, first aid steps to take are:
- Stay calm and move away from the centipede to avoid further stings.
- Wash the affected area gently with soap and water to clean the wound and reduce the risk of infection.
- Apply a cold compress or ice pack wrapped in a cloth to the sting site. This can help alleviate pain and reduce swelling.
- Take over-the-counter pain relievers, such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen, to manage pain if necessary. Follow the instructions and recommended dosage.
- Keep the sting site clean and dry and avoid scratching or irritating the area to prevent infection.

heading: CENTIPEDES
text: If there are signs of an allergic reaction, such as difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or widespread hives, seek immediate medical attention.

heading: MILLIPEDES
text: Millipedes, belonging to the class Diplopoda, are arthropods distinguished by their elongated, segmented bodies with two pairs of legs per body segment, excluding the first few segments. These creatures are commonly found in moist environments such as forests, gardens, and areas with decaying vegetation.

heading: MILLIPEDES
text: Unlike centipedes, millipedes lack venomous pincers or fangs and are generally harmless to humans. However, they possess defensive mechanisms that can release toxins or irritating chemicals, which may cause mild reactions in some individuals, particularly those with sensitive skin.

heading: MILLIPEDES
text:
If a Service member encounters a millipede and experiences irritation or a sting, the recommended first aid steps include:
- Washing the affected area gently with soap and water to cleanse the site and remove any secretions from the millipede.
- Applying a cold compress or an ice pack wrapped in a cloth to reduce swelling and alleviate discomfort at the sting site.
- Using over-the-counter topical antihistamines or hydrocortisone creams to relieve itching or irritation.
- Avoiding scratching or further irritating the site to prevent infection.

heading: MILLIPEDES
text: In cases where there is a severe allergic reaction, characterized by symptoms such as difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or widespread hives, it is crucial to seek immediate medical attention. While millipede stings are typically mild and self-limiting, if symptoms persist, worsen, or if there are concerns about an individual's reaction, consulting a healthcare professional for further advice and treatment is advisable.

heading: FIRE ANTS
text: Fire ants are a type of stinging ant that are native to South America but have spread to various parts of the world, including the southern U.S, Southeast Asia, and Australia. Fire ants are known for their aggressive behavior and painful stings.

heading: FIRE ANTS
text:
When a fire ant stings, it injects venom into the skin, resulting in a sharp, burning sensation and the formation of a raised, reddish bump. Multiple ants may attack simultaneously, leading to multiple stings. If stung by a fire ant, the first aid steps are to:
- Move away from the area where the ants are present to avoid further stings.
- Remove any clothing or jewelry that may have ants trapped in them, as they can continue to sting.
- Gently wash the affected area with soap and water to clean the site.
- Apply a cold compress or ice pack wrapped in a cloth to the sting site. This can help reduce pain and swelling.
- Over-the-counter pain relievers, such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen, can be taken to help manage pain if necessary. Follow the instructions and recommended dosage.
- Avoid scratching the sting site to prevent infection. If itching is severe, over-the-counter antihistamines or hydrocortisone creams may be used under the guidance of a health care professional.
- Monitor the individual for signs of an allergic reaction, such as difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or widespread hives. If these symptoms occur, seek immediate medical attention.

heading: FIRE ANTS
text: Fire ant stings can be particularly problematic for individuals who are allergic or hypersensitive to ant venom. In such cases, immediate medical attention should be sought. These first aid steps are general guidelines, and the severity of the reaction may vary from person to person. If there are concerns about the Service member's health or if the symptoms worsen or persist, consult a health care professional for appropriate advice and treatment.

heading: TICKS
text: A tick is a small arachnid parasite that feeds on the blood of animals, including humans. Ticks are found in various environments, such as forests, grasslands, and shrubby areas. They latch onto their hosts and can transmit diseases through their bites.

heading: TICKS
text:
When a tick bites, it burrows its mouth parts into the skin to feed on blood. If you discover a tick attached to your skin, it's important to remove it promptly and take the following first aid steps:
- Prepare for tick removal: Use fine-tipped tweezers to grasp the tick as close to the skin's surface as possible. Avoid squeezing or crushing the tick's body.
- Remove the tick: Gently and steadily pull the tick upward with even pressure. Do not twist or jerk it. The goal is to remove the entire tick, including its mouthparts. Dispose of the tick by placing it in a sealed bag or container or by submerging it in alcohol.
- Clean the bite area: Thoroughly clean the bite area with soap and water or an antiseptic solution to reduce the risk of infection.
- Apply an antiseptic: After cleaning the bite area, you can apply an antiseptic ointment or cream to further prevent infection.
- Monitor for symptoms: Keep an eye on the bite site for any signs of an allergic reaction, infection, or the appearance of a rash. If you notice any concerning symptoms, seek medical attention.

heading: TICKS
text: Certain tick-borne diseases, such as Lyme disease or Rocky Mountain spotted fever, may take time to manifest symptoms. If in an area where these diseases are prevalent or if you develop symptoms such as fever, rash, joint pain, or flu-like symptoms after a tick bite, it is crucial to consult a health care professional for proper evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment.

heading: TICKS
text: Prevention is key when it comes to ticks. To minimize the risk of tick bites, wear protective clothing when in tick-prone areas, use insect repellents containing DEET, perform regular tick checks after outdoor activities, and take appropriate measures to protect pets from ticks as well. DEET (chemical name, N, Ndiethyl-meta-toluamide) is the active ingredient in many repellent products. It is widely used to repel biting pests such as mosquitoes and ticks.

notices.text: Lyme disease, transmitted by Blacklegged "Deer" tick, can cause long- term neurological disorders and other complications if not identified and treated early.

heading: TICKS
text:
The signs and symptoms of a tick bite can vary depending on factors such as the type of tick, the individual's sensitivity to the tick's saliva, and the presence of any tick-borne diseases. The common signs and symptoms associated with tick bites are:
- Redness and swelling: After a tick bite, it is common to experience localized redness and swelling at the site of the bite. This is a normal reaction to the tick's saliva.
- Itching or irritation: The bite site may be itchy or irritated, like a mosquito bite. Avoid scratching to reduce the risk of infection.
- Tick remnants: If a tick is not promptly and properly removed, parts of the tick's body, such as its mouthparts, may remain embedded in the skin. This can lead to ongoing irritation and a risk of infection.
- Rash: In some cases, a small red spot or rash may develop around the tick bite. This can expand over time and may resemble a target-like pattern. It is important to note that not all tick bites result in a rash.
- Flu-like symptoms: Tick-borne diseases such as Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, or babesiosis can cause flu-like symptoms. These may include fever, fatigue, headache, muscle aches, joint pain, and swollen lymph nodes. However, these symptoms usually develop days or weeks after the tick bite.
- Allergic reaction: In rare cases, individuals may have an allergic reaction to tick bites, resulting in more severe symptoms such as difficulty breathing, swelling, hives, or anaphylaxis. Immediate medical attention is necessary in such cases.

heading: TICKS
text: Not all tick bites lead to the transmission of diseases, and most tick bites are harmless. If a Service member experiences any concerning symptoms or if you live in an area where tick-borne diseases are prevalent, seek medical attention for proper evaluation, diagnosis, and appropriate treatment.
