heading: First Aid for Nerve Agent Poisoning
text: Nerve agents are absorbed rapidly, and the effects are felt immediately upon entry into the body. You will be issued three ATNAAs and one convulsant antidote nerve agent (CANA) or advanced anticonvulsant system (AAS). Each ATNAA consists of a multi-chambered auto injector with the atropine and pralidoxime chloride in separate chambers. You will use the ATNAA in self-aid and buddy aid as issued.

heading: First Aid for Nerve Agent Poisoning
text: If nerve agents are used, mission permitting, watch for persons needing nerve agent antidotes and immediately follow procedures. When you have the signs and symptoms of nerve agent poisoning, you should immediately put on the protective mask and then inject yourself with one set of the ATNAA. First aid for nerve agent poisoning consists of administering the ATNAA, CANA, or AAS.

heading: Convulsant Antidote for Nerve Agent and Advanced Anticonvulsant System
text: Two anticonvulsant autoinjectors are available to control actively seizing patients. CANA (figure 19- 2 on page 197) is the drug diazepam. AAS (figure 19-3 on page 197) is the drug midazolam. CANA and AAS are not intended for self-administration.

heading: Convulsant Antidote for Nerve Agent and Advanced Anticonvulsant System
text: Diazepam or midazolam should be administered with the three ATNAA kits when the casualty's condition warrants the use of three ATNAA kits at the same time. Use either the CANA or the AAS to control an actively seizing patient. Do not administer both for the same series of three ATNAA kits.

heading: Antidote Treatment - Nerve Agent, Auto-Injector
text: The ATNAA (figure 19-4) is a multi-chambered device with the atropine and pralidoxime chloride in separate chambers. Both antidotes will be administered through a single needle. The ATNAA provides atropine injections and pralidoxime chloride injections in separate chambers as sterile, pyrogen-free solutions for intramuscular injection.

heading: Antidote Treatment - Nerve Agent, Auto-Injector
text:
The ATNAA is a specially designed unit for automatic self-aid or buddy aid administration by military personnel. When activated, the ATNAA sequentially administers atropine and pralidoxime chloride through a single needle. The recommended procedure is to inject the contents of the auto-injector into the muscles of an outer thigh or into the buttocks. When activated, each ATNAA dispenses:
- 2.1mg atropine in 0.7 milliliter of a sterile, pyrogen-free solution containing 12.47mg glycerin and not more than 2.8mg of phenol, citrate buffer, and water for injection. The potential hydrogen (pH) range is 4.0 - 5.0.
- 600mg of pralidoxime chloride in 2 milliliters of a sterile, pyrogen-free solution containing 40mg benzyl alcohol, 22.5mg glycine and water for injection. The pH is adjusted with hydrochloric acid. The pH range is 2.0 - 3.0.

heading: Antidote Treatment - Nerve Agent, Auto-Injector
text: The ATNAA should be self-aid or buddy aid administered by military personnel after donning a protective mask and hood but only if some or all the following mild symptoms of nerve agent exposure are present.

heading: Reactive Skin Decontamination Lotion Kit
text: The RSDL kit (figure 19-5) is intended to remove or neutralize chemical warfare agents from the skin. The RSDL contains Dekon 139 and a small amount of 2,3-butanedione monoxime. These compounds are dissolved in a solvent composed of polyethylene glycol monomethyl ether and water. This solvent system is particularly important as it promotes the decontamination reaction by actively desorbing, retaining, and sequestering the chemical agent, while the active ingredient (Dekon 139) chemically reacts with, and rapidly neutralizes the vesicant chemical or the organophosphorus nerve agent. This reaction starts immediately, and neutralization is usually complete within two minutes.

heading: Reactive Skin Decontamination Lotion Kit
text: The RSDL kit is the preferred method of decontamination. If a RSDL kit is not available soap and large amounts of water can be used for decontamination. Although soap and a large amount of water may be effective in physically removing chemical warfare agents, they do not neutralize chemical warfare agents. Soap and water can increase dermal absorption of mustard agents and can result in contaminated runoff that can affect others.

notices.text: For external use only. May be slightly irritating to the eyes. Keep decontaminating powder out of the eyes. Use water to wash the toxic agent out of the eyes.

heading: Injection Site
text: The injection site for administering the antidotes is normally in the outer thigh muscle. The thigh injection site is the area about a hand's width below the hip joint (figure 19-6 step A on page 199). It is important that the injection be given into a large muscle area. If the individual is thinly built, then the injections should be administered into the upper outer quarter (quadrant) of the buttock (figure 19-6 step B on page 199). Injecting in the buttocks of a thinly built individual avoids injury to the thighbone.

notices.text: There is a nerve that crosses the buttocks; hitting this nerve can cause paralysis. Service members that are thinly built, should inject themselves in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock to avoid this nerve.

heading: Injection Site
text: If experiencing any or all of the MILD nerve agent symptoms, IMMEDIATELY self-administer one ATNAA kit and put on your protective mask. Follow the procedure given in table 19-3 on page 200. The ATNAA is carried in your protective mask carrier, pocket of the Mission-Oriented Protective Posture over garment, or other location as specified in your unit tactical SOP. In cold weather, the ATNAA should be stored in an inside pocket of the Service member's clothing to protect the antidote from freezing. A frozen ATNAA cannot be immediately used to provide the antidote, when needed; however, the ATNAA can still be used after complete thawing.

notices.text: DO NOT cover or hold the needle end with your hand, thumb, or fingers--you might accidentally inject yourself. An accidental injection into the hand WILL NOT deliver an effective dose of the antidote, especially if the needle goes through the hand.

heading: Injection Site
text: DO NOT self-administer another set of injections. If the Service member can walk without assistance, know who they are, and where they are, they may not need a second set of injections. Administering not needed additional injections may create a nerve-agent-antidote overdose, which could cause incapacitation or the inability to perform the mission or defend themselves.

heading: Self-Administer Antidote Treatment - Nerve Agent, Auto Injector
text: If you experience any or all of the nerve agent MILD symptoms, you must IMMEDIATELY selfadminister one ATNAA following the procedures given in table 19-3 on page 200.

text: Step 1. Obtain one ATNAA. Step 2. Check injection site. Step 3. Hold ATNAA with dominant hand. Step 4. Grasp safety cap with non-dominant hand and remove from injector. Step 5. Clear hard objects from injection site. Step 6. Inject ATNAA at injection site applying even pressure to the injector. Hold in place for 10 seconds. Step 7. Bend needle of used injector by pressing on a hard surface to form a hook. Step 8. Attach used injector to blouse pocket flap of BDO and or JSLIST. Step 9. Massage injection site, mission permitting.

heading: Combat Lifesaver Assistance for Nerve Agent Poisoning
text: The CLS must check to verify if the individual has received three sets of ATNAAs. If not, the CLS performs first aid as described for buddy aid above. If the individual has received the three sets of, ATNAA, the CLS may administer additional injections at approximately 15-minute intervals until atropinization is achieved (that is a heart rate above 90 beats per minute, reduced bronchial secretions, and reduced salivations). Administer additional atropines at intervals of 30 minutes to four hours to maintain atropinization or until the casualty is placed under the care of medical personnel. Check the heart rate by lifting the casualty's mask hood and feeling for a pulse at the carotid artery. Request medical assistance as soon as the tactical situation permits.

heading: Combat Lifesaver Assistance for Nerve Agent Poisoning
text: The CLS should administer additional CANA or AAS to casualties suffering from convulsions. Administer a second, and if needed, a third CANA or AAS at 5-to-10-minute intervals for a maximum of three injections (30mg diazepam or 30mg midazolam). Follow the steps and procedures described in paragraph 19-49 on page 201 for administering the CANA or AAS. DO NOT give more than two additional injections for a total of three (one self-aid plus two by the CLS).

heading: BLISTER AGENTS
text: Blister agents (vesicants) include mustard, nitrogen mustards, lewisite, and other arsenicals, mixtures of mustards and arsenicals, and phosgene oxime. Blister agents may act on the eyes, mucous membranes, lungs, and skin. They burn and blister the skin or any other body parts they contact. Even relatively low doses may cause serious injury. Blister agents damage the respiratory tract (nose, sinuses, and windpipe) when inhaled and cause vomiting and diarrhea when absorbed. Lewisite and phosgene oxime cause immediate pain on contact. However, mustard agents are deceptive as there is little or no pain at the time of exposure. In some cases, signs of injury may not appear for several hours after exposure.

heading: Protective Measures for Blister Agent Poisoning
text: Your protective mask with hood and protective over garment provides protection against blister agents. If it is known or suspected that blister agents are being used, STOP BREATHING, put on your mask and your protective over garment.

notices.text: Large drops of liquid vesicants on the protective over garment ensemble may penetrate it if allowed to stand for an extended period. Remove large drops as soon as possible.

heading: Signs and Symptoms of Blister Agent Poisoning
text: Immediate and intense pain upon contact with L, LH (lewisite and mustard) mixture, and phosgene oxime. No initial pain upon contact with mustard.

heading: Signs and Symptoms of Blister Agent Poisoning
text: Inflammation and blisters (burns) resulting in tissue destruction. The severity of a chemical burn is directly related to the concentration of the agent and the duration of contact with the skin. The longer the agent is in contact with the tissue, the more serious the injury will be.

heading: Signs and Symptoms of Blister Agent Poisoning
text: Vomiting and diarrhea. Exposure to high concentrations of vesicants may cause vomiting or diarrhea.

heading: Signs and Symptoms of Blister Agent Poisoning
text: The blister agent vapors absorbed during ordinary field exposure will probably not cause enough internal body (systemic) damage to result in death. However, death may occur from prolonged exposure to high concentrations of vapor or from extensive liquid contamination over wide areas of the skin, particularly when decontamination is neglected or delayed.

heading: First Aid Measures for Blister Agent Poisoning
text: Use your RSDL to decontaminate your skin and use water to flush contaminated eyes. Decontamination of vesicants must be done immediately (within one minute is best).

heading: First Aid Measures for Blister Agent Poisoning
text: If blisters form, cover them loosely with a field dressing and secure the dressing.

notices.text: Blisters are burns. DO NOT attempt to decontaminate the skin where blisters have formed, as the agent has already been absorbed.

heading: First Aid Measures for Blister Agent Poisoning
text: If you receive blisters over a wide area of the body, you are considered seriously burned. Seek medical assistance immediately.

heading: First Aid Measures for Blister Agent Poisoning
text: If vomiting occurs, the mask should be lifted momentarily and drained. Make sure, while doing this, the eyes are closed, and the breath is held. As soon as it is complete, replace, clear, and seal the mask.

heading: First Aid Measures for Blister Agent Poisoning
text: Remember, if vomiting or diarrhea occurs after having been exposed to blister agents, seek medical assistance immediately.

heading: CHOKING AGENTS (LUNG-DAMAGING AGENTS)
text: Chemical agents that attack lung tissue, primarily causing fluid buildup (pulmonary edema), are classified as choking agents (lung-damaging agents). This group includes phosgene, diphosgene (known as DP), chlorine (known as Cl), and chloropicrin (known as PS). Of these four agents, phosgene is the most dangerous and is more likely to be employed by the enemy in future conflict. Your protective mask gives adequate protection against choking agents.

heading: Signs and Symptoms for Choking Agents
text:
During and immediately after exposure to choking agents (depending on agent concentration and length of exposure), you may experience some or all the following signs and symptoms:
- Tears (lacrimation).
- Coughing.
- Choking.
- Tightness of chest.
- Nausea and vomiting.
- Headaches.

heading: Self-Aid for Choking Agents
text: The protective mask should be put on immediately when any of the conditions described above exist. Another indication of a phosgene attack is an odor like newly mown hay; however, DO NOT rely upon odor as indication of a chemical attack.

heading: Self-Aid for Choking Agents
text: If some phosgene is inhaled, normal combat duties should be continued unless there is difficulty in breathing, nausea, vomiting, or more than the usual shortness of breath during exertion. If any of the above symptoms occur and the mission permits, remain at quiet rest until MEDEVAC is accomplished.

heading: Death from Choking Agents
text: With ordinary field exposure to choking agents, death will probably not occur. However, prolonged exposure to high concentrations of the vapor and neglect, or delay in masking can be fatal.

heading: Cyanogen (Blood) Agents
text: Cyanogen agents interfere with proper oxygen utilization in the body. Hydrogen cyanide (AC) and cyanogen chloride are the primary agents in this group.

heading: Protective Measures for Cyanogen Agents
text: The protective mask with a fresh filter gives adequate protection against field concentrations of cyanogen agent vapor. Protective over garments, as well as the mask, are needed when exposed to liquid AC hydrogen cyanide.

heading: Signs and Symptoms for Cyanogen Agents
text:
During and immediately after exposure to cyanogen agents (depending on agent concentration and length of exposure), you may experience some or all the following signs and symptoms:
- Tearing (lacrimation).
- Eye, nose, and throat irritation.
- Sudden stimulation of breathing (unable to hold breath).
- Nausea.
- Coughing.
- Tightness of chest.
- Headache.
- Light-headedness (dizziness).
- Unconsciousness.

heading: First Aid for Cyanogen Agents
text: Hydrogen cyanide. During any chemical attack, if you get a sudden stimulation to breathe or detect an odor like bitter almonds, PUT ON YOUR MASK IMMEDIATELY. Speed is essential since this agent acts so rapidly that within a few seconds its effects will make it impossible for Service members to put on their mask by themselves. Stop breathing until the mask is on. This may be very difficult since the agent strongly stimulates respiration.

heading: First Aid for Cyanogen Agents
text: Cyanogen chloride. Put your mask on immediately if you experience any irritation of the eyes, nose, or throat. The nearest Service member should mask Service members who are unable to mask themselves.

notices.text: Before attempting to help anyone else, make sure you appropriately mask yourself first.

heading: Medical Assistance for Cyanogen Agents
text: If exposure to blood agents is suspected, immediate medical assistance is needed. Medical assistance for cyanogen agents is crucial because cyanogen is a highly toxic compound that poses significant health risks to humans. Cyanogen is a colorless gas that can be lethal when inhaled or when it encounters the skin or eyes.

heading: INCAPACITATING AGENTS
text: An incapacitating agent is a chemical agent that produces temporary, disabling conditions, which persist for hours to days after exposure. Unlike riot control agents, which usually are momentary or fleeting in action, incapacitating agents have a persistent effect. It is likely that smoke-producing munitions or aerosols will disseminate such agents, thus making breathing their means of entry into the body. The protective mask is, therefore, essential.

heading: INCAPACITATING AGENTS
text: There are no specific first aid measures to relieve the symptoms of incapacitating agents. Supportive first aid and physical restraint may be indicated. If the casualty is stuporous or comatose, be sure that respiration is unobstructed; then turn them on their side in case vomiting should occur. Complete cleansing of the skin with soap and water, this should be done as soon as possible; or RSDL can be used if washing is impossible. Remove weapons and other potentially harmful items from Service members who are suspected of having these symptoms. Harmful items include cigarettes, matches, medications, and small items that might be swallowed accidentally. Delirious (confused) persons have been known to attempt to eat items bearing only a superficial resemblance to food.

heading: INCAPACITATING AGENTS
text: Incapacitating agents (anticholinergic drugs BZ type) may produce alarming dryness and coating of the lips and tongue; however, there is usually no danger of immediate dehydration. Fluids should be given sparingly, if at all, because of the danger of vomiting and because of the likelihood of temporary urinary retention due to paralysis of bladder muscles.

heading: INCAPACITATING AGENTS
text: Immediate and vigorous cooling of the casualties is indicated if the body temperature is elevated and mucous membranes are dry, (as for heatstroke). The casualty can be cooled by spraying them with cool water and fanning; applying alcohol-soaked cloths and air circulation; and providing maximum exposure to air in a shaded area, along with maximum air circulation. Such cases are usually a result of anticholinergic poisoning.

notices.text: DO NOT use ice for cooling the skin.

heading: INCAPACITATING AGENTS
text: Rapid evacuation should be accomplished since medical treatment with the appropriate medication may be lifesaving. Reassurance and a firm, but friendly, attitude by individuals providing first aid will be beneficial if the casualty appears to comprehend what is being said. Conversation is a waste of time if the Service member is incoherent or cannot understand what is being said. In such cases, the less said, the better it is. These casualties will benefit more from prompt and vigorous restraint and evacuation to an MTF.

heading: INCENDIARIES
text: Incendiaries can be grouped as white phosphorus (WP), thickened gasoline, metal, and oil and metal. You must learn to protect yourself against these incendiaries.

heading: White Phosphorus
text: WP is primarily used as a smoke-producing agent but also serves an incendiary role for igniting field expedients and combustible materials. The burns caused by WP are typically multiple, deep, and vary in size. Once WP particles contact the skin or clothing, they will continue to burn until deprived of air, and they tend to adhere to any surface they contact, requiring physical removal.

heading: White Phosphorus
text: In the event that WP particles ignite clothing, it's crucial to remove the contaminated clothing quickly to prevent the WP from burning through to the skin. If WP particles directly strike the skin, the immediate response should be to smother the flames using water, a wet cloth, or mud. It is important to note that since WP is soluble in oil, one should not use grease or oily substances to extinguish the flames as these can exacerbate the burning.

heading: White Phosphorus
text: To prevent further combustion, keep the WP particles covered with wet material to exclude air. Removal of WP particles from the skin should be done cautiously using a wet cloth to brush them away and a knife, bayonet, stick, or other available tools to pick them out.

heading: White Phosphorus
text: Once immediate first aid measures are taken, it is vital to seek medical assistance as soon as the mission allows us to address any burns or injuries caused by WP exposure properly.

heading: Thickened Fuel Mixtures (Napalm)
text: Thickened fuel mixtures (napalm) tend to cling to clothing and body surfaces, thereby producing prolonged exposure and severe burns. The first aid for these burns is the same as for other heat burns. The heat and irritating gases given off by these combustible mixtures may cause lung damage, which must be treated by medical personnel.

heading: Metal Incendiaries
text: Metal incendiaries pose special problems. Thermite particles on the skin should be immediately cooled with water and then removed. The first aid for these burns is the same as for other heat burns. Particles of magnesium on the skin burn quickly and deeply. Like other metal incendiaries, they must be removed. Ordinarily, medical personnel should do the complete removal of these particles as soon as possible. Immediate medical treatment is required.

heading: Oil and Metal Incendiaries
text: Oil and metal incendiaries, upon contact with skin and clothing, produce effects similar to those caused by white phosphorus. These substances can cause severe burns that require immediate and proper first aid attention to prevent further damage and promote healing. For detailed guidance on administering first aid for burns resulting from exposure to incendiaries like oil and metal, see Chapter 12. This chapter provides comprehensive instructions on the steps to take in treating burns, including how to manage the injury before professional medical help is available.

heading: FIRST AID IN A BIOLOGICAL ENVIRONMENT
text:
Biological hazards can provide important advantages to adversaries who use them because of factors such as--
- Clandestine employment.
- Delayed onset of symptoms.
- Detection, identification, and verification difficulties.
- Agent persistence.
- Communicability.

heading: FIRST AID IN A BIOLOGICAL ENVIRONMENT
text: Biological attacks can result in combat ineffectiveness by introducing disease-causing organisms such as bacteria or viruses into the force through aerosol release; food and water contamination; vectors such as ticks, fleas, mosquitoes, or body fluids from infected animals or humans. The occurrence of the signs and symptoms from a biological hazard may appear in a few minutes to several hours or days to weeks depending on the biological hazard, the Service member's susceptibility, and the amount of biological hazard that is inhaled, ingested, or deposited on the skin. Many biological warfare agents present the same signs and symptoms as the flu or common cold such as fever, cough, runny nose, and tiredness.

heading: FIRST AID IN A BIOLOGICAL ENVIRONMENT
text: First aid or medical treatment is initiated after a disease is identified, depending on the seriousness of the disease. First aid measures are concerned with observable symptoms of the disease such as diarrhea or vomiting. For certain biological warfare hazards, Service members may be directed to take doxycycline or ciprofloxacin from the initial issue medical CBRN defense materiel.

heading: TOXINS
text: Toxins have reportedly been used in past conflicts. Witnesses and survivors have described the employment of the T-2 mycotoxin as toxic rain (or yellow rain) because it was reported to have been released from aircraft as a yellow powder or liquid that covered ground, structures, vegetation, and people.

heading: Signs and Symptoms of Toxin Poisoning
text:
The occurrence of the symptoms from toxins may appear in a period of a few minutes to several hours depending on the toxin, the Service member's susceptibility, and the amount of toxin that is inhaled, ingested, or deposited on the skin. Symptoms from toxins usually involve the central nervous system but are often preceded by less prominent symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cramps, stomach irritation, and burning sensation. Typical neurological symptoms often develop rapidly in severe cases; for example, visual disturbances, inability to swallow, speech difficulty, lack of muscle coordination, and sensory abnormalities (numbness of the mouth, throat, or extremities). Yellow rain (mycotoxins) also may have hemorrhagic symptoms, which could include any or all of the following:
- Dizziness.
- Severe itching or tingling of the skin.
- Formation of multiple, small, or hard blisters.
- Coughing up blood.
- Shock (which could result in death).

heading: Self-Aid of Toxin Poisoning
text:
Upon recognition of an attack employing toxins, you must immediately take the following actions:
- Stop breathing, put on your protective mask with hood, and then resume breathing. Next, put on your protective ensemble.
- Should itching of the face become severe or unbearable, quickly--
- Loosen the cap in your canteen or valve on your water source.
- Take and hold a deep breath and lift your mask.
- While holding your breath, close your eyes and flush your face with generous amounts of water.

notices.text:
DO NOT rub or scratch your eyes. Try not to let the water run onto your clothing or protective over garment.
- Put your protective mask back on, seat it properly, clear it, and check it for a seal; then resume breathing.
- Decontaminate your skin by bathing with soap and water as soon as the mission permits.
- Change clothing and decontaminate your protective mask using soap and water. Replace the filters if directed.

heading: Self-Aid of Toxin Poisoning
text: If vomiting occurs, the mask should be lifted momentarily and drained. While doing this, keep your eyes closed, and hold your breath. The mask is then replaced, cleared, and sealed.

heading: Medical Assistance for Toxin Poisoning
text: If you think you might have been exposed to harmful substances, it's important to get medical help right away. Seeing a doctor quickly can ensure you get the care you need.

heading: FIRST AID IN A RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR ENVIRONMENT
text: Three types of injuries may result from nuclear detonation. These are thermal, blast, and radiation injuries. Many times, the casualty will have a combination of these types of injuries. First aid for thermal and blast injuries is provided based on observable injuries, such as burns, hemorrhage, or fractures.

heading: FIRST AID IN A RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR ENVIRONMENT
text: The signs and symptoms of radiation illness in the initial phase include the rapid onset of nausea, vomiting, and malaise (tiredness) with first aid measures focused on those observable symptoms and decontamination. If radioactive iodine is released, Service members may be directed to take potassium iodide from the initial issue medical CBRN defense materiel. Potassium iodide is only effective if taken within four hours before or after exposure to radiation from a nuclear or radiological incident. For additional information on first aid in a radiological and nuclear environment see paragraph 1-85 on page 16 or refer to DODM 3150.8, JP 3-11, or ATP 4-02.83.

heading: OVERVIEW OF COMBAT AND OPERATIONAL STRESS CONTROL
text: Psychological first aid is just as crucial as physical first aid and is a familiar concept to many. Think back to when a simple comforting gesture from a parent soothed you as a child, or how supportive conversation with a friend helped you navigate through disappointment or grief. These actions are natural responses to emotional distress, similar to how we instinctively want to help someone who is physically hurt.

heading: OVERVIEW OF COMBAT AND OPERATIONAL STRESS CONTROL
text: Just as we use bandages to cover wounds, we use supportive words and actions to help heal emotional wounds. Psychological first aid involves assisting those who are emotionally distressed, whether due to physical injuries, illness, or overwhelming stress. Signs of emotional distress, like overexcitement, severe fear, excessive worry, deep depression, or anger, can sometimes be less visible than physical injuries but are equally important to address.

heading: OVERVIEW OF COMBAT AND OPERATIONAL STRESS CONTROL
text: These emotional reactions are indicators that stress is impacting someone's ability to cope effectively. When these symptoms become more pronounced, the need for psychological support becomes more urgent. Knowing how to offer this support is essential, as it can significantly aid in someone's recovery process, just as much as treating a physical ailment.

heading: PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
text: You must know how to give psychological first aid to be able to help yourself, your team members, and your unit to keep performing the mission. Psychological first aid measures are simple and easy to understand. Your decision of what to do depends upon your ability to observe the Service member and understand their needs. Making the best use of resources requires ingenuity on your part. A stress reaction resulting in poor judgment can cause injury or even death to yourself or others on the battlefield. It can be even more dangerous if other personnel are affected by the judgment of an emotionally upset Service member. If it is detected early enough, the affected Service member stands a good chance of remaining in their unit as an effective member. If it is not detected early and if the Service member becomes more emotionally upset, they may become a threat to themselves and to others.

heading: SITUATIONS REQUIRING PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
text: Psychological first aid (buddy aid) is most needed at the first sign that a Service member cannot perform the mission because of emotional distress. Stress is inevitable in combat, in hostage and terrorist situations, and in civilian disasters such as floods, hurricanes, or industrial accidents. Most emotional reactions to such situations are temporary, and the Service member can still carry on with encouragement. Painful or disruptive symptoms may last for minutes, hours, or days. However, if the stress symptoms are seriously disabling, they may be psychologically contagious and endanger not only the emotionally upset Service member but also the entire unit.

heading: SITUATIONS REQUIRING PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
text: Sometimes people continue to function well during a disastrous event, but suffer from emotional scars, which impair their job performance or quality of life later. Painful memories and dreams may recur for months and years and still be considered a normal reaction. However, an individual needs treatment if the memories are so painful that the person must avoid all situations which arouse them, becomes socially withdrawn, show symptoms of anxiety, depression, or substance abuse. Experience with police, firefighters, emergency medical technicians, and others who deal with disasters have proved that the routine application of psychological first aid to all the participants, including those who have functioned well, greatly reduces the likelihood of future serious post-traumatic stress disorder(s).

heading: INTERRELATIONSHIP OF PSYCHOLOGICAL AND PHYSICAL FIRST AID
text: Psychological first aid should go together with physical first aid. The discovery of a physical injury or cause for an inability to function does not rule out the possibility of a psychological injury (or vice versa). The person suffering from pain, shock, fear of serious injury, or fear of death does not respond well to joking, indifference, or fearful-tearful attention. Fear and anxiety may take as high a toll of on the Service member's strength as does the loss of blood.

heading: GOALS OF PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
text: Psychological First Aid is aimed at supporting Service members in managing immediate stress reactions effectively, ensuring both the well-being of the individual and the operational readiness of the unit. The primary goals of Psychological First Aid are multifaceted, focusing on immediate mental health support, safety, and a swift return to duty.

heading: GOALS OF PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
text: The first and foremost goal of Psychological First Aid is to provide empathetic support to Service members experiencing stress reactions. By offering a supportive presence, responders can help individuals navigate their emotional responses effectively. This involves active listening, acknowledging their feelings without judgment, and providing reassurance. This supportive approach is crucial in helping Service members feel understood and less isolated in their experiences.

heading: GOALS OF PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
text: Another critical aim of Psychological First Aid is to prevent and control behaviors that could be harmful to the individual or others. This includes identifying signs of distress that might lead to harmful actions and implementing strategies to mitigate these risks. The ability to intervene early and effectively can prevent the escalation of stress reactions into more serious mental health issues, thereby maintaining the safety and cohesion of the unit.

heading: GOALS OF PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
text: Finally, Psychological First Aid seeks to return the Service member to duty as efficiently as possible after addressing their immediate psychological needs. This goal underscores the importance of resilience and rapid recovery within military operations, ensuring that personnel are mentally fit to resume their roles. Facilitating a quick return to duty not only helps maintain unit effectiveness but also promotes a sense of normalcy and purpose for the individual, which can be therapeutic in overcoming stress reactions.

heading: RESPECT FOR OTHERS' FEELINGS
text: Accept the Service member you are trying to help without censorship or ridicule. Respect their right to their own feelings. Even though your feelings, beliefs, and behavior are different, do not blame or make light of them for the way they feel or act. Your purpose is to help them in this tough situation, not to be their critic. A person does not want to be upset and worried. When they seek help, they need and expect consideration of their fears, not abrupt dismissal, or ridicule.

heading: RESPECT FOR OTHERS' FEELINGS
text: Realize that people are the products of a wide variety of factors. All people do not react the same way to the same situations. Everyone has complex needs and motivations, both conscious and unconscious, that are uniquely their own. Often the one thing that finally causes the person to become overloaded by a stressful situation is not the stressor itself, but some other problem.

heading: EMOTIONAL AND PHYSICAL DISABILITY
text: Accept emotional disability as being just as real as physical disability. If a Service member's ankle is seriously sprained in a fall, no one expects them to run right away. A Service member's emotions may be temporarily strained by the overwhelming stress of battle or another traumatic incident. Do not demand that they pull themselves together immediately and carry on without a break. Some individuals can pull themselves together immediately, but others cannot. The Service member whose emotional stability has been disrupted has a disability just as real as the Service member who has sprained their ankle. There is an unfortunate tendency in many people to regard as real only what they can see, such as a wound or bleeding. Some people tend to assume that damage involving a person's mind and emotions is just imagined, they are not sick or injured, and that they could overcome their trouble by using their will power.

heading: EMOTIONAL AND PHYSICAL DISABILITY
text: The phrases "it is all in your head", "snap out of it", and "get control of yourself" are often used by people who believe they are being helpful. These terms are expressions of hostility because they show lack of understanding. They only emphasize weakness and inadequacy. The above stated phrases are of no use in psychological first aid.

heading: EMOTIONAL AND PHYSICAL DISABILITY
text: Every physically injured person has some emotional reaction to the fact that they are injured. It is normal for an injured person to feel upset. The more severe the injury, the more insecure and fearful they become, especially if the injury is to a body part that is highly valued. For example, an injury to the eyes or the genitals, even though relatively minor, is likely to be extremely upsetting. An injury to some other part of the body may be especially disturbing to an individual for their own reason. For example, an injury to the hand may be a terrifying blow to a surgeon, or an injury to the eye of a pilot.

heading: EMOTIONAL AND PHYSICAL DISABILITY
text: An injured Service member can sometimes feel less secure, more anxious, and more afraid not only because of what has happened to them but also what they imagine may happen because of their injury. This fear and insecurity may cause them to be irritable, uncooperative, or unreasonable. As you help the Service member, always keep in mind that such behavior has little or nothing to do with you personally. They need your patience, reassurance, encouragement, and support.

heading: COMBAT AND OPERATIONAL STRESS REACTION
text: Stress reaction is a temporary emotional disorder or inability to function, experienced by a previously normal Service member as a reaction to the overwhelming or cumulative stress of combat. Stress reaction gets better with reassurance, rest, physical replenishment, and activities that restore confidence. All Service members are likely to feel stressed under conditions of intense or prolonged stress. They may even become stress reaction casualties and are unable to perform their mission for hours or days. Other combat and operational stress reactions may result in negative behavior, but are not termed stress reaction, as they need treatment that is more intensive. These negative combat and operational stress reactions may result in misconduct and stress behaviors such as drug and alcohol abuse, criminal acts, looting, desertion, and selfinflicted wounds. These harmful combat and operational stress reactions can often be prevented by good psychological first aid. Service members who commit misconduct stress behaviors may require disciplinary action rather than medical treatment.

heading: REACTIONS TO STRESS
text: Most Service members react to stressful incidents after the situation has passed. Service members feel some fear. This fear may be greater than they have experienced at any other time, or they may be more aware of their fear. In such a situation, they should not be surprised if they feel shaky or become sweaty, nauseated, or confused. These reactions are normal and are not a cause for concern. However, some reactions, either short- or long-term, will cause problems if left unchecked.

heading: Emotional Reactions
text:
The most obvious combat and operational stress reaction is inefficient performance. This can be demonstrated by--
- Slow thinking (or reaction time).
- Difficulty recognizing priorities and seeing what needs to be done.
- Difficulty getting started.
- Indecisiveness and having trouble focusing.
- Tendency to do familiar tasks and be preoccupied with familiar details. (This can reach the point in which the person is very passive, sitting or wandering, and not knowing what to do).

heading: Emotional Reactions
text: A less common reaction may be uncontrolled emotional outbursts; this can be demonstrated by crying, screaming, or laughing. Some Service members will react in the opposite way. They can show signs of being very withdrawn, silent, and try to isolate themselves from everyone. These Service members should be encouraged to remain with their assigned unit. Uncontrolled reactions may appear by themselves or in any combination. The person may be crying uncontrollably one minute and then laughing the next. In this state, the person is restless and cannot keep still. They may run about, apparently without purpose. Inside, they feel a great rage or fear and their physical acts may show this. In their anger, they may indiscriminately strike out at others.

heading: Loss of Adaptability
text: In a desperate attempt to get away from the danger, which has overwhelmed them, a Service member may panic and become confused. Their mental ability may be so impaired they cannot think clearly or even follow simple commands. Their judgment may be faulty, and they may not be aware of their actions, such as standing up in their fighting position during an attack.

heading: Loss of Adaptability
text: In other cases, overwhelming stress may produce symptoms that are often associated with head injuries. For example, the Service member may appear dazed or be found wandering around aimlessly. They may appear confused and disoriented and may seem to have a complete or partial loss of memory. In such cases, especially when no eyewitnesses can provide evidence that the Service member has NOT suffered a head injury, it is necessary for them to be rapidly evacuated. DO NOT allow the Service members to expose themselves to further personal danger until the cause of the problem has been determined.

heading: Sleep Disturbance and Repetition of Dreams
text: A person who has been overwhelmed by stress, often has difficulty sleeping. The Service member may experience nightmares related to the stressors. Remember that nightmares, in themselves, are not considered abnormal when they occur soon after a period of intensive stress. As time passes, the nightmares usually become less frequent and less intense. In extreme cases, a Service member, even when awake, may think repeatedly of the incident, feel as though it is happening again, and act out parts of their stress repeatedly.

heading: Sleep Disturbance and Repetition of Dreams
text: For some individuals, this repetitious re-experiencing of the stressful event may be necessary for eventual recovery; therefore, it should not be discouraged or viewed as abnormal. For the person reexperiencing the event, such reaction may be disruptive. The Service member needs to be encouraged to ventilate about the incident. Ventilation is a technique where the Service member is given the opportunity to talk extensively and often repetitiously about the experience.

heading: Severe Stress or Stress Reaction
text: You do not need specialized training to recognize severe stress or stress reaction that will cause problems for the Service member, the unit, or the mission. Reactions that are less severe, however, are more difficult to detect. To determine whether a person needs help, you must observe them to see whether they are doing something meaningful, performing their duties, taking care of themselves, behaving in an unusual fashion, or acting out of character.

heading: APPLICATION OF PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
text: The emotionally disturbed Service member has built a barrier against fear. They do this for their own protection, although they are probably not aware that they are doing it. If they find that they do not have to be afraid and that there are normal, understandable things about them, they will feel safer in dropping this barrier. Persistent efforts to make them realize that you want to understand them will be reassuring, especially if you remain calm. Nothing can cause an emotionally disturbed person to become even more fearful than feeling that others are afraid of them. Try to remain calm. Familiar things, such as a cup of coffee, the use of their name, attention to a minor wound, being given a simple job to do, or the sight of familiar people and activities, will add to their ability to overcome their fear. They may not respond well if you get excited, angry, or abrupt.

heading: Ventilation
text: After the Service member becomes calmer, they are likely to have dreams about the stressful event. They also may think about it when they are awake or even repeat their personal reaction to the event. One benefit of this natural pattern is that it helps them master the stress by going over it just as one master the initial fear of parachuting from an aircraft by doing it repeatedly. Eventually, it is difficult to remember how frightening the event was initially. In giving first aid to the emotionally disturbed Service members, you should let them follow this natural pattern. Encourage them to talk. Be a good listener. Let them tell you, in their own words, what happened. If home front problems or worries have contributed to stress, it will help them to talk about these problems. Your patient listening will prove to the Service member that you are interested in them, and by describing their personal problem, they can work at mastering their fear. If they become overwhelmed, suggest a cup of coffee or a break. Whatever you do, assure them that you will listen again as soon as they are ready. Try to help put the Service member's perception of what happened back into realistic perspective; but DO NOT argue about it.

heading: Activity
text: A person who is emotionally disturbed as the result of a combat action is a casualty of anxiety and fear. The person may feel as though they are disabled because they have become temporarily overwhelmed by their anxiety. A good way to control fear is through activity. For example, almost all Service members experience a considerable sense of anxiety and fear while they are poised, awaiting the opening of a big offensive; but this is normally relieved, and they feel better once they begin to move into action. They take pride in effective performance and pleasure in knowing that they are a good Service member, perhaps being completely unaware that overcoming their initial fear was their first major accomplishment.

heading: Activity
text: Useful activity can be very beneficial to Service members who are emotionally disturbed and not physically incapacitated. After you help a Service member get over their initial fear, help them to regain some self-confidence. Help them realize their job continues by finding them something useful to do. Encourage them to be active. Get them to help load trucks, clean up debris, or dig fighting positions. If possible, get them back to their usual duty. Seek out their strong points and help them apply these attributes. Avoid having them just sit around. You may have to provide directions by telling them what to do and where to do it. The instructions should be clear, simple, and should be repeated. A person who has panicked is likely to argue. Respect their feelings, but point out more immediate, obtainable, and demanding needs. Channel their excessive energy and, above all, DO NOT argue. If you cannot get them to become interested in doing profitable work, it may be necessary to enlist aid in controlling their over-activity before it results in more panic. Prevent the spread of such infectious feelings by restraining and segregating if necessary.

heading: Activity
text:
Involvement in an activity helps the Service member in three ways; they--
- Place their thoughts on something more productive.
- Have an outlet for their excessive tensions.
- Prove to them that they can do something useful.

heading: Rest
text: There are times, particularly in combat, when physical exhaustion is a principal cause for emotional reactions. A unit sleep plan should be established and implemented. When possible, Service members should be given a safe and relatively comfortable area in which to sleep. Examples would be an area away from heavy traffic, noise, congestion, a place that is clean, dry, and protected from environmental conditions. The more uninterrupted sleep a Service member gets the better they will be able to function in the tactical environment.

heading: Hygiene
text: Field hygiene is an important ingredient in a Service member's morale. A Service member who is lacking personal hygiene will not function as well as others who have had the opportunity to bathe and put on clean, dry clothing. During combat, unit leaders should stress the importance of personal hygiene. Good personal hygiene not only improves morale, but it is also a preventive measure against disease and disease and nonbattle injury.

heading: Group Activity
text: You have probably already noticed that a person who works, faces danger, and handles serious problems better if they are a member of a closely-knit group. Each Service member in the team supports the other team members. Esprit de corps is built because the Service members have the same interests, goals, and mission. As a result, they are more productive; and are less worried because everyone is involved. This is one of the most effective tools you have in your psychological first aid bag. Getting the Service member back into the team or squad activities will re-establish their sense of belonging and security. This will go far toward making them a useful member of the unit.

heading: REACTIONS AND LIMITATIONS
text: Up to this point, the discussion has been primarily about the feelings of the emotionally distressed Service member. What about your feelings towards them? Whatever the situation, you will have emotional reactions (conscious or unconscious) toward this Service member. Your reactions can either help or hinder your ability to help them. When you are tired or worried, you may very easily become impatient with them if they are unusually slow or exaggerated. You may even feel resentful toward them. Physical wounds can be seen and easily accepted. Emotional reactions are more difficult to accept as injuries. On the other hand, you tend to be overly sympathetic. Excessive sympathy for an incapacitated person can be as harmful as negative feelings in your relationship with them. They need strong help, but not your sorrow. To overwhelm them with pity may make them feel even more inadequate. You must expect your buddy to recover, to be able to return to duty, and to become a useful Service member again. This expectation should be displayed in your behavior and attitude as well as in what you say. If they can see your calmness, confidence, and competence, they will be reassured and will feel a sense of greater security. For more information on stress reactions see tables 20-1, table 20-2 on page 215 and table 20-3 on page 216.

heading: PHYSICAL SIGNS* EMOTIONAL SIGNS*
text: 1. Trembling, tearful. 1. Anxiety, indecisiveness. 2. Jumpiness, nervousness. 2. Irritable, complaining. 3. Cold sweat, dry mouth. 3. Forgetful, unable to concentrate. 4. Pounding heart, dizziness. 4. Easily startled by noise, movement. 5. Insomnia, nightmares. 5. Grief, tearful. 6. Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. 6. Anger, beginning to lose confidence in self and unit. 7. Fatigue. 8. Thousand-yard stare. 9. Difficulty thinking, speaking, and communicating.

heading: SELF- AND BUDDY AID
text:
1. Continue mission performance and focus on the immediate mission. 2. Expect Service members to perform the assigned duties. 3. Always remain calm; be directive, and in control. 4. Let Service member know their reaction is normal, and that there is nothing seriously wrong with them. 5. Keep the Service member informed of the situation, objectives, expectations, and support. Control rumors. 6. Build Service members' confidence, talk about succeeding. 7. Keep Service member productive (when not resting) through recreational activities, equipment, maintenance, and resupply. 8. Ensure Service members maintain good personal hygiene. 9. Ensure Service member eats, drinks, and sleeps as soon as possible. 10. Let the Service member talk about their feelings. Do not "put down" their feelings of grief or worry. Give practical advice and put emotions into perspective.
- Most or all of these signs are present in mild stress reaction. They can be present in any normal Service member in combat, yet they can still do their job.

heading: PHYSICAL SIGNS * EMOTIONAL SIGNS *
text: 1. Constantly moves around. 1. Rapid and/or inappropriate talking. 2. Argumentative, reckless movements, or 2. Flinching or ducking at sudden sounds. actions. 3. Shaking, trembling (whole body or arms). 3. Inattentive to personal hygiene. 4. Cannot use parts of the body, no physical reason 4. Indifferent to danger. (hands, arms, or legs). 5. Cannot see, hear, or feel (partial or complete loss of 5. Memory loss. senses). 6. Severe stuttering, mumbling, or cannot speak 6. Physical exhaustion, crying. at all. 7. Freezing under fire, or total immobility. 7. Insomnia, nightmares. 8. Vacant stares, staggers, and sways when they stand. 8. Seeing or hearing things that do not exist. 9. Panic running under fire. 9. Rapid emotional shifts. 10. Social withdrawal. 11. Apathetic. 12. Hysterical outbursts. 13. Frantic or strange behavior.

heading: TREATMENT PROCEDURES **
text:
1. If a Service member's behavior endangers the mission, self, or others, do whatever is necessary to control them. 2. If the Service member is upset, calmly talk them into cooperating. 3. If concerned about the Service member's reliability:
- Unload their weapon.
- Take weapons if seriously concerned.
- Physically restrain them only when necessary for safety or transportation. 4. Reassure everyone that the signs are probably just stress reaction and will quickly improve. 5. If stress reaction signs continue:
- Get the Service member to a safer place.
- Do not leave the Service member alone, keep someone they know with them.
- Notify the senior noncommissioned officer or officer.
- Have the Service member examined by medical personnel. 6. Give the Service member easy tasks to do when they are not sleeping, eating, or resting. 7. Assure the Service member they will return to full duty in 24 hours; and return them to normal duty as soon as they are ready.
- These signs are present in addition to the signs of mild stress reaction. ** Do these procedures in addition to the self- and buddy aid care.

heading: Preventive Measures
text:
1. Welcome new Service members into your team and get to know them quickly. If you are new, be active in making friends. 2. Be physically fit (strength, endurance, and agility). 3. Know and practice lifesaving self- and buddy aid. 4. Practice rapid relaxation techniques. 5. Help each other out when things are tough at home or in the unit. 6. Keep informed; ask your leader questions, ignore rumors. 7. Work together to give everyone food, water, shelter, hygiene, and sanitation. 8. Sleep when the mission and safety permit; let everyone get time to sleep. Follow these sleep rules:
- Sleep only in safe places and by standard operating procedure.
- If possible, sleep six to nine hours per day.
- Try to get at least four hours of sleep per day.
- Get good sleep before going on sustained operations.
- Take a nap when you can but allow time to wake up fully.
- Catch up on sleep after going without.

heading: SUPPORTING AT-RISK SERVICE MEMBERS
text: Taking care of fellow Service members is a fundamental duty within the DOD, emphasizing the critical role of teamwork and the inherent value of each individual. Essential to this dynamic is the implementation of the battle-buddy concept, particularly when addressing COSR. Vigilance, appropriate intervention, and thorough follow-through are key elements in fostering a supportive environment.

heading: SUPPORTING AT-RISK SERVICE MEMBERS
text: The optimal initial response to Service member stress involves the caring and observant presence of battle buddies and leaders. The DOD supports this approach through a robust framework that extends from individual Service members to the highest levels of leadership, facilitating COSC. It is imperative that Service members recognize signs of distress among their peers, seek help, and provide consistent support.

heading: SUPPORTING AT-RISK SERVICE MEMBERS
text:
In the context of handling COSRs, the "ACE" acronym--standing for Acknowledge, Care, and Escort--serves as a concise and memorable strategy. This method is crucial for both Service members and leaders in managing stress reactions effectively:
- Acknowledge: The first critical step is recognizing potential stress reactions in colleagues. This requires alertness to behavioral and emotional shifts that may suggest a Service member is struggling. Trusting one's instincts and taking any signs of distress seriously are essential in this initial phase.
- Care: After recognizing a colleague's distress, providing immediate support is vital. This support can include offering reassurance, listening with empathy, and creating a safe, non-judgmental environment for the individual to share their experiences. It's important to affirm that their reactions are normal responses to the stressful situations they have encountered.
- Escort: The final step involves guiding the affected Service member to suitable professional resources. This could mean directing them to a mental health expert, a chaplain, or another unit leader who can offer further support and advice. Ensuring the individual receives appropriate help is crucial and helps to mitigate any stigma associated with seeking mental health support.

heading: SUPPORTING AT-RISK SERVICE MEMBERS
text: The Acknowledge, Care, and Escort framework underscores the importance of timely intervention and the need to connect distressed Service members with suitable resources. It offers a practical guide for those who may lack extensive mental health training but are committed to assisting their colleagues.

heading: SUPPORTING AT-RISK SERVICE MEMBERS
text: The Acknowledge, Care, and Escort approach is a preliminary measure and does not substitute for professional mental health evaluation and treatment. Involving mental health professionals is crucial for a comprehensive assessment and care of Service members experiencing COSRs, ensuring they receive the full spectrum of necessary support.

heading: WARRIOR AID AND LITTER KIT
text: The warrior aid and litter kit (WALK) (figure B-1) allows first aid treatment and immediate evacuation of one patient in a CASEVAC vehicle and treatment of multiple trauma patients at the POI. The total weight of the WALK can weigh approximately 29 pounds, 15 ounces. The WALK offers an option for a vehicle life-saving kit.

heading: WARRIOR AID AND LITTER KIT
text:
The system holds a quad-fold litter (see figure B-2 on page 225) and a pocket system containing medical supplies. The WALK contains a hypothermia prevention kit to help stabilize patients during transport. The WALK also includes the following:
- Five pairs of nitrile trauma gloves.
- Two NPAs, size 28 French with lubricant.
- One casualty equipment bag.
- Two CoTCCC approved occlusive chest seals.
- Two combat application TQs.
- Six trauma dressings, six inches.
- Four rolls of rolled gauze, 4.5 inches by 4.1 yards.
- One abdominal emergency trauma dressing.
- Two moldable fracture splints.
- One pair of trauma shears, 7.25 inches.
- One roll surgical tape, two inches.
- One role multipurpose tape.
- Six polycarbonate eye shields.
- Two TCCC cards.
- One aviation panel (Recognition, Orange).
- Four tie-down straps (universal litter).

heading: WARRIOR AID AND LITTER KIT
text: The WALK fits into any standard or nonstandard CASEVAC asset and is useful as part of the prepositioning of medical supplies or cache on a forward operating base, CCP, or at a patrol base.

heading: POLYMER FLEXIBLE LITTER SYSTEM
text: The CoTCCC approved polymer flexible litter system (figure B-3 on page 226) uses a sled design to allow the evacuator to continue returning fire as the casualty is evacuated. It is used for confined space, high angle, or technical rescue, and it provides casualty protection while allowing the aid and litter teams to have their hands free for weapons and security.

heading: POLYMER FLEXIBLE LITTER SYSTEM
text: It is equipped for horizontal hoisting by helicopter or vertical hoisting in caves or industrial confined spaces. When the patient is packaged, the litter becomes rigid. It is rolled for storage in a backpack, which is included with the system. The litter system weighs approximately 17 pounds. This page intentionally left blank.

heading: battalion aid station
text: The forward-most medically staffed treatment location organic to the maneuver battalion. (ATP 4-02.4).

heading: *care under fire
text: The first phase of care in tactical combat casualty care where very limited care is provided for the casualty while the enemy threat is still active. Also known as CUF or care under threat.

heading: casualty
text: Any person who is lost to the organization by having been declared dead, duty status - whereabouts unknown, excused absence-whereabouts unknown, missing, ill, or injured. (JP 4-02).

heading: casualty collection point
text: A location that may or may not be staffed, where casualties are assembled for evacuation to a medical treatment facility. (ATP 4-02.2).

heading: casualty evacuation
text: (Joint) The unregulated movement of casualties aboard any vehicle. Also called CASEVAC. (JP 4-02). (Army) The movement of casualties aboard nonmedical vehicles or aircraft without en route medical care. (ATP 4-02.13).

heading: *casualty response
text: The immediate and organized care, evacuation and reporting of those injured or killed in action.

heading: *combat lifesaver
text: (Joint) Nonmedical Department of Defense person who has received additional trauma training and equipment, providing enhanced medical treatment beyond self-aid/buddy aid. (JP 4-02). (Army) A Soldier trained and equipped to provide enhanced first aid as a secondary mission, known as CLS.

heading: *first aid
text: The immediate lifesaving measures performed on casualties or military working animals.

heading: first responder
text: Is anyone who provides initial and immediate treatment to self or others. (JP 4-02).

heading: medical evacuation
text: The timely and effective movement of the wounded, injured, or ill to and between medical treatment facilities on dedicated and properly marked medical platforms with en route care provided by medical personnel. Also called MEDEVAC. (ATP 4-02.2).

heading: medical treatment facility
text: (Joint) A facility established for the purpose of furnishing medical and/or dental care to eligible individuals. Also called MTF. (JP 4-02). (Army) Any facility established for the purpose of providing medical treatment. (FM 4-02).

heading: patient
text: (Joint) A sick, injured, wounded, or other person receiving medical care, dental care, or other medical treatment. (JP 4-02). (Army) A patient is a wounded, ill and injured Soldier who receives medical care or treatment from medically trained personnel. (ATP 4-02.10).

heading: tactical combat casualty care
text: The deliberate integration of tactics and medicine to treat casualties during combat. Also called TCCC. (JP 4-02).

heading: *tactical evacuation care
text: The third phase of care in tactical combat casualty care. Care provided during transportation from the battelefield to a medical treatment facility.

heading: *tactical field care
text: The second phase of care in tactical combat casualty care. Care provided once the threat has been neutralized, the scene is safe or the casualty has moved or been moved out of the immediate threat situation. Also known as TFC.

heading: triage
text: Triage is the system of sorting and prioritizing casualties based on the tactical situation, mission, and available resources (FM 4-02).
